cons: May introduce change in default behavior for other clients

template_adherence.title: JetStream Encryption At Rest
template_adherence.context:
Present a way to have the nats-server itself provide encryption at rest for all stored JetStream data. This should be seen as an alternative to an encrypted filesystem or block storage that would be provided by a cloud provider.

End user documentation for this feature can be found in the official documentation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly list decision drivers as a separate section, but the drivers can be inferred from the context and design sections, such as the need for encryption at rest, alternatives to encrypted filesystems, and the use of authenticated encryption.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is described mainly in the Design and Encryption sections: to use a master key to generate keys for asset encryption within JetStream, using ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD for encryption, with keys managed as EK, KEK, and AEK. The design includes per-asset and per-message block keys.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences are not explicitly stated in a dedicated section, but can be inferred: positive consequences include providing encryption at rest natively in nats-server, avoiding reliance on external encrypted filesystems; potential future support for KMS and key rolling; and client-side EK control. Negative consequences or risks are not explicitly discussed.

alternatives.description: Use an encrypted filesystem or block storage provided by a cloud provider instead of native encryption in nats-server.
pros: Leverages existing, possibly well-tested encryption solutions.
No need to implement encryption logic in nats-server.
cons: Less control over encryption keys within nats-server.
May not be portable across different environments.

alternatives.description: Allow clients to provide the External Key (EK) in a header, enabling client-side control over encryption keys.
pros: Clients can control their own encryption keys.
Adds flexibility in key management.
cons: Requires TLS to secure the key transmission.
Not as secure as a KMS or cloud provider encrypted storage.
Introduces complexity in client-server interaction.

template_adherence.title: JWT library free jwt user generation
template_adherence.context: Users writing programs to issue user jwt, ask if this can be done in languages other than go. We assume that these programs stamp out a set number of identical user profiles. With the addition of scoped signing keys, limits and permissions are attached to the signing key instead of the user. As a consequence, user jwt generating programs, do not need the data model the jwt library provides. The use of scoped signing keys is highly encouraged as a compromised key can only be used to issue certain user, NOT user with arbitrary permissions. Thus, a simple utility function, added to nkey supporting client libraries, can replace the need for the go only jwt library, for most use cases. This can be a series of standalone repositories as well. Because this is a single and small utility function, adding it to suitable client libraries seems easiest for usage as it meets the users where they are (similar to nkey functions in some languages). Furthermore, this may not be needed for every client library. Initially we'd focus on languages widely used by corporate user where jwt generating programs are to be expected. Those would be: go, java, csharp
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support jwt user generation in languages other than Go.
- Simplify user jwt generation by leveraging scoped signing keys.
- Avoid dependency on the full jwt library and data model.
- Provide a simple utility function in client libraries where users are.
- Focus initially on widely used corporate languages: Go, Java, C#.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a simple utility function, IssueUserJWT, added to nkey supporting client libraries, to generate user JWTs without the full jwt library. This function will handle only the values not covered by scoped signing keys and will be available in selected client libraries for widely used languages.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Removes the need for the full jwt library when programmatically generating user JWTs using scoped signing keys.
- Simplifies the process of user JWT generation across multiple languages.
- Encourages use of scoped signing keys for better security.
- May limit functionality to the simplified use case described.
- Requires client libraries to implement the utility function.

alternatives.description: Continue using the full Go jwt library for all user jwt generation.
pros: Full feature set and data model available.
Mature and tested library.
cons: Limited to Go language.
More complex than needed for scoped signing key use case.
Not portable to other languages easily.

alternatives.description: Create standalone repositories for the utility function in each language.
pros: Modular and language-specific implementations.
Can be maintained independently.
cons: More overhead in maintaining multiple repos.
Users have to find and integrate separate repos.
Less discoverable than inclusion in client libraries.

template_adherence.title: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views
template_adherence.context: This document describes a design on how to support API prefixes for materialized JS views. API prefixes allow the client library to disambiguate access to independent JetStreams that run either in different domains or different accounts. By specifying the prefix in the API, a client program can essentially pick which one it wants to communicate with. This mechanism needs to be supported for materialized JS views as well.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to disambiguate API access to JetStream instances across different accounts and domains, ensuring that materialized views like KV and object store support the same API prefix mechanism. The solution must maintain backward compatibility and avoid accidental API overlaps.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to treat the first token of any API or materialized view as the default API prefix with local semantics. For concrete views, tokens like $KV and $OBJ are treated as default API prefixes. For publishes and subscribes, the API replaces the first token with the specified (non-default) prefix. This approach leverages existing account export/import and domain leaf node connection mappings to handle prefix translation and traffic routing.
template_adherence.consequences: The change is backward compatible with existing materialized views. It requires avoiding starting the first token after the API prefix with '$' to prevent accidental overlaps. A potential issue is the clash between two-token API prefixes (e.g., $JS.API) and single-token prefixes used by materialized views, which could be resolved by unifying API namespaces to always use two tokens, though this would break backward compatibility.

alternatives.description: Do not support API prefixes for materialized views, keeping them fixed to default prefixes.
pros: Simpler implementation.
No changes to existing materialized views.
cons: Cannot disambiguate access across accounts or domains.
Limits flexibility and scalability.

alternatives.description: Unify API namespaces to always use two tokens with the second token being 'API' (e.g., $JS.API, $KV.API, $OBJ.API).
pros: Avoids clashes between API prefixes and materialized view tokens.
Provides a consistent namespace structure.
cons: Not backward compatible.
Requires significant changes to existing APIs and clients.

template_adherence.title: NATS Service Latency Distributed Tracing Interoperability
template_adherence.context:
The goal is to enable the NATS internal latencies to be exported to distributed tracing systems, here we see a small architecture using Traefik, a Go microservice and a NATS hosted service all being observed in Jaeger.

The lowest 3 spans were created from a NATS latency Advisory.

These traces can be ingested by many other commercial systems like Data Dog and Honeycomb where they can augment the existing operations tooling in use by our users. Additionally Grafana 7 supports Jaeger and Zipkin today.

Long term I think every server that handles a message should emit a unique trace so we can also get visibility into the internal flow of the NATS system and exactly which gateway connection has a delay - see our current HM issues - but ultimately I don't think we'll be doing that in the hot path of the server, though these traces are easy to handle async

Meanwhile, this proposal will let us get very far with our current Latency Advisories.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to export NATS internal latencies to distributed tracing systems.
- Support for existing tracing systems like Jaeger, Zipkin, and emerging standards like W3C Trace Context.
- Desire to augment existing operations tooling used by users.
- Long term goal to trace internal flow of NATS system without impacting hot path performance.
- Current limitation of static 50% sampling configuration.
- Need to interpret HTTP headers for sampling decisions to support interoperability.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to support Jaeger, Zipkin, and W3C Trace Context header formats for distributed tracing interoperability. This includes interpreting incoming HTTP headers to determine sampling decisions rather than relying solely on static sampling rates. The proposal includes updating the NATS latency advisory with a headers field containing relevant headers used for sampling decisions. This approach balances current capabilities with future extensibility and interoperability with popular tracing systems.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Enables integration with multiple distributed tracing systems.
- Provides more dynamic and accurate sampling based on incoming headers.
- Enhances observability and debugging capabilities for NATS services.
- Aligns with emerging standards for trace context propagation.

Negative consequences:
- Increased complexity in interpreting multiple header formats.
- Potential performance impact if not handled asynchronously.
- Requires updates to existing NATS latency advisory structures and clients consuming them.

alternatives.description: Continue using static sampling rate (e.g., 50%) without interpreting headers.
pros: Simple to implement and maintain.
No changes to existing advisory formats or clients.
cons: Lacks interoperability with distributed tracing systems.

template_adherence.title: Lame Duck Notification
template_adherence.context: This document describes the _Lame Duck Mode_ server notification. When a server enters lame duck mode, it removes itself from being advertised in the cluster, and slowly starts evicting connected clients as per  [`lame_duck_duration`](https://docs.nats.io/nats-server/configuration#runtime-configuration). This document describes how this information is notified to the client, in order to allow clients to cooperate and initiate an orderly migration to a different server in the cluster.
template_adherence.decision: The server notififies that it has entered _lame duck mode_ by sending an [`INFO`](https://docs.nats.io/nats-protocol/nats-protocol#info) update. If the `ldm` property is set to true, the server has entered _lame_duck_mode_ and the client should initiate an orderly self-disconnect or close. Note the `ldm` property is only available on servers that implement the notification feature.
template_adherence.consequences: By becoming aware of a server changing state to _lame duck mode_ clients can orderly disconnect from a server, and connect to a different server. Currently clients have no automatic support to _disconnect_ while keeping current state. Future documentation will describe strategies for initiating a new connection and exiting the old one.

template_adherence.title: JetStream Consumer Idle Heartbeats
template_adherence.context:
The JetStream ConsumerConfig option `idle_heartbeat` enables server-side heartbeats to be sent to the client. To enable the option on the consumer simply specify it with a value representing the number of nanoseconds that the server should use as notification interval.

The server will only notify after the specified interval has elapsed and no new messages have been delivered to the consumer. Delivering a message to the consumer resets the interval.

The idle heartbeats notifications are sent to the consumer's subscription as a regular NATS message. The message will have a `code` of `100` with a `description` of `Idle Heartbeat`. The message will contain additional headers that the client can use to re-affirm that it has not lost any messages:

- `Nats-Last-Consumer` indicates the last consumer sequence delivered to the client. If `0`, no messages have been delivered.
- `Nats-Last-Stream` indicates the sequence number of the newest message in the stream.

Here's an example of a client creating a consumer with an idle_heartbeat of 10 seconds, followed by a server notification.

```
$JS.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.FRHZZ447RL7NR8TAICHCZ6 _INBOX.FRHZZ447RL7NR8TAICHCQ8.FRHZZ447RL7NR8TAICHDQ0 136␍␊
{"config":{"ack_policy":"explicit","deliver_subject":"my.messages","idle_heartbeat":10000000000},
"stream_name":"FRHZZ447RL7RL7NR8TAICHCZ6"}␍␊
...

> HMSG my.messages 2  75 75␍␊NATS/1.0 100 Idle Heartbeat␍␊Nats-Last-Consumer: 0␍␊Nats-Last-Stream: 0␍␊␍␊␍␊
alive - last stream seq: 0 - last consumer seq: 0
```

This feature is intended as an aid to clients to detect when they have been disconnected. Without it the consumer's subscription may sit idly waiting for messages, without knowing that the server might have simply gone away and recovered elsewhere.
template_adherence.consequences: Clients can use this information to set client-side timers that track how many heartbeats have been missed and perhaps take some action such as re-create a subscription to resume messages.

template_adherence.title: Handling Database Corruption
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of users encountering corrupt SQLite databases, which renders the related component unusable. It focuses on two main questions: (A) When and how to identify corrupted databases? and (B) What actions to take upon identifying corrupted databases? The goal is to avoid deleting valid user data while effectively handling persistent corruption errors.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Key drivers include avoiding deletion of valid user data, the negative impact of keeping corrupted databases, and the current lack of a reliable method to distinguish persistent from transient errors, which could be improved by analyzing telemetry and sentry data.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to (A2) check for errors when opening a database and compare against known corruption error types, and (B1) delete the database file and recreate the database. This approach is conservative, simpler to implement, and expected to fix many cases, with plans to monitor telemetry for future improvements.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision allows users with corrupted databases to regain component usability by deleting and recreating the database. However, there is a risk of data loss if corruption is misidentified. The approach balances conservatism with practicality and plans for future enhancements based on monitoring.

alternatives.description: Assume all errors when opening a database are from corrupt databases.
pros: Sentry data indicates many errors occur during opening.
Migrations likely trigger corruption errors.
Natural time to delete database before queries run.
cons: Will delete valid user data in common situations like migration logic errors, OOM errors, disk full.

alternatives.description: Check for errors when opening a database and compare against known corruption error types.
pros: Eliminates possibility of deleting valid user data.
Sentry data indicates many errors during opening.
Natural time to delete database before queries run.
cons: Currently no good list of corruption errors.

alternatives.description: Check for errors for all database operations and compare against known corruption error types.
pros: Sentry data shows errors outside opening time.
Eliminates possibility of deleting valid user data.
cons: Consumer code may not expect database deletion mid-query.
No good list of corruption errors.

alternatives.description: Delete the database file and recreate the database.
pros: Allows users with corrupted databases to use components again.
cons: Misidentification leads to data loss.

alternatives.description: Move the database file and recreate the database.
pros: Possibility to recover data if misidentified.
Allows user-initiated data deletion.
cons: Recovery function is complex and hard to test.
Adds complexity to database opening code.
User experience may be confusing with data disappearing and reappearing.

alternatives.description: Return a failure code.
pros: No chance of user data deletion.
Simplest to implement.
cons: Component unusable if database is corrupt.
No way for users to delete corrupted data.

template_adherence.title: Running experiments on first run early startup
template_adherence.context: As an experimenter, I would like to run experiments early on a user's first run of the application. However, the experiment data is only available on the second run. We would like to have that experiment data available before the user's first run.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Availability of experiments early on the first run
* No impact on experimentation data analysis
* Flexibility in creating experiments
* Ability to quickly disable experiments
* Simplicity of releases
* Mobile's expectations of Nimbus (The SDK should be idempotent)
template_adherence.decision:
None of the options were feasible, so for now we are sticking with option **(A) Do Nothing** until there are experiments planned that are expected to run on early startup on the first run, then we will revaluate our options.

The **(B) Bundle Experiment data with app on release** option was rejected mainly due to difficulty in disabling experiments and pausing enrollments. This can create a negative user experience as it prevents us from disabling any problematic experiments. Additionally, it ties experiment creation with application release cycles.

The **(C) Retrieve Experiment data on first run, and deal with delay** option was rejected due to the fact it changes the Nimbus SDK will no longer be idempotent,and the possibility of introducing undesirable UI.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to do nothing means that experiments will not run early on the user's first run, maintaining the current state. This preserves flexibility in experiment creation, allows disabling experiments remotely, and keeps the Nimbus SDK idempotent. However, it does not solve the problem of exposing experiments to users on their first run, potentially delaying experimentation benefits.

cons: Bad, because it doesn't address the main problem of exposing experiments to user on their first run

Later on the first run, the client would retrieve the actual experiment data from remote-settings and overwrite the bundled data.
pros: Good, because it allows us to run experiments early on a user's first run

Bad, because it requires investment from the console team, and can modify existing flows.

pros: Good, because it enables us to retrieve experiments for users on their first run
Good, because it keeps the flexibility in experiment creation
Good, because disabling experiments can still done remotely for all experiments
cons: Bad, because experiments may not be ready early on the user's experience

Bad, because it forces the customer application to deal with either the delay, or changing the configuration shortly after startup. e.g. a loading spinner or a pre-onboarding screen not under experimental control; delaying initialization of onboarding screens until after experiments have been loaded.

template_adherence.title: 1. Deployment on-prem & as a SaaS
template_adherence.context:
In global health there are two deployment constraints that push against one another:  the desire for iNGO's, government agencies, multi-laterals, etc to lower the barrier to acquiring software solutions by utilizing a SaaS model, and that of many governments to exercise self-reliance and sovereignty of their software and their data by being able to reasonably deploy software on premise in their own data center.

With regards to SaaS, most customers of the software are able and willing to pay reasonable monthly fees, especially if those fees are predictable over a suitable project timeline.  For organizations that want to offer PCMT as a SaaS they likely will expect the number of instances to be quite low:  likely less than 25 in the next 5 years.  Thus the key attributes for those running PCMT as a SaaS and for those consuming PCMT as a SaaS are reasonable fees and lead-times for signing a new instance on.

When a government agency deploys the software in their own data center a principal concern is that of limited resources.  Limited both in hardware and the maturity of the data center, as well as on the technical staff available. There are few organizations within PCMT's user-base that have extensive experience running highly available services or complicated deployment stacks.

We have a number of choices that are available to us:

1. Multi-tenancy development in theory can achieve the greatest cost-per-customer since the same application code on the same hardware can serve more than one customer.  However it can significantly increase the scope and development of each feature as each needs to consider how many customers would share the same resources without impacting one-another. It can also increase deployment cost and complexity as each instance needs to be configured and monitored for many clients.
1. Multi-single-tenancy is really a single tenancy model that utilizes advances in containerization, oftentimes cloud providers, and deployment tools to manage many single instances, one per customer, in such an automated fashion as to make it nearly indistinguishable from multi-tenancy.
1. Serverless is an approach to reduce overhead for developers by shifting resource management to a provider.  It's included here for completeness, and while it may make development practices easier, the deployment of a serverless architecture on-prem in PCMT's context is non-trivial.

template_adherence.title: 3. Cloud Provisioning through Terraform
template_adherence.context:
Deploying to the cloud is a fundamental part of increasing software delivery frequency. However once the frequency is increased, it becomes increasingly needed to manage the provisioning and configuration of those cloud resources lest a step is forgotten, a security vulnerability is found, or an instance is corrupted. Following patterns found in software development, such as managing infrastructure as code (IaC) and tracking changes in source control, are widely regarded as good practice today.

Many cloud providers have bespoke tooling that helps manage the creation of resources on their infrastructure. While this tooling is hugely powerful, the context of PCMT is that our cloud resources should be kept as simple as possible, in part due to our constraint to allow for on-prem deployments. Further an organization that chooses to deploy PCMT as a SaaS may not use the same cloud provider as the one the PCMT project uses.
template_adherence.decision: We will use Terraform to provision cloud resources:  compute instances, storage, DNS, etc.

template_adherence.title: 7. Versioning and Release Mechanism

template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include the need for careful and intentional setting of semantic versions by release-designated personnel, and control of builds, pre-releases, and stable releases through semantic version settings in SCM and CI commits.

template_adherence.title: Data Resilience on ingest
template_adherence.context: We want to ensure that the Data resilience (this is what we are calling the guarantee that data once sent to the ingest pipeline will be ingested into A2) in our system is well understood. We also want to make sure that this is captured here for future reference.
template_adherence.decision:
1) Data resilience / durability - our current approach on leaving retries to the edges (Chef Infra Client, Chef Infra Server, Chef InSpec) is still valid and we will not change that at this time. However, there is no retry logic built into Chef Infra Server or Chef InSpec. We will add that to those products' backlog and triage according to those teams' priorities.
2) For Notifications right now, this is built in a way where notifications might get triggered but the data has not yet been fully ingested. We will change that behavior so that notifications only get triggered upon successful ingestion of data
3) There is an event service in compliance right now that we all agreed can be extracted and enhanced to use across the system. However, the right time to look at this is when there is a new use-case for it. While the approach is agreed upon, we will await a use-case before proceeding
template_adherence.consequences: The system will behave as above in terms of data consistency. We may need to revisit this as / when / if the requirement to guarantee 100% data resilience (no data loss once sent to ingest) changes.

template_adherence.title: Names Not UUIDs for IAM API
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the current state of the IAM implementation where some services use human-readable names and others use UUIDs for entity identification. It outlines the pros and cons of using UUIDs versus names, the challenges with renaming entities, and the need for consistency across the A2 API. It also references Google's API design guidance and the decision to standardize on using 'name' for new APIs while evolving existing ones.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for consistency across APIs, usability concerns (human-readable names vs UUIDs), technical challenges with renaming and cascading changes, alignment with external standards (Google's API design guide), and the impact on existing systems and protocols.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use human-readable resource identifiers ('names') for the IAMv2 public API, disallow renames to these names, support a separate 'display_name' field that can be changed, use UUIDs internally in the data store, and continue using 'id' in GRPC messages for the unique identifier. The decision also includes considerations for delete operations and identifier reuse.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision will be implemented and assessed by 2019-03-10. It will impact API design, data store usage, and handling of entity identifiers across bounded contexts, including delete and rename operations.

template_adherence.title: APIs live together in a top level folder
template_adherence.context:
In A2, we use protobufs to describe our APIs and config. Services talk to each other using clients generated from these protobuf files. The `deployment-service` uses the protobufs for config to allow users to configure A2.

While this works, it has a few flaws. First, there is no clean separation between a service's implementation and its API. This means that when certain services update a service, but not the API, dependent services must be rebuilt. A similar thing is true for config, where `deployment-service` ends up depending on all services, and chaining any of them causes `deployment-service` to be rebuilt.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a clean separation between service implementation and API.
- Avoid unnecessary rebuilds of dependent services when only service implementation changes.
- Manage dependencies in config to prevent cascading rebuilds.
template_adherence.decision:
We will define APIs and config in our top-level `api` directory. This top-level `api` directory will have 3 subdirectories:

* external - Our public facing API, which is currently exposed by `automate-gateway`
* internal - API definitions for each of our services
* config - The config definitions for the services and the global config definition

Services that want to communicate with each other should do so by using the clients that are in the `internal` API subdirectory. When taking such a dependency, the service must update the `.expeditor/config.yml` file with this information. Components which are services should not have dependencies to other components which are services in the `.expeditor/config.yml` file.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Clear separation of APIs and config, reducing unnecessary rebuilds.
- Positive: Organized API directory structure improves maintainability.
- Negative: Requires discipline to update `.expeditor/config.yml` correctly.
- Negative: Potential initial overhead in reorganizing existing APIs and configs.

alternatives.description: Keep the current approach where protobufs are used directly without a top-level API directory.
pros: No immediate restructuring needed.
Developers are familiar with the current setup.
cons: No clean separation between service implementation and API.
Dependent services must be rebuilt even if only service implementation changes.
`deployment-service` depends on all services, causing cascading rebuilds.

template_adherence.title: ADR 2019-01-15: Nodemanager Package
template_adherence.context:
We would like for the Nodes Service to be a central store of all the node objects across a user's infrastructure.
This will allow us to provide the user with a way to easily map nodes between client-runs and compliance reports.
The Nodes Service maps to the `/nodes` endpoint.
In today's world, nodes are added to that endpoint via manual node creation and cloud integration creation. Upon ingestion of a compliance report, the compliance ingest service makes a call to the ProcessNode endpoint in the Node Manager Service with some metadata information about the node.  The node is then updated or created.
In order to allow us to have a central store of all the nodes, we will need to have the client runs ingestion call the same ProcessNode endpoint with metadata about each incoming node.
The Node Manager Service and Nodes Service grew out of needs in the compliance service, and currently exists as part of that service/package. In order to enable the client run ingestion to make the call to Node Manager Service, the Node Manager service will need to be pulled out into its own independent package/service in A2.

### Current Architecture
![current nodemanager diagram](../images/current-nodemanager.png)

### Desired Architecture
![desired nodemanager diagram](../images/desired-nodemanager.png)

template_adherence.title: Backwards Compatibility for Automate UI Routes
template_adherence.context:
Previously, we did not have any rules for governing Automate UI route lifecycle. In the past, we likely broke backwards compatibility when re-naming or moving routes.

Additionally, the top nav highlighting in Automate UI was driven off the root route (e.g. everything under the `Settings` tab must live under the `/settings` route or it will not be highlighted properly for pages that live under it). This means that if you want to move a page to a new tab, it will require a new route.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain backwards compatibility for Automate UI routes to ensure deep linking from internal and external sources continues to work until the original resource is removed. Also, the requirement to maintain proper top navigation highlighting and to have automated tests verifying route redirections.
template_adherence.decision: Every route that originally linked to a page that is still in use in the webapp must still work and backwards compatibility must be maintained. Only when the webpage that the original route linked to is being removed from the app can a route be removed. To maintain backwards compatibility, the original route must redirect to the new route (achievable in `app-routing.module.ts`) and an e2e test must be added to verify that redirection in `deprecated-routes.e2e-spec.ts`.
template_adherence.consequences: All deprecated Automate UI routes redirect to their new location until the relevant content is removed from the webapp (with e2e testing verifying that the redirection works). This also means that any route you add to the app will exist until the corresponding part of the app is deleted, so choose your route namespaces carefully!

template_adherence.title: ADR 1: Logging
template_adherence.context:
Current logging system in Tendermint is very static and not flexible enough.

Issues: [358](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/358), [375](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/375).

What we want from the new system:

- per package dynamic log levels
- dynamic logger setting (logger tied to the processing struct)
- conventions
- be more visually appealing

"dynamic" here means the ability to set smth in runtime.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a more flexible and dynamic logging system that supports per-package dynamic log levels, dynamic logger settings tied to processing structs, conventions for logging, and improved visual appeal. Also, compatibility with existing libraries and ease of use are important.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a new logging interface inspired by go-kit Logger interface but tailored to Tendermint's needs, implement a stdout logger with current formatting style, enable dynamic logger settings tied to processing structs, and establish conventions for key-value ordering in logs.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Dynamic logger that can be turned off for some modules at runtime.
- Public interface for other projects using Tendermint libraries.

Negative:
- Potential loss of ability to color keys in key-value pairs due to limitations in go-kit coloring.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use the go-kit Logger interface as is for all libraries.
pros: Standardized interface with composability.
Supports colored logging and log levels.
cons: Too big a change for current codebase.
May not support all needed log levels directly.

alternatives.description: Use logrus as the logging backend.
pros: Popular and feature-rich.
Supports hooks and has familiar API and output.
cons: Less flexible than go-kit.
May not conform easily to the new interface.

alternatives.description: Stick with the current static logging system.
pros: No changes needed.
Stable and familiar to current users.
cons: Lacks flexibility and dynamic features.
Does not support per-package dynamic log levels or dynamic logger settings.

template_adherence.title: Event Subscription
template_adherence.context: In the light client (or any other client), the user may want to subscribe to a subset of transactions (rather than all of them) using `/subscribe?event=X`. For example, I want to subscribe for all transactions associated with a particular account. Same for fetching. The user may want to fetch transactions based on some filter (rather than fetching all the blocks). For example, I want to get all transactions for a particular account in the last two weeks (`tx's block time >= '2017-06-05'`). Now you can't even subscribe to "all txs" in Tendermint. The goal is a simple and easy to use API for doing that.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for users to subscribe to a subset of transactions rather than all.
- Desire for a simple and easy to use API.
- Support for fetching transactions based on filters.
- Limitations in current Tendermint subscription capabilities.
- Need to support multiple indexers with different APIs.
- Performance considerations with many queries/subscribers.
- Handling large number of transactions in the database.
template_adherence.decision: ABCI app will return tags with a `DeliverTx` response inside the `data` field (for now, later possibly a separate field). Tags are a list of key-value pairs, protobuf encoded. These tags will be parsed and matched with current queries (subscribers). If the query matches the tags, the subscriber will get the transaction event. A new package will be developed to replace the current `events` package to allow clients to subscribe to different types of events in the future. For fetching transactions, an indexing storage (Postgres, SQLite, etc.) will be needed for historic queries.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Same format for event notifications and search APIs.
- Powerful enough query capabilities.

Negative:
- Performance concerns with the `match` function when there are too many queries/subscribers.
- Issues with handling too many transactions in the database.

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implied alternatives include: continuing with the current Tendermint subscription model which does not support subscribing to all transactions or filtered subsets.
pros: No changes to existing system, no development effort.
cons: Does not meet user needs for filtered subscriptions.
Limited functionality.

alternatives.description: Develop a new package to replace the current `events` package to support more flexible subscriptions and queries.
pros: Allows subscribing to different types of events.
Supports powerful query capabilities.
cons: Requires development effort.
Potential performance issues with many queries/subscribers.

template_adherence.title: ADR 002: Sampling erasure coded Block chunks
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need for nodes in the Celestia network to sample row-/column-chunks of the erasure coded block (extended data square) from the network for Data Availability proofs. It describes the high-level requirements, defines the API for different components, and documents implementation decisions. It references existing implementations, specifications, and prototypes, and discusses integration with IPFS and IPLD.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a high-level API independent of the underlying stack, reuse of existing networking and p2p stacks (go-ipfs), performance considerations, and the complexity of integrating Data Availability proofs into Tendermint. Concerns include latency, dependency on a large codebase, and the coexistence of two p2p layers in celestia-core.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a two-package library: a lower-level package under p2p/ipld handling IPFS/IPLD objects and a higher-level API closer to Celestia core types. The implementation will use IPFS CoreAPI, IPLD nodes, and Namespaced Merkle Trees. The ADR outlines detailed API methods and an implementation plan for integration and replacement of existing block gossiping mechanisms.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simplicity, ease of implementation, reuse of existing stacks, and community support. Negative consequences include potential latency, overkill of using public IPFS network, and dependency on a large codebase. Neutral consequence is the existence of two p2p layers in celestia-core.

Could require more custom implementation work.

pros: Potentially better performance.

template_adherence.title: Must an ABCI-app have an RPC server?
template_adherence.context:
ABCI-server could expose its own RPC-server and act as a proxy to Tendermint.

The idea was for the Tendermint RPC to just be a transparent proxy to the app.
Clients need to talk to Tendermint for proofs, unless we burden all app devs
with exposing Tendermint proof stuff. Also seems less complex to lock down one
server than two, but granted it makes querying a bit more kludgy since it needs
to be passed as a `Query`. Also, **having a very standard rpc interface means
the light-client can work with all apps and handle proofs**. The only
app-specific logic is decoding the binary data to a more readable form (eg.
json). This is a huge advantage for code-reuse and standardization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:

- Desire to avoid burdening app developers with exposing Tendermint proof logic.
- Complexity considerations in managing one server versus two.
- Importance of code reuse and standardization for light-client compatibility.
- Trade-offs between interface simplicity and query complexity.
template_adherence.decision: We dont expose an RPC server on any of our ABCI-apps.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Unified interface for all apps

### Negative

- `Query` interface

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Historical Validators
template_adherence.context:
Right now, we can query the present validator set, but there is no history.
If you were offline for a long time, there is no way to reconstruct past validators. This is needed for the light client and we agreed needs enhancement of the API.
template_adherence.decision:
For every block, store a new structure that contains either the latest validator set,
or the height of the last block for which the validator set changed. Note this is not
the height of the block which returned the validator set change itself, but the next block,
ie. the first block it comes into effect for.

Storing the validators will be handled by the `state` package.

At some point in the future, we may consider more efficient storage in the case where the validators
are updated frequently - for instance by only saving the diffs, rather than the whole set.

An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Can query old validator sets, with proof.

### Negative

- Writes an extra structure to disk with every block.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: Keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
pros: Might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed.
cons: More complex.
Likely less efficient.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Consensus Params
template_adherence.context: Consensus critical parameters controlling blockchain capacity have until now been hard coded, loaded from a local config, or neglected. Since they may be need to be different in different networks, and potentially to evolve over time within networks, we seek to initialize them in a genesis file, and expose them through the ABCI. While we have some specific parameters now, like maximum block and transaction size, we expect to have more in the future, such as a period over which evidence is valid, or the frequency of checkpoints.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have consensus critical parameters configurable per network and evolvable over time, to avoid hard coding or local config limitations. The desire to have parameters initialized in genesis and exposed through ABCI, and to maintain sanity checks and flexibility for future parameters.
template_adherence.decision: Consensus critical parameters should not be in the config.toml but optionally included in the genesis.json file and loaded into the State. Parameters not included get default values; 0 means undefined, -1 means not applicable. Parameters determine block and transaction validity. The ConsensusParams struct can evolve by adding new structs. Certain parameters must be greater than 0 for sanity. The ABCI InitChain and EndBlock methods are extended to handle ConsensusParams appropriately, with updates applied for the next block.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to specify alternative capacity limits and consensus parameters without recompiling software, and the ability to change them over time under application control. Negative consequences include increased complexity due to more exposed parameters and complications in fast sync due to different rules at different blockchain heights. Neutral consequence is potential conflict between TxSize validity checks and config's max_block_size_tx proposal sizes.

alternatives.description: Keep consensus parameters hard coded or loaded from local config only.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need to extend genesis or ABCI interfaces.
cons: Lack of flexibility to change parameters per network or over time.
Requires recompilation for parameter changes.
Does not support evolving parameters easily.

alternatives.description: Include all consensus parameters directly in the ABCI InitChain call.
pros: Centralizes all initial parameters in one call.
Simplifies parameter passing at chain start.
cons: May expose parameters the application shouldn't know about.
Less modular and flexible.
Could complicate ABCI interface unnecessarily.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Decouple the PartSetHeader from the BlockID

This means that we will remove the `PartSetHeader` from as many places as possible, but keep it in the `Proposal` struct.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:

- Other designs exist but are more experimental and require more extensive changes.

template_adherence.title: ADR 006: Consensus Block Gossiping with Rows
template_adherence.context:
It's a long story of relations between Celestia, Tendermint, and consensus block gossiping. Celestia's team discussed multiple ideas, several ADRs were made, and nothing yet was finalized. This ADR is another attempt to bring valuable changes into block gossiping and hopefully successful.

Currently, we inherit the following from Tendermint. Our codebase relies on the blocks Parts notion. Each Part is a piece of an entire serialized block. Those Parts are gossiped between nodes in consensus and committed with `PartSetHeader` containing a Merkle Root of the Parts. However, Parts gossiping wasn't designed for Celestia blocks.

Celestia comes with a different block representation from Tendermint. It lays out Blocks as a table of data shares, where Rows or Columns can be and should be gossiped instead of Parts, keeping only one system-wide commitment to data.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to adapt block gossiping mechanism to Celestia's block representation (Rows instead of Parts).
- Desire to keep Tendermint consensus as a black box with minimal changes.
- Improve data integrity verification and resource usage.
- Maintain compatibility and leverage previous work.
- Address performance and security concerns such as DOS vectors and resource waste.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to still treat Tendermint's consensus as a black box, but with few amendments to gossiping mechanism:
- Introduce `RowSet` that mimics `PartSet`.
- Replace `PartSet` with `RowSet` within consensus.
- Keep `DAHeader` in `Proposal`.
- Remove `PartSetHeader` from `Proposal`.

These changes are required to implement the decision. Later, other clean-up changes like entirely removing `PartSetHeader` and `PartSet` and relying solely on `DAHeader` are likely to be implemented.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include:
- Hardening of consensus gossiping with erasure coding.
- Immediate rejection of oversized blocks on Proposal.
- More control over Row message size.
- Less bandwidth usage.
- Only required block data is gossiped.
- Single system-wide block data commitment schema.
- Continuation and leveraging of prior work.

Negative consequences:
- Additional development time (~1.5 weeks).
- Remaining implementation and peer review work.

Neutral consequences:
- Change in chunk size characteristics on the wire.
- Gossiped chunks size proportional to block data size.
- Divergence from original Tendermint codebase behavior.

alternatives.description: Treat Tendermint consensus as a black box, keeping two data commitments: one for consensus with `PartSetHeader` and another for the world outside consensus with `DAHeader`.
pros: Less work
cons: Pulls two data commitments to Celestia's specs
Brings ambiguity to data integrity verification
Controversial from software design perspective
Brings DOSing vector for big Blocks. Every Block would need to be represented in two formats in RAM
Wastes more resources on building and verifying additional

alternatives.description: Get rid of the PartsHeader from BlockID without changing block propagation at all.
pros: Maintains existing block propagation mechanism
cons: Does not address the mismatch with Celestia's block representation

alternatives.description: Change block propagation to fixed-sized chunks based on the ODS instead of current Parts.
pros: Empirically better performance
cons: Requires significant changes to block propagation

alternatives.description: Send the block as a whole (only works with smaller blocks).
pros: Simplifies propagation for small blocks
cons: Not scalable for large blocks

alternatives.description: Block propagation based on sending the header and Tx-IDs and then requesting missing Tx/Messages on demand.
pros: Potentially efficient for certain scenarios
cons: Complexity in implementation and verification

template_adherence.title: ADR 006: Trust Metric Design
template_adherence.context: The proposed trust metric will allow Tendermint to maintain local trust rankings for peers it has directly interacted with, which can then be used to implement soft security controls. The calculations were obtained from the TrustGuard project. Background information explains the need for tracking peer trustworthiness to improve security and reliability, and discusses challenges such as strategic oscillation by malicious nodes and the use of fading memories to balance adaptability and history preservation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve Tendermint security and reliability by tracking peer behavior over time, the challenge of malicious nodes adapting behavior to circumvent trust metrics, the desire to maintain a history of trust data without excessive storage, and the need for a flexible, resilient trust metric that can be queried and updated efficiently.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a trust metric that counts good and bad events over intervals, calculates a trust value using a PID-controller-like equation combining proportional, integral, and derivative components, employs fading memories to manage history data efficiently, and provides a trust metric store to manage metrics per peer with persistence across node executions. An interface with methods to record events, query trust values, and manage metric state is defined, along with configuration options for weights and intervals.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling non-binary security decisions, implementing soft security controls, and providing profiling information for peer performance analysis. Negative consequences include the requirement to save trust metric history data across node executions. Neutral considerations include the need to record both good and bad events.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implicitly alternatives could include simpler trust metrics without history, or metrics without PID-like calculations.
pros: Simpler implementation
Less storage requirements
cons: Less resilient to strategic oscillation
Less adaptive to recent events
Potentially less accurate trust assessments

template_adherence.title: ADR 007: From Ukraine, with Love
template_adherence.context:
Currently, our fork of tendermint includes changes to how to erasure block data, minor changes to the header to commit to that data, additions to serve data availability sampling, along with some miscellaneous modification to adhere to the spec. Instead of incorporating all of these changes into our fork of tendermint, we will only make the strictly necessary changes and the other services and their code to the new celestia-node repo. Notably, we will also refactor some of the remaining necessary changes to be more isolated from the rest of the tendermint codebase. Both of these strategies should significantly streamline pulling updates from upstream, and allow us to iterate faster since most changes will be isolated to celestia-node.

Update: many of the changes described below have since been minimized or removed. Please see ADR 008 for a summarized list of changes. Notably, we removed intermediate state roots, adopted two new methods from ABCI++ instead of PreprocessTxs, and are still signing over the PartSetHeader.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to minimize changes to the tendermint fork to ease upstream updates
- Desire to isolate Celestia-specific logic into a separate process (celestia-node)
- Improve iteration speed by separating concerns
- Refactor to isolate necessary changes from tendermint codebase
- Maintain compatibility and ease of maintenance
- Prepare for future design changes
template_adherence.decision: Treat tendermint more as a "black box" by keeping minimal necessary changes in the tendermint fork (celestia-core) and moving other Celestia-specific logic to a separate process (celestia-node) communicating via RPC. Refactor additions to tendermint into their own packages to ease future updates and maintainability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Streamlined pulling changes from upstream
- Separation of functionality aids faster iteration
- Opportunity to reconsider past design choices without starting from scratch
- Prepares for future designs
- Avoids having two p2p stacks in a single repo

Negative:
- Some computations may be performed multiple times
- Running multiple nodes is less convenient for node operators if full celestia-node participates in consensus

alternatives.description: Incorporate all changes directly into the tendermint fork without separation.
pros: Simpler deployment with a single node/process
No need for inter-process communication
cons: Harder to pull updates from upstream tendermint
Slower iteration due to tightly coupled code
More complex codebase with mixed concerns

alternatives.description: Use a monolithic approach with heavy modifications to tendermint and no separate process.
pros: All logic in one place
Potentially better performance without RPC overhead
cons: Difficult to maintain and update
Increased risk of bugs due to complex integration
Less modular and flexible

template_adherence.title: ADR 009: ABCI UX Improvements
template_adherence.context: The ABCI was first introduced in late 2015 as a generic interface between state machines and their replication engines, designed to be language-agnostic and replication-engine-agnostic. Recent community discussions identified pain points such as Amino encoded types, managing validator sets, and protobuf imports, which affect developer experience and compatibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include improving developer experience, removing dependencies on Amino encoding in the short term, maintaining compatibility with protobuf and gogoproto, simplifying address computation, and ensuring flexibility and efficiency in validator and public key handling.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to move away from gogoproto in the short term by maintaining a second protobuf file without gogoproto annotations, eventually using Amino in the long term. Amino will be removed from ABCI in the short term to simplify development. PubKey encoding will use a type string and bytes data without enforcing Amino. Addresses will be simplified to SHA256-based computation. Validator messages will include addresses. RequestBeginBlock will include complete validator sets with voting info but exclude public keys to reduce overhead. ResponseEndBlock will include validator addresses. RequestInitChain and ResponseInitChain will be changed to provide and allow specification of full genesis and validator info. The ABCI Header will match the Tendermint header for identical serialization.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier development on ABCI and identical serialization of ABCI and Tendermint headers. Negative consequences include maintenance overhead of alternative encoding schemes and performance overhead of passing validator info every block. Neutral consequences include the requirement for ABCI developers to understand validator addresses.

alternatives.description: Continue using gogoproto exclusively for protobuf code generation.
pros: Leverages existing gogoproto features and community adoption.
No need to maintain multiple protobuf files.
cons: Creates additional dependency on gogoproto.
Reported failures compiling protobuf types for other languages.
Less flexibility for cross-language compatibility.

pros: Unified encoding scheme.
Potentially better performance and usability in cryptographic applications in the future.
cons: Current incompatibility with protobuf.
Frustration among developers due to Amino requirements.
Not yet mature enough to replace protobuf fully.

alternatives.description: Maintain current protobuf with gogoproto and Amino dependencies without changes.
pros: No immediate development effort required.
Stable existing implementation.
cons: Continued developer pain points.
Lack of simplification and flexibility.
Potential incompatibility issues remain.

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Crypto Changes
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint is a cryptographic protocol that uses and composes a variety of cryptographic primitives.

After nearly 4 years of development, Tendermint has recently undergone multiple security reviews to search for vulnerabilities and to assess the the use and composition of cryptographic primitives.

### Hash Functions

Tendermint uses RIPEMD160 universally as a hash function, most notably in its Merkle tree implementation.

RIPEMD160 was chosen because it provides the shortest fingerprint that is long enough to be considered secure (ie. birthday bound of 80-bits).
It was also developed in the open academic community, unlike NSA-designed algorithms like SHA256.

That said, the cryptographic community appears to unanimously agree on the security of SHA256. It has become a universal standard, especially now that SHA1 is broken, being required in TLS connections and having optimized support in hardware.

### Merkle Trees

Tendermint uses a simple Merkle tree to compute digests of large structures like transaction batches
and even blockchain headers. The Merkle tree length prefixes byte arrays before concatenating and hashing them.
It uses RIPEMD160.

### Addresses

ED25519 addresses are computed using the RIPEMD160 of the Amino encoding of the public key.
RIPEMD160 is generally considered an outdated hash function, and is much slower
than more modern functions like SHA256 or Blake2.

### Authenticated Encryption

Tendermint P2P connections use authenticated encryption to provide privacy and authentication in the communications.
This is done using the simple Station-to-Station protocol with the NaCL Ed25519 library.

While there have been no vulnerabilities found in the implementation, there are some concerns:

- NaCL uses Salsa20, a not-widely used and relatively out-dated stream cipher that has been obsoleted by ChaCha20
- Connections use RIPEMD160 to compute a value that is used for the encryption nonce with subtle requirements on how it's used
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context section and the concerns listed under 'Authenticated Encryption' imply the drivers: the need for more secure, modern, and widely accepted cryptographic primitives; concerns about outdated or less secure algorithms; and hardware acceleration and standardization.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is clearly stated under the 'Decision' section with subsections for each cryptographic primitive:
- Hash Functions: Use the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 hash instead of RIPEMD160 for everything
- Merkle Trees: TODO (not yet decided)
- Addresses: Compute ED25519 addresses as the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 of the raw 32-byte public key
- Authenticated Encryption: Use xChaCha20 instead of xSalsa20 and use an HKDF instead of RIPEMD160 to compute nonces

template_adherence.title: Secp256k1 Signature Malleability
template_adherence.context:
Secp256k1 has two layers of malleability. The signer has a random nonce, and thus can produce many different valid signatures. This ADR is not concerned with that. The second layer of malleability basically allows one who is given a signature to produce exactly one more valid signature for the same message from the same public key. (They don't even have to know the message!) The math behind this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Note that in many downstream applications, signatures will appear in a transaction, and therefore in the tx hash. This means that if someone broadcasts a transaction with secp256k1 signature, the signature can be altered into the other form by anyone in the p2p network. Thus the tx hash will change, and this altered tx hash may be committed instead. This breaks the assumption that you can broadcast a valid transaction and just wait for its hash to be included on chain. One example is if you are broadcasting a tx in cosmos, and you wait for it to appear on chain before incrementing your sequence number. You may never increment your sequence number if a different tx hash got committed. Removing this second layer of signature malleability concerns could ease downstream development.

### ECDSA context

Secp256k1 is ECDSA over a particular curve. The signature is of the form `(r, s)`, where `s` is a field element. (The particular field is the `Z_n`, where the elliptic curve has order `n`) However `(r, -s)` is also another valid solution. Note that anyone can negate a group element, and therefore can get this second signature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to remove the second layer of signature malleability to ensure transaction hashes remain consistent and reliable in downstream applications. The desire to have a simple, canonical form for ECDSA signatures to prevent malleability. Compatibility with existing solutions such as Ethereum's approach. The trade-off between implementation complexity and security guarantees.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to distinguish a canonical form for the ECDSA signatures and require that all ECDSA signatures be in this canonical form. Signatures not in canonical form will be rejected. The canonical form is defined as the smaller of the two possible `s` values, checked lexicographically, specifically `s <= (n - 1)/2`. This approach is simple to check and aligns with Ethereum's solution to secp256k1 malleability.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include maintaining the ability to expect a transaction hash to appear in the blockchain reliably. Negative consequences include additional work in all future implementations, though the check is simple, and the requirement to maintain a fork of the btcd repository. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Do nothing and accept the malleability as is.
pros: No additional implementation work required.
No need to maintain forks or additional checks.
cons: Transaction hashes can be altered by third parties, breaking assumptions in downstream applications.
Potential for sequence number and transaction tracking issues in systems like Cosmos.

alternatives.description: Implement a different canonical form or signature scheme to prevent malleability.
pros: Potentially stronger or more elegant cryptographic guarantees.
May align better with other cryptographic standards or future-proofing.
cons: Increased complexity in implementation.
Potential incompatibility with existing systems like Ethereum.
More development and maintenance effort.

template_adherence.title: Limiting txs size inside a block
template_adherence.context: We currently use MaxTxs to reap txs from the mempool when proposing a block, but enforce MaxBytes when unmarshaling a block, so we could easily propose a block thats too large to be valid. We should just remove MaxTxs all together and stick with MaxBytes, and have a `mempool.ReapMaxBytes`. But we can't just reap BlockSize.MaxBytes, since MaxBytes is for the entire block, not for the txs inside the block. There's extra amino overhead + the actual headers on top of the actual transactions + evidence + last commit. We could also consider using a MaxDataBytes instead of or in addition to MaxBytes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to unify block size limiting parameters to avoid proposing invalid blocks, reduce configuration complexity, and provide a clear upper bound on block size. Considerations include the overhead bytes in blocks, the complexity of having both MaxBytes and MaxDataBytes, and the practical use of MaxGas for transaction throttling.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove MaxTxs entirely and rename MaxTxsBytes to MaxBytes. The mempool will use ReapMaxBytes with an upper bound calculated by subtracting overheads (amino overhead, last commit bytes, evidence bytes, header bytes) from MaxBytes. Constants for overhead sizes are defined in the types package. ChainID is limited to 50 symbols. A test should ensure constants remain accurate if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a clear way to limit block size and fewer configuration variables. Negative consequences include the need to adjust constants if underlying data structures change. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Keep both MaxBytes and MaxDataBytes to separately control total block size and transaction data size.
pros: Allows fine-grained control over block size components.
Can optimize resource usage by separately bounding data and overhead.
cons: Adds complexity to configuration and understanding.
Requires additional calculations and maintenance.

alternatives.description: Continue using MaxTxs and MaxBytes separately as before.
pros: Maintains existing behavior and compatibility.
No immediate changes required.
cons: Risk of proposing blocks too large to be valid.
More variables to configure and potential confusion.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: ABCI Events
template_adherence.context: ABCI tags were first described in ADR 002. They are key-value pairs used to index transactions. Currently, ABCI messages return a list of tags describing an event during Check/DeliverTx/Begin/EndBlock, with each tag referring to a property of the event. Since there is only one list of tags, recording data for multiple events in a single message must be done using prefixes in the key space. Alternatively, groups of tags can be separated by a special tag to denote breaks between events, allowing encoding of multiple events without prefixing, at the cost of special tags.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to represent multiple distinct events within a single ABCI message and improve the clarity and power of event indexing and querying, while balancing complexity in query syntax and implementation.
template_adherence.decision: Instead of returning a list of tags, return a list of events, where each event is a list of tags, naturally capturing multiple events during a single ABCI message.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to track distinct events separate from ABCI calls and more powerful query abilities. Negative consequences include more complex query syntax and more complex search implementation. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using a single list of tags with prefixes to distinguish multiple events.
pros: Simple to implement with existing system.
No change to query syntax.
cons: Less clear separation of events.
More complex key management with prefixes.

alternatives.description: Use special tags to separate groups of tags representing different events within a single list.
pros: Allows encoding multiple events without prefixing.
Maintains a single list structure.
cons: Requires special tags to denote event breaks.
Potentially more complex parsing and indexing.

template_adherence.title: ADR 024: SignBytes and validator types in privval
template_adherence.context: Currently, the messages exchanged between tendermint and a (potentially remote) signer/validator, namely votes, proposals, and heartbeats, are encoded as a JSON string (e.g., via `Vote.SignBytes(...)`) and then signed. JSON encoding is sub-optimal for both hardware wallets and for usage in ethereum smart contracts. Both is laid down in detail in [issue#1622]. Also, there are currently no differences between sign-request and -replies. Also, there is no possibility for a remote signer to include an error code or message in case something went wrong. The messages exchanged between tendermint and a remote signer currently live in [privval/socket.go] and encapsulate the corresponding types in [types].
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a binary encoding format easily parseable by hardware devices and smart contracts.
- Clear separation between sign-requests and sign-replies.
- Ability to include error codes and messages in responses.
- Compatibility with existing code that assumes Vote with signature included.
- Support for remote signers such as KMS.
- Maintainability and clarity in message types and encoding.
template_adherence.decision:
- Restructure vote, proposal, and heartbeat messages to use a binary encoding format (amino).
- Split messages exchanged between tendermint and remote signers into requests and responses.
- Include an error type in responses.
- Remove ChainID parameter from SignBytes interface.
- Define new protobuf-like message structures for Vote, Proposal, Heartbeat, and their corresponding sign request and reply messages.
- Postpone decisions on PubKey handling for KMS and multiple keys.
- Partially accept the proposal as described.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Signing bytes can be easily parsed by hardware modules and smart contracts.
- Clearer separation between requests and responses.
- Added error messages enable better error handling.

Negative:
- Relatively large refactoring affecting many parts of the code.
- Many places assume a Vote with signature included; interfaces will need modification.

Neutral:
- No neutral consequences explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSON encoding for messages and keep current message structure without separating requests and responses or adding error codes.
pros: No changes required to existing codebase.
No refactoring needed.
cons: JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and smart contracts.
No error codes or messages in responses.
No clear separation between requests and responses, leading to potential confusion and less robust error handling.

alternatives.description: Include the signature directly in the type X (e.g., Vote) instead of separating it in SignedXReply.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025 Commit
template_adherence.context:
Currently the `Commit` structure contains a lot of potentially redundant or unnecessary data. It contains a list of precommits from every validator, where the precommit includes the whole `Vote` structure. Thus each of the commit height, round, type, and blockID are repeated for every validator, and could be deduplicated, leading to very significant savings in block size.

The original tracking issue for this is #1648. We have discussed replacing the `Vote` type in `Commit` with a new `CommitSig` type, which includes at minimum the vote signature. The `Vote` type will continue to be used in the consensus reactor and elsewhere.

A primary question is what should be included in the `CommitSig` beyond the signature. One current constraint is that we must include a timestamp, since this is how we calculuate BFT time, though we may be able to change this in the future.

Other concerns include whether to include Validator Address, how to represent absent votes, and how to represent votes for nil and other block IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include reducing redundancy and block size by deduplicating repeated fields in the `Commit` structure, maintaining necessary information for BFT time calculation (timestamp), ergonomic and debugging advantages of including ValidatorAddress, handling absent votes explicitly to resolve serialization issues, and clarifying representation of votes for nil and other block IDs. Also, the need to maintain compatibility and consider future breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to deduplicate the fields and introduce a new `CommitSig` type that includes BlockIDFlag, ValidatorAddress, Timestamp, and Signature. The `Commit` struct will have Height, Round, BlockID, and a slice of `CommitSig` as Precommits.

Timestamp is kept for now to avoid breaking changes.
ValidatorAddress is included for ergonomic and debugging benefits despite increasing block size.
Absent votes are included explicitly with no Signature or Timestamp but with ValidatorAddress.
Only three BlockIDFlag values are allowed: Absent, Commit, and Nil, disallowing votes for other block IDs.
Future changes may reconsider these decisions.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Significant savings in block size (up to 8kB per block for 100 validators) by removing redundant fields.

Negative:
- Large breaking change to block and commit structure.
- Added complexity in code to differentiate between Vote and CommitSig objects.

Neutral:
- Commit.Precommits no longer contains nil values, improving serialization.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing `Commit` structure with full `Vote` objects for each precommit.
pros: No breaking changes to existing structures.
Simpler code as no differentiation between Vote and CommitSig needed.
cons: High redundancy leading to larger block sizes.
Inefficient serialization and storage.

alternatives.description: Remove timestamp from `CommitSig` to reduce size further.
pros: Further reduces block size.
Simplifies `CommitSig` structure.
cons: Requires more analysis and work, potentially breaking BFT time calculations.
Deferred to future breaking change.

alternatives.description: Exclude ValidatorAddress from `CommitSig` to save space.
pros: Reduces block size by 20 bytes per validator.
Simplifies commit structure.
cons: Loses ergonomic and debugging advantages.
Lite clients cannot verify commits without validator set.
Requires fetching validator set to interpret commits.

template_adherence.title: ADR 029: Check block txs before prevote
template_adherence.context:
We currently check a tx's validity through 2 ways.

1. Through checkTx in mempool connection.
2. Through deliverTx in consensus connection.

The 1st is called when external tx comes in, so the node should be a proposer this time. The 2nd is called when external block comes in and reach the commit phase, the node doesn't need to be the proposer of the block, however it should check the txs in that block.

In the 2nd situation, if there are many invalid txs in the block, it would be too late for all nodes to discover that most txs in the block are invalid, and we'd better not record invalid txs in the blockchain too.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to check transaction validity earlier in the consensus process to avoid committing invalid transactions.
- Desire to prevent blocks full of invalid transactions from being proposed and committed.
- Performance considerations and impact on application logic.
- Avoid redundant validations and excessive data transmission over ABCI.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to reject the proposed solution of checking all transactions in a block before sending out a prevote due to the performance impact being too great, as referenced in issue #2384.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- More robust defense against adversaries proposing blocks full of invalid transactions.

Negative:
- Requires adding a new interface method, necessitating adjustments in application logic.
- Involves sending all transaction data over ABCI twice.
- Potentially redundant validations (e.g., signature checks in both CheckBlock and DeliverTx).

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Implement a method in BlockExecutor to check all transactions' validity in a block by calling CheckTxAsync for each transaction.
pros: Allows early detection of invalid transactions before prevote.
Uses existing CheckTx mechanism.
cons: CheckTx shares state with mempool, which may cause inconsistencies.
May not reflect the same state as deliverTx, leading to incorrect validation results.

alternatives.description: Define a new interface method checkBlock in Application to check block validity using the same state as deliverTx.
pros: Ensures consistency by using the same state as deliverTx.
Allows applications to implement block-level transaction validation.
Prevents invalid transactions from being recorded in the blockchain.
cons: Requires all applications to implement a new interface method.
Adds complexity to application logic.
Potential performance impact due to additional validation steps.

alternatives.description: Optimize by altering deliverTx to deliverBlock, caching the block after checkBlock validation to avoid redundant checks.
pros: Saves network and computation resources by avoiding redundant validations.
Improves performance by applying cached blocks directly.
cons: Adds complexity to application implementation.
Requires careful state management and caching mechanisms.
