template_adherence.title: ADR 030: Consensus Refactor
template_adherence.context:
One of the biggest challenges this project faces is to proof that the implementations of the specifications are correct, much like we strive to formaly verify our alogrithms and protocols we should work towards high confidence about the correctness of our program code. One of those is the core of Tendermint - Consensus - which currently resides in the `consensus` package. Over time there has been high friction making changes to the package due to the algorithm being scattered in a side-effectful container (the current `ConsensusState`). In order to test the algorithm a large object-graph needs to be set up and even than the non-deterministic parts of the container makes will prevent high certainty. Where ideally we have a 1-to-1 representation of the [spec](https://github.com/tendermint/spec), ready and easy to test for domain experts.

Addresses:

- [#1495](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1495)
- [#1692](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1692)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve confidence in correctness of the consensus algorithm implementation.
- Current implementation is scattered and side-effectful, making testing and reasoning difficult.
- Desire to isolate the consensus algorithm into a pure function and finite state machine.
- Maintain backward compatibility and allow gradual, non-invasive refactoring.
- Improve testability and separation of concerns.
template_adherence.decision: To remedy these issues we plan a gradual, non-invasive refactoring of the `consensus` package. Starting of by isolating the consensus alogrithm into a pure function and a finite state machine to address the most pressuring issue of lack of confidence. Doing so while leaving the rest of the package in tact and have follow-up optional changes to improve the sepration of concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- isolated implementation of the algorithm
- improved testability - simpler to proof correctness
- clearer separation of concerns - easier to reason

Negative:
- None explicitly stated

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated

alternatives.description: Keep the current implementation without refactoring, accepting the complexity and testing difficulties.
pros: No immediate development effort required.
No risk of introducing new bugs due to refactoring.
cons: Continued difficulty in testing and reasoning about the consensus algorithm.
High friction in making changes to the consensus package.
Low confidence in correctness of implementation.

alternatives.description: Rewrite the consensus algorithm from scratch with a new design.
pros: Opportunity to design a clean, well-structured implementation from the ground up.
Potentially better long-term maintainability.
cons: High development effort and risk.
Potentially long transition period.
Risk of introducing new bugs and regressions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 033: pubsub 2.0
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses issues with the initial pubsub design, including problems with synchronous vs asynchronous message publishing, blocking vs non-blocking sends, and the choice between channels and callbacks for message transmission. It outlines the challenges of ensuring strict event ordering, handling slow subscribers, and the interface design for subscription and message delivery.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for strict ordering of events, avoiding deadlocks caused by slow subscribers, providing subscribers with information about message tags, and improving the interface to be more idiomatic and informative about subscription cancellation reasons.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a MsgAndTags struct for messages, change Subscribe() to return a Subscription struct with methods Out(), Canceled(), and Err(), use buffered channels with capacity 1 by default for Out(), provide a separate SubscribeUnbuffered() for unbuffered channels, treat buffered and unbuffered channels differently in publishing (blocking on unbuffered, non-blocking on buffered), and terminate slow subscribers to avoid deadlocks.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a more idiomatic interface, subscribers knowing message tags, and awareness of subscription cancellation reasons. Negative consequences include no concurrency in publishing messages since version 1. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use synchronous publishing with goroutines per subscriber or per message.
pros: Greater performance by asynchronous publishing.
Avoids slow client problem by not blocking other subscribers.
cons: Cannot guarantee strict ordering of events.
More complex implementation with potential resource overhead.
Unclear benefits for goroutine per subscriber approach.

alternatives.description: Use non-blocking send with select default case to avoid blocking on slow subscribers.
pros: Fixes slow client problem by skipping messages when buffer is full.
Avoids system halt due to slow or unresponsive clients.
cons: Slow clients have no way to know if they missed messages.
Requires additional mechanisms to notify subscription termination.
Places burden on developers to ensure subscriber handling code does not block.

alternatives.description: Use callback functions instead of channels for message transmission.
pros: Gives subscribers more flexibility in handling messages.
Allows use of mutexes, channels, goroutines as needed.
cons: Can cause memory leaks or increased memory usage due to local scope.
Less idiomatic in Go compared to channels.

template_adherence.title: ADR 034: PrivValidator file structure
template_adherence.context:
For now, the PrivValidator file `priv_validator.json` contains mutable and immutable parts. Even in an insecure mode which does not encrypt private key on disk, it is reasonable to separate the mutable part and immutable part.

References:
[#1181](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1181)
[#2657](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2657)
[#2313](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2313)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate mutable and immutable parts of the PrivValidator file to improve structure and security, and to specify file paths in configuration.
template_adherence.decision: Split the PrivValidator file into two structs representing mutable and immutable parts (`FilePVKey` and `FilePVLastSignState`), then combine them into `FilePV`. Store `FilePV` in `config` and `FilePVLastSignState` in `data`, with file paths specified in `config.yml`.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Separation of mutable and immutable parts of PrivValidator.
Negative:
- Additional configuration needed for file paths.
Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences listed)

alternatives.description: Keep the PrivValidator file as a single structure without separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Simpler file structure.
No need to change existing methods or configuration.
cons: Less clear separation of concerns.
Potential security and maintainability issues.

alternatives.description: Encrypt the private key on disk instead of separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Improved security by encrypting sensitive data.
cons: Increased complexity in handling encryption/decryption.
Does not address separation of mutable and immutable data concerns.

template_adherence.title: ADR 035: Documentation
template_adherence.context: The Tendermint documentation has undergone several changes until settling on the current model. Originally, the documentation was hosted on the website and had to be updated asynchronously from the code. Along with the other repositories requiring documentation, the whole stack moved to using Read The Docs to automatically generate, publish, and host the documentation. This, however, was insufficient; the RTD site had advertisement, it wasn't easily accessible to devs, didn't collect metrics, was another set of external links, etc.
template_adherence.decision:
For two reasons, the decision was made to use VuePress:

1) ability to get metrics (implemented on both Tendermint and SDK)
2) host the documentation on the website as a `/docs` endpoint.

This is done while maintaining synchrony between the docs and code, i.e., the website is built whenever the docs are updated.
template_adherence.consequences:
Because of the organizational seperation between Tendermint & Cosmos, there is a challenge of "what goes where" for certain aspects of documentation.

### Positive

This architecture is largely positive relative to prior docs arrangements.

### Negative

A significant portion of the docs automation / build process is in private repos with limited access/visibility to devs. However, these tasks are handled by the SRE team.

template_adherence.title: Deliver Block
template_adherence.context:
Initial conversation: https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2901

Some applications can handle transactions in parallel, or at least some
part of tx processing can be parallelized. Now it is not possible for developer
to execute txs in parallel because Tendermint delivers them consequentially.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to allow applications to execute transactions in parallel or at least partially parallelize tx processing.
- Current Tendermint delivers transactions sequentially, limiting parallelism.
- Desire to simplify and speed up communication between application and Tendermint.
- Consideration that not all applications will benefit; some may slow down.
- Need to support two types of ABCI applications to avoid forcing all apps to change completely.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to merge the existing `BeginBlock`, `EndBlock`, `Commit`, and `DeliverTx` steps into a single `DeliverBlock` step. This new step allows application developers to decide how to execute transactions (in parallel or sequentially) and simplifies the interface and communication. Additionally, a new ABCI type will be introduced to support this change alongside the existing one.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Simpler introduction and tutorials for new developers (only 3 methods to implement instead of 5).
- Transactions can be handled in parallel.
- Simpler interface.
- Faster communications between Tendermint and application.

Negative consequences:
- Tendermint must support two kinds of ABCI applications.

alternatives.description: Keep the current ABCI interface with separate BeginBlock, DeliverTx, EndBlock, and Commit steps.
pros: No need to change existing applications.
No additional complexity in Tendermint to support multiple ABCI types.
cons: Does not allow parallel transaction processing.
More complex interface for developers.
Slower communication between Tendermint and application.

template_adherence.title: ADR 039: Peer Behaviour Interface
template_adherence.context: The responsibility for signaling and acting upon peer behaviour lacks a single owning component and is heavily coupled with the network stack. Reactors maintain a reference to the `p2p.Switch` which they use to call `switch.StopPeerForError(...)` when a peer misbehaves and `switch.MarkAsGood(...)` when a peer contributes in some meaningful way. While the switch handles `StopPeerForError` internally, the `MarkAsGood` method delegates to another component, `p2p.AddrBook`. This scheme of delegation across Switch obscures the responsibility for handling peer behaviour and ties up the reactors in a larger dependency graph when testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decouple signaling peer behaviour from acting upon it.
- Reduce coupling between reactors and the network stack.
- Improve testability by reducing dependencies.
- Centralize responsibility for managing peer behaviour.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a `PeerBehaviour` interface and concrete implementations which provide methods for reactors to signal peer behaviour without direct coupling to `p2p.Switch`. Introduce `ErrorBehaviourPeer` and `GoodBehaviourPeer` types to provide concrete reasons for stopping peers and ways peers contribute, respectively. Provide a concrete implementation wrapping the switch and another for testing purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Decouples signaling from acting upon peer behaviour.
- Reduces coupling of reactors and the Switch and network stack.
- Centralizes responsibility for managing peer behaviour.

Negative:
- Initial iteration adds a level of indirection by wrapping the Switch.

Neutral: None specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing approach where reactors directly call methods on `p2p.Switch` and `p2p.AddrBook` to signal peer behaviour.
pros: No additional abstraction or interface needed.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: High coupling between reactors and network stack components.
Responsibility for peer behaviour handling is split and unclear.
Difficult to unit test reactors due to large dependency graph.

alternatives.description: Introduce a different interface or mechanism for signaling peer behaviour, such as event-based messaging or observer pattern.
pros: Potentially more flexible and extensible.
Can decouple components further than a direct interface.
cons: More complex implementation.
May introduce overhead or latency.
Requires more significant refactoring and design changes.

template_adherence.title: ABCI Evidence Handling
template_adherence.context:
Evidence is a distinct component in a Tendermint block and has its own reactor for high priority gossipping. Currently, Tendermint supports only a single form of evidence, an explicit equivocation, where a validator signs conflicting blocks at the same height/round. It is detected in real-time in the consensus reactor, and gossiped through the evidence reactor. Evidence can also be submitted through the RPC.

Currently, Tendermint does not gracefully handle a fork on the main chain. If a fork is detected, the node panics. At this point manual intervention and social consensus are required to reconfigure. We'd like to do something more graceful here, but that's for another day.

It's possible to fool lite clients without there being a fork on the main chain - so called Fork-Lite. See the fork accountability document for more details. For a sequential lite client, this can happen via equivocation or amnesia attacks. For a skipping lite client this can also happen via lunatic validator attacks. There must be some way for applications to punish all forms of misbehaviour.

The essential question is whether Tendermint should manage the evidence verification, or whether it should treat evidence more like a transaction (ie. arbitrary bytes) and let the application handle it (including all the signature checking).

Currently, evidence verification is handled by Tendermint. Once committed, evidence is passed over ABCI in BeginBlock in a reduced form that includes only the type of evidence, its height and timestamp, the validator it's from, and the total voting power of the validator set at the height. The app trusts Tendermint to perform the evidence verification, as the ABCI evidence does not contain the signatures and additional data for the app to verify itself.

Arguments in favor of leaving evidence handling in Tendermint:
1) Attacks on full nodes must be detectable by full nodes in real time, ie. within the consensus reactor.
2) Amensia attacks can not be easily detected - they require an interactive protocol among all the validators to submit justification for their past votes.
3) Evidence gossipping is similar to tx gossipping, but it should be higher priority.
4) All ABCI application frameworks will benefit from most of the heavy lifting being handled by Tendermint.

Arguments in favor of moving evidence handling to the application:
5) Skipping lite clients require us to track the set of all validators that were bonded over some period.
6) Applications supporting cross-chain validation will be required to process evidence from other chains.
7) Evidence from lite clients may be large and constitute some form of DoS vector against full nodes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for real-time detection of attacks on full nodes, the complexity of detecting amnesia attacks requiring interactive protocols, the priority and handling of evidence gossipping, the benefit of centralized evidence verification logic in Tendermint, the need to track historical validator sets for skipping lite clients, cross-chain validation requirements, and concerns about denial of service (DoS) vectors from large evidence submissions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is that evidence detection belongs in Tendermint. Points (5) and (6) do not impose large obligations on Tendermint and can be managed by the application using Tendermint libraries. Point (7) raises concerns about DoS, but this can be mitigated by out-of-band mechanisms such as payment channels or banning client IPs sending bad data. The burden of sending large data lies on the client. A separate ADR will describe how Tendermint will handle new forms of evidence, including monitoring protocols, tracking past validators, and managing DoS issues.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include no real changes to ABCI and Tendermint handling evidence for all applications. Neutral consequences include the need to be careful about denial of service on the Tendermint RPC. Negative consequences include Tendermint duplicating data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period.

alternatives.description: Leave evidence handling in Tendermint, where Tendermint manages evidence verification and gossipping with high priority.
pros: Real-time detection of attacks on full nodes within the consensus reactor.
Centralized handling reduces duplication of verification logic across applications.
Evidence gossipping can be prioritized appropriately.
Simplifies ABCI applications as Tendermint handles heavy lifting.
cons: Tendermint must track historical validator sets, duplicating data.
Potential DoS vectors if evidence from lite clients is large.
May require Tendermint to evolve to handle new evidence types and protocols.

alternatives.description: Move evidence handling to the application, treating evidence as arbitrary transactions and letting the application handle verification and processing.
pros: Avoids duplicating historical validator set tracking in Tendermint.
Supports cross-chain validation by processing evidence from other chains as transactions.
Engages application fee mechanisms to mitigate DoS by requiring fees for evidence submission.
cons: Applications must implement complex evidence verification logic.
Real-time detection of attacks on full nodes may be compromised.
Evidence gossipping priority is harder to manage without Tendermint support.
Increased complexity and potential inconsistency across applications.

template_adherence.title: Improved Trusted Peering
template_adherence.context:
When `max-num-inbound-peers` or `max-num-outbound-peers` of a node is reached, the node cannot spare more slots to any peer by inbound or outbound. Therefore, after a certain period of disconnection, any important peering can be lost indefinitely because all slots are consumed by other peers, and the node stops trying to dial the peer anymore.

This is happening because of two reasons, exponential backoff and absence of unconditional peering feature for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain stable and persistent peering connections despite limits on inbound and outbound peer slots, and to overcome issues caused by exponential backoff and lack of unconditional peering for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce two new parameters in `config.toml`: `unconditional-peer-ids` to allow certain peers to connect regardless of peer limits, and `persistent-peers-max-dial-period` to limit the dial period during exponential backoff for persistent peers. This approach was chosen over modifying persistent-peers due to complexity.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Allows node operators to ensure stable connections with trusted peers by configuring new parameters, improving peering stability.

Negative: Introduces new configuration parameters that require explanation to node operators.

Neutral: None specified.

alternatives.description: Use only persistent-peers for outbound connections and try to handle unconditional peers by putting id-only items into persistent-peers.
pros: Simplifies configuration by using existing persistent-peers structure.
cons: Persistent-peers only cover outbound connections, not full utility of unconditional-peer-ids.
Requires complicated structural exceptions for different item types in persistent-peers, increasing complexity.

template_adherence.title: ADR 051: Double Signing Risk Reduction
template_adherence.context:
To provide a risk reduction method for double signing incidents mistakenly executed by validators
- Validators often mistakenly run duplicated validators to cause double-signing incident
- This proposed feature is to reduce the risk of mistaken double-signing incident by checking recent N blocks before voting begins
- When we think of such serious impact on double-signing incident, it is very reasonable to have multiple risk reduction algorithm built in node daemon
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce risk of double signing incidents caused by validator mistakes
- Validators mistakenly running duplicated validators causing double-signing
- Serious impact of double-signing incidents requires robust risk reduction
- Desire to have multiple risk reduction algorithms built into the node daemon
template_adherence.decision: We would like to suggest a double signing risk reduction method. - Methodology : query recent consensus results to find out whether node's consensus key is used on consensus recently or not - When to check - When the state machine starts `ConsensusReactor` after fully synced - When the node is validator ( with privValidator ) - When `cs.config.DoubleSignCheckHeight > 0` - How to check 1. When a validator is transformed from syncing status to fully synced status, the state machine check recent N blocks (`latest_height - double_sign_check_height`) to find out whether there exists consensus votes using the validator's consensus key 2. If there exists votes from the validator's consensus key, exit state machine program - Configuration - We would like to suggest by introducing `double_sign_check_height` parameter in `config.toml` and cli, how many blocks state machine looks back to check votes - `double_sign_check_height = {{ .Consensus.DoubleSignCheckHeight }}` in `config.toml` - `tendermint node --consensus.double_sign_check_height` in cli - State machine ignore checking procedure when `double_sign_check_height == 0`
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Validators can avoid double signing incident by mistakes. (eg. If another validator node is voting on consensus, starting new validator node with same consensus key will cause panic stop of the state machine because consensus votes with the consensus key are found in recent blocks)
- We expect this method will prevent majority of double signing incident by mistakes.

### Negative

- When the risk reduction method is on, restarting a validator node will panic because the node itself voted on consensus with the same consensus key. So, validators should stop the state machine, wait for some blocks, and then restart the state machine to avoid panic stop.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text. The ADR focuses on the chosen method without listing other alternatives.
pros: N/A
cons: N/A

template_adherence.title: ADR 052: Tendermint Mode
template_adherence.context:
- Full mode: full mode does not have the capability to become a validator.
- Validator mode : this mode is exactly same as existing state machine behavior. sync without voting on consensus, and participate consensus when fully synced
- Seed mode : lightweight seed node maintaining an address book, p2p like TenderSeed
template_adherence.decision:
We would like to suggest a simple Tendermint mode abstraction. These modes will live under one binary, and when initializing a node the user will be able to specify which node they would like to create.

- Which reactor, component to include for each node
- full
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- *~~no privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)~~*
- validator
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- with privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)
- seed
- switch, transport
- reactor
- p2p/pex
- Configuration, cli command
- We would like to suggest by introducing `mode` parameter in `config.toml` and cli
- `mode = "{{ .BaseConfig.Mode }}"` in `config.toml`
- `tendermint start --mode validator`  in cli
- full | validator | seednode
- There will be no default. Users will need to specify when they run `tendermint init`
- RPC modification
- `host:26657/status`
- return empty `validator_info` when in full mode
- no rpc server in seednode
- Where to modify in codebase
- Add  switch for `config.Mode` on `node/node.go:DefaultNewNode`
- If `config.Mode==validator`, call default `NewNode` (current logic)
- If `config.Mode==full`, call `NewNode` with `nil` `privValidator` (do not load or generation)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `privValidator` to related functions
- If `config.Mode==seed`, call `NewSeedNode` (seed node version of `node/node.go:NewNode`)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `reactor`, `component` to related functions
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Node operators can choose mode when they run state machine according to the purpose of the node.
- Mode can prevent mistakes because users have to specify which mode they want to run via flag. (eg. If a user want to run a validator node, she/he should explicitly write down validator as mode)
- Different mode needs different reactors, resulting in efficient resource usage.

### Negative

- Users need to study how each mode operate and which capability it has.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 053: State Sync Prototype
template_adherence.context:
State sync will allow a new node to receive a snapshot of the application state without downloading blocks or going through consensus. This bootstraps the node significantly faster than the current fast sync system, which replays all historical blocks.

Background discussions and justifications are detailed in ADR-042. Its recommendations can be summarized as:

- The application periodically takes full state snapshots (i.e. eager snapshots).
- The application splits snapshots into smaller chunks that can be individually verified against a chain app hash.
- Tendermint uses the light client to obtain a trusted chain app hash for verification.
- Tendermint discovers and downloads snapshot chunks in parallel from multiple peers, and passes them to the application via ABCI to be applied and verified against the chain app hash.
- Historical blocks are not backfilled, so state synced nodes will have a truncated block history.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for faster node bootstrap than current fast sync.
- Requirement for deterministic, consistent, asynchronous, and chunked snapshots.
- Need for a small and general ABCI interface for maximum application flexibility.
- Security concerns such as verifying snapshots via light client and handling invalid snapshots.
- Practical considerations like snapshot scheduling, garbage collection, and chunk size limits.
- Compatibility with existing systems and plans for incremental improvements.
template_adherence.decision: The ADR proposes a state sync prototype with a defined snapshot data structure and ABCI interface. Snapshots are taken periodically, split into chunks, and verified against a trusted chain app hash obtained via the light client. The node restores state by discovering peers, verifying trusted headers, selecting suitable snapshots, downloading chunks in parallel, applying them sequentially, and then switching to fast sync and normal consensus. The ABCI interface is mandatory and designed to be minimal and general. The prototype includes detailed message definitions and outlines both Tendermint and Gaia perspectives on snapshot handling.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include significantly faster node bootstrap, a clear and minimal ABCI interface for snapshot handling, and a flexible design allowing application-specific snapshot formats. Negative consequences include the complexity of implementing snapshot chunk verification and handling, potential breaking changes due to mandatory ABCI interface, and the need for careful snapshot scheduling and garbage collection. The approach also requires trust in the light client and peer snapshot availability.

alternatives.description: Do not implement state sync and continue using the existing fast sync method that replays all historical blocks.
pros: Simplicity: no changes to existing system.
No need to design and maintain snapshot and chunking mechanisms.
cons: Slow node bootstrap times.
Higher resource consumption during sync.
Does not address the problem of faster node startup.

alternatives.description: Implement state sync with an optional ABCI service instead of a mandatory one.
pros: Less disruptive to existing applications.
Allows gradual adoption.
cons: Increased complexity in handling optional interfaces.
Potential fragmentation in application implementations.
May delay adoption and benefits of state sync.

alternatives.description: Use a streaming API for ListSnapshots instead of request/response.
pros: Potentially more scalable for large numbers of snapshots.
More efficient data transfer.
cons: Increased complexity in implementation.
Not necessary given max message size constraints.
Adds complexity without clear immediate benefit.

template_adherence.title: ADR 054: Crypto encoding (part 2)
template_adherence.context:
Amino has been a pain point of many users in the ecosystem. While Tendermint does not suffer greatly from the performance degradation introduced by amino, we are making an effort in moving the encoding format to a widely adopted format, Protocol Buffers. With this migration a new standard is needed for the encoding of keys. This will cause ecosystem wide breaking changes.

Currently amino encodes keys as <PrefixBytes> <Length> <ByteArray>.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Amino encoding has performance and usability issues.
- Need to adopt a widely used and supported encoding format (Protocol Buffers).
- Desire to minimize user impact during migration.
- Backwards compatibility concerns.
- Need for ecosystem-wide standardization.
- Requirement for a hardfork upgrade due to breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision: The Cosmos-SDK will define its own protobuf type for keys, allowing Tendermint to define only the keys used in its codebase (ed25519). All encoding of keys will shift to protobuf, and where amino encoding is still relied upon, custom marshal and unmarshal functions will be used. This approach aims to minimize headaches for users. The migration will be done in stages via multiple PRs merged into a proto-breakage branch.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Keys will move to protobuf encoding.
- Amino marshal and unmarshal functions will be used where backwards compatibility is needed.
- Protocol Buffer encoding will be stable going forward.
- Removing amino overhead will improve key management.
- A hardfork is required to integrate these changes into running chains.
- The ecosystem benefits from a large set of supported languages.
- Migration requires coordinated effort and multiple PRs.

alternatives.description: Continue using amino encoding for keys without migrating to protobuf.
pros: No breaking changes or hardfork needed.
No immediate migration effort required.
cons: Continued performance and usability issues with amino.
Lack of adoption of a widely supported encoding format.
Potential ecosystem fragmentation.

alternatives.description: Define all key types in Tendermint instead of Cosmos-SDK.
pros: Centralized key definitions.
Potentially simpler for Tendermint codebase.
cons: Less flexibility for Cosmos-SDK.
May complicate maintenance and upgrades.
Does not address amino encoding issues directly.

template_adherence.title: ADR 055: Protobuf Design
template_adherence.context: Currently we use go-amino throughout Tendermint. Amino is not being maintained anymore (April 15, 2020) by the Tendermint team and has been found to have issues. Amino enables quick prototyping and development of features but does not provide the performance and developer convenience expected. For Tendermint to see wider adoption as a BFT protocol engine a transition to an adopted encoding format is needed. Several options are explored including Protobuf, FlatBuffers, and CapnProto.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for better performance, developer convenience, wider adoption, and support for multiple languages. The current solution (Amino) is unmaintained and has known issues. The ecosystem and tooling support are important factors.
template_adherence.decision: Transition Tendermint to Protobuf because of its performance and tooling. The ecosystem behind Protobuf is vast and has outstanding support for many languages. The design involves keeping current handwritten types and creating a /proto directory for .proto files, with utility functions to transition between handwritten Go types and protobuf generated types, following recommended file structure from buf.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling modular types in the future, less refactoring, ability to pull proto files into the spec repo, improved performance, and tooling support in multiple languages. Negative consequence is the need for developers to update proto types when updating types. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Use Protobuf as the serialization format.
pros: Widely adopted and supported in many languages.
Good performance and tooling.
Proven in production for many years.
cons: Requires maintaining proto files alongside handwritten types.

alternatives.description: Use FlatBuffers as the serialization format.
pros: More efficient than Protobuf due to no parsing/unpacking step.
Tested and used in production.
cons: Not widely adopted.

alternatives.description: Use CapnProto as the serialization format.
pros: Very fast data interchange format.
No encoding/decoding step.
Supports random access and canonical form useful for determinism.
cons: Not widely adopted throughout the industry.

template_adherence.title: ADR 058: Event hashing
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the problem of proving that certain events are part of the result in Tendermint's consensus process. Previously, only certain fields were included in the Merkle tree for DeliverTx results, and events were not provable unless included in the state tree. The ADR explains the introduction of events in BeginBlock, EndBlock, and DeliverTx responses and the challenges of including them in the LastResultsHash without requiring hard-forks when events change.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to prove events as part of the consensus results, the desire to avoid hard-forks when events are added or removed, and the need for a stable and explicit mechanism to manage which events are hashed into the LastResultsHash.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add a new consensus parameter Block#LastResultsEvents, a list of event types to be hashed into the LastResultsHash. This list can be updated via InitChain or EndBlock, allowing networks to manage event hashing without hard-forks. The initial list is empty, and applications can specify which events to include by updating this list.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to update the list of hashed events via parameter changes, avoiding hard-forks, and allowing applications to add events without breaking consensus. Negative consequences include adding another consensus parameter and increased state tracking complexity in Tendermint.

alternatives.description: Add a Hash boolean flag to each Event to indicate whether it should be hashed into LastResultsHash.
pros: Allows per-event control over hashing.
Integrates directly with event structure.
cons: Logic is implicit and depends on node operator's application code choice.
Less explicit and harder to upgrade via governance.

template_adherence.title: ADR 059: Evidence Composition and Lifecycle
template_adherence.context: This ADR addresses the challenges in the composition and lifecycle of evidence in Tendermint, particularly with the introduction of new evidence types like LightClientAttackEvidence that differ significantly from the existing DuplicateVoteEvidence. The document aims to find a solution for how evidence should be formatted and processed from inception to application, excluding verification and detection specifics.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support multiple types of evidence with different structures and verification requirements.
- Desire to minimize disruption to existing processes.
- Performance considerations related to database operations and network bandwidth.
- Ability to verify evidence accurately and prevent forgery.
- Need to understand the severity of attacks.
- Compatibility with ABCI application requirements.
- Avoidance of denial-of-service attacks via evidence flooding.
- Backwards compatibility and upgrade considerations.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a hybrid design allowing both individual and batch evidence to coexist. Verification is done depending on the evidence type, with the bulk of work handled in the evidence pool, including forming evidence to be sent to the application.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Better containment of evidence within the evidence pool/module.
- LightClientAttackEvidence remains intact, facilitating verification and reducing bandwidth.
- Avoids multiple permutations of evidence due to commit signature variations.
- Address-to-evidence mapping helps prevent denial-of-service attacks.

Negative:
- Changes the Evidence interface, causing a block-breaking change.
- Changes the ABCI Evidence format, causing an ABCI-breaking change.
- Querying evidence by address/time is not possible without the evidence pool.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

template_adherence.title: ADR 061: P2P Refactor Scope
template_adherence.context: The `p2p` package responsible for peer-to-peer networking is rather old and has a number of weaknesses, including tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilites, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior. A refactor has been discussed for several years ([#2067](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2067)). Informal Systems are also building a Rust implementation of Tendermint, [Tendermint-rs](https://github.com/informalsystems/tendermint-rs), and plan to implement P2P networking support over the next year. As part of this work, they have requested adopting e.g. [QUIC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-transport/) as a transport protocol instead of implementing the custom application-level `MConnection` stream multiplexing protocol that Tendermint currently uses. This ADR summarizes recent discussion with stakeholders on the scope of a P2P refactor. Specific designs and implementations will be submitted as separate ADRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to address weaknesses in the current P2P package such as tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilities, poor performance, and custom protocols. There is also a desire to improve interoperability by adopting standardized protocols like QUIC and Noise, improve usability with better observability and simpler configuration, and reduce maintenance burden. Concerns include the resource intensity of maintaining a custom P2P stack, potential loss of advanced transport features due to abstraction, and disruption caused by breaking API and protocol changes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to refactor and improve the P2P stack iteratively in three phases: Phase 1 focusing on code and API refactoring while maintaining protocol compatibility; Phase 2 adding additional transports and incremental protocol improvements; and Phase 3 involving disruptive protocol changes. The scope of phases 2 and 3 will be revisited after completing the preceding phases.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a cleaner, simpler architecture that is easier to reason about and test, improved performance and robustness, reduced maintenance burden, increased interoperability, and improved usability. Negative consequences include the resource-intensive nature of maintaining a custom P2P stack, potential limitations due to transport abstraction, and disruption from breaking changes to APIs and protocols.

alternatives.description: Adopting LibP2P instead of maintaining the current P2P networking stack.
pros: Potentially good idea in principle, leveraging a well-known P2P library.
cons: Highly breaking protocol change.
Might require forking and modifying LibP2P.
Concerns about the abstractions used.

template_adherence.title: ADR 063: Privval gRPC
template_adherence.context:
Validators use remote signers to help secure their keys. This system is Tendermint's recommended way to secure validators, but the path to integration with Tendermint's private validator client is plagued with custom protocols.

Tendermint uses its own custom secure connection protocol (`SecretConnection`) and a raw tcp/unix socket connection protocol. The secure connection protocol until recently was exposed to man in the middle attacks and can take longer to integrate if not using Golang. The raw tcp connection protocol is less custom, but has been causing minute issues with users.

Migrating Tendermint's private validator client to a widely adopted protocol, gRPC, will ease the current maintenance and integration burden experienced with the current protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a widely adopted, secure, and maintainable communication protocol.
- Existing use of protobuf in Tendermint making gRPC a natural fit.
- Desire to simplify integration and reduce custom protocol maintenance.
- Security concerns with previous protocols.
- Need for language agnostic and standardized service definitions.
template_adherence.decision: After discussing with multiple stake holders, gRPC was decided on to replace the current private validator protocol. gRPC is a widely adopted protocol in the micro-service and cloud infrastructure world. gRPC uses protocol-buffers to describe its services, providing a language agnostic implementation. Tendermint uses protobuf for on disk and over the wire encoding already making the integration with gRPC simpler.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Adoption of a standard secure communication protocol (TLS), multiplexed requests over HTTP/2, language agnostic service definition, and improved security.
- Negative: Users must generate certificates for TLS and find a supported gRPC key management system.
- Neutral: Additional upgrade coordination required for validator operators and key management systems.
- The change is largely breaking and requires a planned upgrade path.

alternatives.description: JSON-RPC was considered but not chosen because Tendermint extensively uses protobuf, making gRPC a more natural choice.
pros: JSON-RPC is a known protocol and widely used in some contexts.
cons: Does not align with Tendermint's existing protobuf usage.
Less efficient and less standardized for this use case compared to gRPC.

template_adherence.title: ADR 064: Batch Verification
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint uses public private key cryptography for validator signing. When a block is proposed and voted on validators sign a message representing acceptance of a block, rejection is signaled via a nil vote. These signatures are also used to verify previous blocks are correct if a node is syncing. Currently, Tendermint requires each signature to be verified individually, this leads to a slow down of block times.

Batch Verification is the process of taking many messages, keys, and signatures adding them together and verifying them all at once. The public key can be the same in which case it would mean a single user is signing many messages. In our case each public key is unique, each validator has their own and contribute a unique message. The algorithm can vary from curve to curve but the performance benefit, over single verifying messages, public keys and signatures is shared.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve verification speed to reduce block times.
- Validators sign unique messages, which affects choice of verification method.
- Desire to minimize mistakes in verification API usage.
- Compatibility with existing Tendermint consensus and syncing processes.
- Support for curves that allow batch verification (starting with ed25519).
template_adherence.decision: Adopt Batch Verification as the method for verifying validator signatures in Tendermint, introducing a new BatchVerifier interface with methods to add entries and verify them in batch. This approach balances performance improvements with the constraints of unique messages per validator and minimizes user errors in verification.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Faster verification times for supported curves.

Negative:
- Cannot identify which specific key failed if batch verification fails.
- On failure, must revert to slower single signature verification.

Neutral:
- No other significant impacts noted.

Overall, this decision improves performance while maintaining correctness, with some trade-offs in failure diagnostics.

alternatives.description: Signature aggregation as an alternative to batch verification.
pros: Leads to fast verification and smaller block sizes.
cons: Not suitable currently because every validator signs a unique message, preventing aggregation before verification.
Potential slow down of 10x-100x in verification speeds if implemented with BLS in current context.

template_adherence.title: ADR 66: End-to-End Testing
template_adherence.context:
The current set of end-to-end tests under `test/` are very limited, mostly focusing on P2P testing in a standard configuration. They do not test various configurations (e.g. fast sync reactor versions, state sync, block pruning, genesis vs InitChain setup), nor do they test various network topologies (e.g. sentry node architecture). This leads to poor test coverage, which has caused several serious bugs to go unnoticed.

We need an end-to-end test suite that can run a large number of combinations of configuration options, genesis settings, network topologies, ABCI interactions, and failure scenarios and check that the network is still functional. This ADR outlines the basic requirements and design for such a system.

This ADR will not cover comprehensive chaos testing, only a few simple scenarios (e.g. abrupt process termination and network partitioning). Chaos testing of the core consensus algorithm should be implemented e.g. via Jepsen tests or a similar framework, or alternatively be added to these end-to-end tests at a later time. Similarly, malicious or adversarial behavior is out of scope for the first implementation, but may be added later.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for comprehensive end-to-end test coverage beyond current limited P2P tests.
- Ability to test various configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios.
- Feasibility constraints due to combinatorial explosion of test cases.
- Desire to have reproducible test environments locally and in CI.
- Limitations on scope: excluding comprehensive chaos testing and adversarial behavior initially.
- Engineering resource constraints for building a custom test framework.
- Operational considerations such as CI time and infrastructure costs.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a custom end-to-end test suite that covers a broad range of configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios using Docker Compose for reproducibility. The test suite will run tests in stages (setup, initialization, perturbation, testing) and focus on black-box testing via RPC against network nodes. The testnets will be configured via YAML files, and the existing testnet command may be extended to support needed topologies. Comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing are out of scope for the initial implementation.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include comprehensive end-to-end test coverage of basic Tendermint functionality, reproducible test environments, and exercising common code paths as users would.

Negative consequences include limited coverage of consensus correctness and adversarial behavior, the need to develop a custom test framework requiring engineering effort, potentially slower CI times, and increased operational costs.

Neutral consequences include lack of support for alternative infrastructure platforms like Kubernetes or VMs.

alternatives.description: Continue with the existing limited end-to-end tests focusing on P2P in standard configurations.
pros: No additional engineering effort required.

cons: Poor test coverage leading to serious bugs going unnoticed.

template_adherence.title: ADR 067: Mempool Refactor
template_adherence.context: The ADR provides a detailed context describing the current Tendermint Core mempool design as a FIFO queue and the challenges it presents, such as lack of transaction prioritization and associated DoS attack vectors. Negative consequences include increased size of the `ResponseCheckTx` type, loss of causal ordering which may cause some transactions to fail during block proposal, and the possibility of eviction of transactions that previously passed `CheckTx`. Neutral consequences include the eviction behavior under full mempool conditions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 068: Reverse Sync
template_adherence.context:
The advent of state sync and block pruning gave rise to the opportunity for full nodes to participate in consensus without needing complete block history. This also introduced a problem with respect to evidence handling. Nodes that didn't have all the blocks within the evidence age were incapable of validating evidence, thus halting if that evidence was committed on chain.

[RFC005](https://github.com/tendermint/spec/blob/master/rfc/005-reverse-sync.md) was published in response to this problem and modified the spec to add a minimum block history invariant. This predominantly sought to extend state sync so that it was capable of fetching and storing the `Header`, `Commit` and `ValidatorSet` (essentially a `LightBlock`) of the last `n` heights, where `n` was calculated based from the evidence age.

This ADR sets out to describe the design of this state sync extension as well as modifications to the light client provider and the merging of tm store.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to enable full nodes to participate in consensus without complete block history.
- Problem with evidence handling when nodes lack blocks within evidence age.
- Desire to extend state sync to fetch and store recent light blocks.
- Need for a P2P based light client provider to improve UX and performance.
- Maintainability concerns due to increased code complexity.
- Integration with existing state sync and store mechanisms.
- Constraints around pruning blocks within evidence age.
template_adherence.decision: The state sync reactor will be extended by introducing 2 new P2P messages (LightBlockRequest and LightBlockResponse) and a new channel to support a "reverse sync" protocol that fetches, verifies, and stores prior light blocks. This enables nodes to safely participate in consensus and validate evidence. Additionally, a new light client provider will be implemented to use the P2P stack instead of RPC. The reverse sync process will run after state sync and before fast sync or consensus, with modifications to state and block stores to support persistence of headers, commits, and validator sets.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- All nodes have sufficient history to validate all types of evidence.
- State syncing nodes can use the P2P layer for light client verification, potentially improving UX and speed.

Negative:
- Introduces more code, increasing maintenance burden.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly alternatives include not extending state sync with reverse sync, or continuing to rely solely on RPC for light client verification.
pros: Simplicity by not adding new P2P messages and protocols.
Less code to maintain.
cons: Nodes may be unable to validate evidence if lacking block history.
Poor UX and potentially slower verification using RPC only.

template_adherence.title: Restore Requests for Comments
template_adherence.context:
In the past, we kept a collection of Request for Comments (RFC) documents in `docs/rfc`. Prior to the creation of the ADR process, these documents were used to document design and implementation decisions about Tendermint Core. The RFC directory was removed in favor of ADRs, in commit 3761aa69 (PR #6345).

For issues where an explicit design decision or implementation change is required, an ADR is generally preferable to an open-ended RFC: An ADR is relatively narrowly-focused, identifies a specific design or implementation question, and documents the consensus answer to that question.

Some discussions are more open-ended, however, or don't require a specific decision to be made (yet). Such conversations are still valuable to document, and several members of the Tendermint team have been doing so by writing gists or Google docs to share them around. That works well enough in the moment, but gists do not support any kind of collaborative editing, and both gists and docs are hard to discover after the fact. Google docs have much better collaborative editing, but are worse for discoverability, especially when contributors span different Google accounts.

Discoverability is important, because these kinds of open-ended discussions are useful to people who come later -- either as new team members or as outside contributors seeking to use and understand the thoughts behind our designs and the architectural decisions that arose from those discussion.

With these in mind, I propose that:

-  We re-create a new, initially empty `docs/rfc` directory in the repository, and use it to capture these kinds of open-ended discussions in supplement to ADRs.

-  Unlike in the previous RFC scheme, documents in this new directory will _not_ be used directly for decision-making. This is the key difference between an RFC and an ADR.

Instead, an RFC will exist to document background, articulate general principles, and serve as a historical record of discussion and motivation.

In this system, an RFC may _only_ result in a decision indirectly, via ADR documents created in response to the RFC.

**In short:** If a decision is required, write an ADR; otherwise if a sufficiently broad discussion is needed, write an RFC.

Just so that there is a consistent format, I also propose that:

-  RFC files are named `rfc-XXX-title.{md,rst,txt}` and are written in plain text, Markdown, or ReStructured Text.

-  Like an ADR, an RFC should include a high-level change log at the top of the document, and sections for:

* Abstract: A brief, high-level synopsis of the topic.
* Background: Any background necessary to understand the topic.
* Discussion: Detailed discussion of the issue being considered.

-  Unlike an ADR, an RFC does _not_ include sections for Decisions, Detailed Design, or evaluation of proposed solutions. If an RFC leads to a proposal for an actual architectural change, that must be recorded in an ADR in the usual way, and may refer back to the RFC in its References section.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to distinguish between ADRs and RFCs for documenting architectural decisions and open-ended discussions.
- Desire for better discoverability and collaborative editing of open-ended discussions.
- Maintain a consistent format for RFCs similar to ADRs but without decision sections.
- Avoid confusion between RFCs and ADRs by clearly defining their roles and contents.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to restore the RFC documents as a supplement to ADRs by creating a new `docs/rfc` directory in the repository. RFCs will be used for open-ended discussions that do not directly result in decisions, while ADRs will continue to document specific architectural decisions. RFCs will have a consistent format including Abstract, Background, and Discussion sections but will not include Decisions or Detailed Design sections. This approach balances the need for documenting discussions and formal decisions distinctly.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Improved discoverability of open-ended discussions.

Negative:
- Potential confusion among contributors regarding the distinction between RFCs and ADRs.

pros: No additional process or documentation overhead.

cons: Open-ended discussions remain hard to discover and collaborate on.
Lack of formal place for non-decision discussions.

template_adherence.title: The GCS Library represents optional parameters as variadic function arguments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are not explicitly titled or separated, but can be inferred from the context and consequences sections. They include ease of use of optional parameters, avoiding the need to create new handles for parameter changes, concerns about compilation time due to template usage, API overloading complexity, and integration with other optional parameters like timeouts.
template_adherence.decision:
The parameters are passed as variadic arguments into any function that needs them. That is, all APIs look like this:

```C++
class Bucket /* or Object as applicable */ { public:
template <typename... Parameters>
ReturnType ApiName(
FixedArgument1 a1, FixedArgument2 a2,
Parameters&&... p);
```

and are used like this:

```C++
void AppCode(Bucket b, FixedArgument1 foo, FixedArgument2 bar) {
b.ApiName(
foo, bar, storage::IfMetagenerationMatch(7), UserProject("my-project"));
```
template_adherence.consequences:
The advantages of this approach include:

- It is easier to use parameters in an API, it does not require to create a new bucket or object or client handle just for changing the parameters in one request.

The downsides include:

- All APIs become templates, we should be careful not to create massive header files that are slow to compile.
- It is harder to overload APIs.
- It is not clear how other optional parameters of the APIs, such as timeouts, fit with this structure.

alternatives.description: Use a new bucket or object handle with applied modifiers for optional parameters, so that the API calls do not take optional parameters directly but use the modified handle.
pros: Allows grouping optional parameters in a handle, potentially cleaner API calls.
cons: Requires creating new bucket or object handles for parameter changes.
May be less convenient for one-off parameter changes.

alternatives.description: Pass optional parameters as variadic function arguments directly in the API calls.
pros: Easier to use parameters in an API.
Does not require creating new handles for changing parameters in one request.
cons: All APIs become templates, which may slow compilation.
Harder to overload APIs.
Unclear integration with other optional parameters like timeouts.

template_adherence.title: Do not duplicate validation performed by the server-side.
template_adherence.context: many APIs impose restrictions on their parameters. Names may have length limits, or strings may need to conform to specific formats, or ranges must be non-empty. It is tempting to validate these arguments in the client-side, since we *know* the API will fail if it is allowed to continue with the invalid parameters. However, any such validation is redundant, since the server is going to validate its inputs as well. Furthermore, any such validation is wasteful: most of the time the application will pass on valid arguments, checking them twice is just wasting client-side CPU cycles. Moreover, the server-side is the source of truth, so having the validations performed on the client side will require extra work if the server restrictions are ever modified.

template_adherence.title: The GCS Library uses optional fields only for sub-objects.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- The underlying protocol is JSON, which allows fields to be absent.
- The application can filter fields using the `fields` query parameter.
- Need to decide how to represent optional fields in the client library classes.
- Desire to balance ease of use with semantic correctness regarding presence or absence of fields.
template_adherence.decision:
- For string fields where there is no semantic difference between an empty string and the field not present we just use `std::string<>`.
- For array fields where there is no semantic difference between field not present and an empty array we just use `std::vector<>`.
- For integer and boolean fields we default to `0` (and `false`) if the field is not present.
- For object fields we default to wrapping the field in `optional<>`.

Additionally, for fields wrapped in `optional<>` convenience functions are provided such as `has_foo()`, `foo()`, `foo_as_optional()`, `reset_foo()`, and `set_foo()` to facilitate usage.
template_adherence.consequences:
Advantages:
- Most fields are easy to use most of the time.

Disadvantages:
- Ambiguity when the application filters returned fields; the value may be the default because the client did not get the field.
- As applications evolve and filter different fields, code may assume a field's value is valid when it is actually a default.
- Using optionals can help catch such issues during testing or encourage defensive programming.
- Requires more thoughtful class design to handle different semantics for "not there" vs. "default value".

alternatives.description: Use `optional<T>` for all fields regardless of type.
pros: Explicitly represents presence or absence of all fields.
Avoids ambiguity between default values and missing fields.
cons: More cumbersome to use for simple types like strings, integers, booleans.
Increases complexity of the API and client code.

alternatives.description: Use native types with default values for all fields, no optionals.
pros: Simpler API and usage for client code.
No need to check for presence explicitly.
cons: Cannot distinguish between missing fields and default values.
May lead to incorrect assumptions about data presence.

template_adherence.title: Functions should report errors using `StatusOr<T>` instead of throwing exceptions.
template_adherence.context: We know there will be users of these C++ libraries who want to use C++ exceptions as well as those who are not able to. Our C++ libraries must work for all of our users, regardless of their ability to use exceptions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Users have varying abilities and preferences regarding exception handling in C++. The libraries must support both users who can use exceptions and those who cannot. Consistency and usability across all users are important drivers.
template_adherence.decision: None of our APIs will throw exceptions to indicate errors. Instead, our APIs will typically report errors to callers by returning a `Status` or `StatusOr<T>` object, unless the library we're using has another non-throwing way to report errors (e.g., badbit in the standard I/O library).
template_adherence.consequences: This decision results in a single set of APIs and a consistent vocabulary for all users, whether or not they choose to compile with exceptions. It does not prevent callers from using exceptions in their own code. A downside is that the APIs will not be natural or idiomatic for the majority of users who might prefer exceptions for error reporting. Changing existing APIs from throwing exceptions to returning `StatusOr<T>` is a breaking change, with plans to change some components immediately and others later, communicated separately.

alternatives.description: Continue using exceptions for error reporting in APIs.
pros: Natural and idiomatic for users who prefer exceptions.
Leverages standard C++ exception handling mechanisms.
cons: Not all users can or want to use exceptions.
Inconsistent experience for users unable to use exceptions.

alternatives.description: Use other non-throwing error reporting mechanisms specific to each library.
pros: May leverage existing library-specific error reporting.
Avoids exceptions where not supported.
cons: Inconsistent error reporting across different APIs.
Increases complexity for users to learn multiple error handling methods.

template_adherence.title: We will not distribute/own/maintain binary packages, but we will support others doing so within reason.
template_adherence.context: Compiling google-cloud-cpp from source is not always possible nor desired by all users. Some users may want to install a binary package that contains our public headers and pre-compiled libraries so that they can link against our library. There is no single standard binary package manager in C++, instead there are a variety of others that users might want to use (e.g., dpkg, rpm, vcpkg).
template_adherence.decision: We will not directly support nor provide any binary packages. We will not test binary distributions of our code. And we will not host configs for binary distributions, since that would involve hosting files which we do not test. However, we will do our best to make our code easily packageable by others in a wide variety of formats. For more context, see [#333](https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-cpp/issues/333).
template_adherence.consequences: This decision will shield from endorsing any particular binary package management system. Other individuals who want to build and maintain a binary distribution of our code may do so without our permission or knowledge. If they need small and reasonable tweaks from us to support their binary distributions, they may file an issue and we'll do our best to accommodate them within reason.

template_adherence.title: Credential refresh failures participate in retry loop.
template_adherence.context: many credential types require fetching tokens from a remote service. For example, service account impersonation credentials must obtain an access token (which are time limited) by contacting the [IAM service account credentials] service. Likewise, for services without [self-signed JWT] support (e.g. GCS) the access tokens must be obtained via a separate service. The question arises: should we use a retry loop to refresh the credentials? Or should rely on the retry loop of the RPC that triggers a token refresh?
template_adherence.decision: no separate loop to refresh credentials, the failures participate in the overall retry loop.
template_adherence.consequences:
for customers this means one less retry loop to think about. A separate refresh loop would be surprising as some random RPCs could take longer (or shorter) to fail than configured by the main retry loop.

The downside is failures on a token refresh that is triggered by a non-idempotent operation. Obviously token refreshes **are** retryable, even if the operation that triggered the refresh is not retryable. We can minimize these problems by using background threads (if they exist) to refresh the tokens. As tokens can be cached for several minutes, we can start a refresh before they expire, and these background refreshes should be retryable.

alternatives.description: Retry the token refresh but only use remaining time: in this approach we would run the retry loop for the token refresh, using the existing retry strategy (and consuming its "time" or "error count"). This is feasible, but requires changing *all* stubs and decorators to consume a retry policy.
pros: Allows retrying token refreshes within the existing retry strategy.
cons: Requires changing all stubs and decorators to consume a retry policy.

template_adherence.title: ADR 001 - Adding Navigation Overrides
template_adherence.context:
LRUD navigation trees already work very well when every component you need to render is included inside the same tree. e.g if you can render an entire page and all elements are inside the same tree, eventually pointing to the same root container.

The current SSR request/response system has to build multiple LRUD trees, however.

This is because the Partial Page Update System (PPUS) inside our mountains relys on a "Region" system (where each Region defines both its markup and LRUD navigation tree) and the ability to "hot swap" these Regions in and out of a page, along with their navigation nodes.

When new Regions are loaded in, there is a "primary tree" that is rebuilt from all the navigation nodes of each loaded-in Region.

Because this "primary tree" is made up purely from the concatonated nodes of the Region trees, none of the Regions have information about how they relate to _each other_. For example, no 2 Regions can currently be horizontally aligned next to each other.

Alongside this, there are _also_ situations arising where desired journeys around the page don't align exactly with the layout. For example, any given page may want to land on node "X" from node "Y" when the user presses "UP", even through in the navigation tree those 2 nodes are horizontally aligned next to each other (product/UX requirements, etc.)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support multiple LRUD trees combined into a primary tree without losing inter-region navigation context.
- Requirement to support navigation journeys that do not strictly follow the layout alignment.
- Flexibility to update navigation overrides dynamically based on app state.
- Maintainability and clarity in navigation logic.
template_adherence.decision: Implement an `overrides` system into an LRUD instance. The overrides will be an array of objects representing navigation overrides for directions from one node to another. These overrides live alongside the `navigation` object and are checked at runtime, allowing dynamic updates based on application state.
template_adherence.consequences:
- LRUD now handles more information than just a navigation tree, adding complexity.
- Any LRUD implementation that moves data around must also handle the `overrides` data.
- Naive overrides can cause unexpected behavior, such as focus ending on the first focusable child of a target node, which may be unintuitive initially.

alternatives.description: Do not implement an overrides system and rely solely on the concatenated LRUD trees from Regions.
pros: Simpler implementation with no additional complexity.
No need to manage extra override data.
cons: Cannot represent navigation relationships between Regions.
Cannot support navigation journeys that differ from layout alignment.

alternatives.description: Implement overrides but as a separate global mapping outside the LRUD instance.
pros: Keeps LRUD instance simpler.
Overrides can be managed independently.
cons: Increases complexity in managing synchronization between LRUD and overrides.
Potential performance overhead in lookup and maintenance.

template_adherence.title: ADR 002 - Adding Navigation Overrides
template_adherence.context:
After much usage of LRUD V2, we (Lovely Horse 🐴) have ended up with a laundry list of things we want LRUD to do that V2 doesn't support. We also have a desire for a more maintainable codebase that utilises more up-to-date terminology for the expected behaviour of LRUD.

The list of desired functionality currently sits at;

- a real tree structure
- cleaner/easier to understand "grid" functionality
- supporting a concept of "column span"/"column width"
- real definition of which node is the “root” node
- all focusable nodes to maintain an "index" for easier understanding or sorting
- better handling of unregistering
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for enhanced functionality not supported by LRUD V2, maintainability improvements, adoption of modern terminology, and the desire to rewrite the codebase in Typescript for better maintainability.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to re-write LRUD from the ground up, maintaining many of the concepts from V2, while addressing the list of desired functionality.

This will also give us an opportunity to re-write LRUD into Typescript, further increasing the maintainability of the codebase in future.
template_adherence.consequences:
- user land usages of LRUD will need to update their code in order to make use of the new version. We are planning to keep breaking changes to a minimum, but some changes will be necessary.

- slightly increased library size, affecting response payload sizes. The increase in size is small enough (an increase of 2.6kb when minified) that we deem this acceptable. Furthermore, the changes mean that current "workaround" code in service land can be removed, reducing payload size in other areas.

- slightly increased runtime computation. Usage of a real tree in memory requires extra computation. Dedicated testing will take place to ensure LRUD is still performant enough on low powered devices, but initial testing of 92 test cases in 2.4s suggests this is well within limits.

alternatives.description: Continue using LRUD V2 without changes.
pros: No need to rewrite or refactor existing code.
No immediate impact on users or codebase size.
cons: Does not support desired new functionalities.
Maintains outdated terminology and less maintainable codebase.

alternatives.description: Incrementally add features to LRUD V2.
pros: Avoids full rewrite, potentially less initial effort.
Users can adapt gradually.
cons: May increase code complexity and technical debt.
Harder to maintain and understand over time.
May not fully address maintainability and terminology issues.

template_adherence.title: ADR 003 - Handling duplicate node IDs
template_adherence.context: The registration of a node requires an ID to be given. This ID is then used internally in LRUD for retrieving/manipulating the specific Node. IDs are also "surfaced" and used as part of the API, in functions such as `getNode(<node id>)`. Questions have been raised around whether or not LRUD should support duplicate IDs. It is technically feasible by combining the node's own ID with its parents or concatenating with a UUID. The question is whether to allow duplicate IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include technical feasibility, API simplicity, internal state complexity, and service code complexity. Pros of allowing duplicates include simpler data input for navigation trees. Cons include confusion, API complications, service code complications, and internal state complexity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to not allow duplicate IDs until a need arises. If `registerNode()` is called with an already registered ID, an exception will be thrown.
template_adherence.consequences: The registration data and processes must ensure no duplicate IDs are used. This maintains API simplicity and avoids complications in internal state and service code.

alternatives.description: Allow duplicate IDs by combining node ID with parent IDs or appending UUIDs.
pros: Allows simpler data input for navigation trees with duplicate IDs under different parents.
cons: Causes confusion due to multiple identical IDs at different levels.
Complicates API methods like `getNode()` which must handle duplicates.
Increases complexity in service code tracking nodes by parent.
Complicates internal state and pathing mechanisms of LRUD.

template_adherence.title: 8. Migrate certificate structure to conform to ERC-1888
template_adherence.context:
Our current certificate structure is based on ERC-721 non-fungible tokens. This presents an issue when a part of a certificate's volume has to be transferred to another owner.
In cases like these, we currently "split" the certificate into 2 smaller certificates, and then transfer one of the certificates to the new owner, and leave the original certificate to the original owner - deprecating the old certificate.
This approach is not ideal, so we started looking into better ways of changing owners for smaller parts of the certificates.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to use the [ERC-1888](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/issues/1888) Certificate structure so that we can comply and work on standardizing Certificates.
template_adherence.consequences: We would no longer need to split certificates and lose the certificate history whenever we want to transfer a part of the certificate to a new owner.

template_adherence.title: 11. transition-to-event-driven-architecture
template_adherence.context:
Origin as an open-source platform should stay open for custom modules. This should not come with a cost of forking core projects but should be allowed from the topmost application layer.

A good example is features like WebSockets, reporting services, or analytics. While this is not a core concern of the Origin domain, it is definitely important from the operations point of view. Additionally, given the number of specialized solutions, it is virtually impossible for Origin to provide solutions for them.
template_adherence.decision:
We decided to start the transition to event-based architecture for core components. Currently leveraging `@nestjs/cqrs` component of Nest.JS framework for Event emitting and handling parts.

This approach allows developers to create custom event handlers and provide them in the runner projects for e.g @energyweb/origin-backend-app.
template_adherence.consequences: As a consequence, the Origin platform becomes open for additional modules that can listen to core events.
