template_adherence.title: Environments after GOV.UK PaaS migration
template_adherence.context:
We're migrating the Teacher Vacancy application to GOV.UK PaaS and we want to rethink and simplify our delivery process and what environments we're using to aid development, testing and deployment.

This is especially relevant as we are moving away from Gitflow toward a simple usage of Git (refer to ADR003). Not having long-living branches we can utilise a simpler environments setup.

The current setup is this:

- testing - user researchers to conduct usability testing sessions
- edge - devs to test or debug features, code and integrations in isolation
- staging - final quality assurance step and demos
- production - the live service
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify delivery process and environment usage
- Moving away from Gitflow to simpler Git usage
- Desire to reduce maintenance overhead
- Need to support development, testing, and deployment effectively
- Ability to spin up temporary environments quickly with GOV.UK PaaS
template_adherence.decision:
We will reduce the number of environment to:

- staging - used for User Acceptance testing, quality assurance testing and demos
- production - the live service, runs the latest version of the main branch

Developers will use local environments to test or debug features, code and integrations.
The same applies to user researchers when conducting usability testing sessions.

Having a staging environment is also handy to test builds and deployments before going to production. Keeping a staging environment close to production reduces the risk of having unexpected issues when deploying a release.
template_adherence.consequences:
Reducing the number of environments results in less maintenance overhead.
It's also worth mentioning that GOV.UK PaaS makes the process to spin up a new environment fairly trivial.
In case there's a need for an extra environment for a short amount of time we're able to spin a new one, deploy to it and tear it down reasonably quickly.

template_adherence.title: Switch from ElasticSearch to Algolia for search functionality
template_adherence.context: ElasticSearch (ES) is used as the search engine for UI search for vacancies and querying vacancies to construct email job alerts based on a user's criteria. Current search has been identified as not giving optimal search results and job alerts are based on very simplistic search rules. There is a need to find a better tool that is more easily configurable. Currently, indexing and maintaining ranking of search terms is an engineering task.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for improved search results, better configurability, faster performance, and easier management of search rankings and weightings.
template_adherence.decision: Algolia was chosen as the alternative because it offers easier and improved 'out of the box' functionality yielding better search results, is up to 200x faster than ElasticSearch, provides a comprehensive dashboard UI for managing rankings and weightings by a wider range of people, and includes a comprehensive toolset with UI components and libraries.
template_adherence.consequences: Data needs to be indexed in Algolia using their ruby tool. UI search will be re-implemented using Algolia's instantSearch JavaScript client with markup and CSS refactored accordingly. Job alert search will implement the ruby Algolia client with query refactoring. Existing UI search code can be removed. This implies some development effort but promises better search performance and configurability.

alternatives.description: Continue using ElasticSearch with current setup.
pros: No migration effort required.
Existing codebase and infrastructure remain unchanged.
cons: Current search results are suboptimal.
Job alerts use simplistic search rules.
Indexing and ranking maintenance is an engineering task, which is less flexible.

alternatives.description: Switch to Algolia for search functionality.
pros: Easier and improved out-of-the-box functionality.
Up to 200x faster than ElasticSearch.
Comprehensive dashboard UI for managing rankings and weightings by a wider range of people.
Comprehensive toolset including UI components and libraries.
cons: Requires data indexing in Algolia.
UI search and job alert search need to be re-implemented or refactored.
Some development and migration effort required.

template_adherence.title: Continue to use Algolia as search engine
template_adherence.context:
The current technical implementation of the Teaching Vacancies web application adopts Algolia as Search Engine to serve job search results to teachers. The development team migrated from Elastic Search to Algolia in April 2020. The reasons behind the migration are outlined in this document:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1SjmXcnjJyAuAE8WRPrGX7MRrn6UQAfOQyb9GjGsa43c/edit?usp=sharing


A deeper analysis of TVS search requirements can be found in Search Analysis document:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fEQINBHTjI-TqcDfZ6IEDpNAghRGsnQg0EGJoD4E5wg/edit?usp=sharing

Teaching Vacancies conducted a review into which search engine option to take forward in April 2020 and Algolia was compared to Elastic Search. Despite limited technical justification, Algolia was selected as the preferred option to take forward, and the switch to Algolia standard plan was completed on the 18th of May 2020. Since that time a number of features closely linked to search have been introduced and improved.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to evaluate search engine options for Teaching Vacancies.
- Technical and financial considerations.
- Team expertise and knowledge sharing.
- Testing capabilities and integration complexity.
- Cost differences between Algolia and Elastic Search.
- Future scalability and customization needs.
template_adherence.decision: Based on a technical and financial review of the search engines assessed, the recommendation put forward is that Teaching Vacancies should continue to use the Algolia standard plan, and not revert back to using Elastic Search.
template_adherence.consequences: The technical review did not produce any compelling reasons to justify the opportunity cost and ongoing effort required to facilitate the adoption of Elastic Search. In addition, the financial cost of the Algolia standard plan is currently much less than Elastic Search, supporting this decision.

alternatives.description: Do nothing, stay with Algolia
pros: Algolia is already in use and integrated.
Lower financial cost compared to Elastic Search.
No additional migration effort required.
cons: Limited testing capabilities at contract level only.
Algolia not adopted by other teams in DfE, hindering knowledge sharing.

alternatives.description: Migrate back to Elastic Search
pros: Highly customizable and powerful search capabilities.
Can fulfill all current and future needs of Teaching Vacancies.
cons: Requires significant team expertise and continuous effort to maintain.
Higher financial cost.
Migration effort and opportunity cost.

alternatives.description: Use PostgreSQL
pros: Already used as main data store for the application.
Relational nature facilitates application operations.
cons: Not a search engine; lacks keyword, fuzzy search, and indexing features.
Significant engineering effort needed to build and maintain search functionalities from scratch.

template_adherence.title: Migrate from Algolia to Postgres-based search
template_adherence.context: Given the user needs we want to meet with our search functionality, and the cost and complexity involved in our integration with Algolia, would we be better off with a simpler solution of leveraging our existing database for search?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Financial cost of Algolia (and risk of eventually losing our cheap grandfathered legacy plan)
* Technical complexity and brittleness of Algolia integration
* Lack of customisability and lack of configuration-as-code on Algolia
* Simplicity of underlying search requirements means enterprise-grade search engine is overkill
* Lack of ability to integration test search results when using SaaS search engine
* Availability of constantly improving full-text search functionality in our database (PostgreSQL)
* Potential for richer geographical querying using PostGIS
template_adherence.decision: Decided to migrate away from Algolia and move to using our database for search functionality.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Simplified infrastructure and one fewer third-party service integration
* Significant complexity savings in search code
* Ability to integration test search results and keep search configuration in code (versioned and auditable)
* End of reliance on Algolia's goodwill in keeping us grandfathered on their legacy plan
* Minor cost savings in the short term (and we no longer need to avoid potential increases in queries in the long term)
* Improved performance and reliability due to not having to interact with a third-party service
* Ability to completely control and debug all aspects of how search works
* Richer geographical querying through use of PostGIS

Negative Consequences:
* Some implementation effort (estimated at 2x developers for ~3-4 sprints)
* Synonym logic will need custom implementation (but at the same time, this allows us to make it significantly "smarter" than on Algolia)
* Typo tolerance/fuzzy search will need custom implementation (but this is an edge-case for us because the majority of queries are straightforward)

template_adherence.title: Encourage use of devcontainers for local development
template_adherence.context: Setting up the Teaching Vacancies app for local development is a frustrating process involving many steps and multiple dependencies driven by manually updated setup documentation. A workflow based on devcontainers would alleviate much of this setup pain, and provide a trivially reproducible environment for local development, benefitting both developers and non-developers on the team.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Complex and time-consuming onboarding and "re-boarding" experience of the application
- Difficulties experiences by non-developers in getting the app set up locally, and getting it running again after major dependency changes (e.g. our recent addition of PostGIS)
- Increasing adoption of devcontainers as a de-facto standard in the wider development community including Ruby on Rails
- Possible use of cloud-based development environments such as Github Codespaces in the future to enable users on restricted organisation-managed devices to contribute to the application
template_adherence.decision: Add devcontainers as an option for now, with a view to iterate on it and improve it to the point where we can consider it the "official" default way of running Teaching Vacancies (while still allowing other development workflows for developers who prefer different ways of working).
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Drastically easier onboarding and "re-boarding" (e.g. on a new device or after an OS upgrade causing developer tooling issues)
- Dependencies reduced to just Git, Docker, and VS Code
- A fully functioning development environment is ready in 10 minutes from scratch, with no user interaction beyond opening the repository in VS Code and selecting "Reopen in container"
- Moving entirety of development experience into a container fixes past Docker development workflow issues experienced on the team
- Developers and other team members can develop on any host OS (macOS/Linux/Windows) but we only need to support one single consistent environment
- Does away with all the Mac vs Linux vs WSL setup steps in our current documentation
- Reduces likelihood of "works on my machine" development environment issues
- "Leave no trace" on the host machine and complete isolation from other projects
- Removes possibility of "dependency hell" when working on multiple projects
- Removes need to clutter local environment with applications and dependencies that need to be kept up to date and in sync
- Removes need for language version managers
- Provides executable documentation of project setup and dependencies
- Removes need for manually updated setup documentation that can become stale
- Experienced developers who have a different preferred workflow can get a clear, in-code view of setup steps and dependencies
- Good workflow for everyone, but excellent additional integration with Visual Studio Code
- Automatic passthrough of SSH and GPG keys
- Language extensions run within the container itself, and can be specified in the devcontainer configuration file for instant setup of useful extensions for new users
- Automatic bootstrapping of personal dotfiles
- Ability to easily move to cloud-based workflows in the future
- Ability to easily propagate new tools and improved configuration to all developers on the team
- Trivial rebuilds to a known good state when performing "dangerous" operations in the container

Negative Consequences:
- Slightly reduced performance on some host OSs (non-Linux) due to Docker being Linux-native technology
- Somewhat mitigated by use of volumes for IO-intensive cache directories
- Can be worked around entirely by moving workspace root into the container
- Container layers need occasional pruning on the host as Docker can fill up disk space quickly
- Some duplication of Docker configuration between production and development configuration (but that is to be expected given that use cases are very different)

Consistent development environment
cons: Requires initial setup and maintenance

pros: No additional setup required

template_adherence.title: Do not use Azure Search Service highlighting
template_adherence.context: Azure Search Service has the ability to return results with the search term hits highlighted. The searches submitted by the application add a wildcard character (`*`) to each term to match the beginning of words. However, this causes the highlighting to return full word matches rather than exact term matches, and there is no option within the search service to highlight only the exact term entered.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main driver is the requirement to highlight only the exact term entered in search results, which the Azure Search Service cannot fulfill due to its wildcard search behavior and highlighting limitations.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to perform highlighting on the application server after receiving results from the search service, rather than using the Azure Search Service's built-in highlighting feature.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision results in additional code within the application to handle highlighting. However, it also reduces the complexity and size of requests and responses to and from the search service.

alternatives.description: Use Azure Search Service's built-in highlighting despite its limitations.
pros: Simpler implementation as highlighting is handled by the search service.

Does not meet the requirement for exact term highlighting.

template_adherence.title: 8. Provide an End To End Stub
template_adherence.context:
We wish to run regular user research and testing against the prototype Service Provider.

To support user research we need to provide a user journey that resembles a typical Verify journey.

The area we are most interested in is the interface between the Service and the Hub.
template_adherence.decision:
We will create a Stub Verify Hub that will allow for end-to-end testing of the prototype.

It will not provide a SAML implementation.

It will expect a form submission on a web resource that mimics the behaviour of receiving an AuthnRequest.

If the form post is successful then a browser redirect will be issued to a page explaining where the user is in their
journey.  Continuing from this page will take the user to a page containing a series of possible response scenarios that
can be selected.

Any information that needs to be stored from the original request or between pages will be stored in a session
cookie. The session cookie does not need to be signed or encrypted initially.

Some scenarios will require additional user input such as a providing a pid value or user account creation attributes.
These will be provided on subsequent pages. In every case the user will need to provide the URL that the stub-hub should
send its responses to.

Each response will mimic the shape of a Hub SAML Response form that can be submitted back to the Service and SP
prototype.

The details of each canned response will be encoded as base64 encoded JSON in the SAMLResponse parameter of the form.

The prototype service provider will be able to understand each canned response and produce a specific response to the
Service/client.

Using these responses it will be possible able to test different scenarios in the client, Service, and browser.

The Stub Verify Hub will provide the following responses:

| Response Scenario     | Message                                                                                                                   |
| --                    | --                                                                                                                         |
| Successful Match      | scenario: SUCCESS_MATCH, levelOfAssurance: ${specified loa}, pid: ${specified PID}                                         |
| Account Creation      | scenario: ACCOUNT_CREATION, levelOfAssurance: ${specified loa}, pid: ${specified PID}, attributes: [${user attributes}]  |
| No Match              | scenario: NO_MATCH                                                                                                         |
| Cancellation          | scenario: CANCELLATION                                                                                                     |
| Authentication failed | scenario: AUTHENTICATION_FAILED                                                                                           |
| Requestor Error       | scenario: REQUEST_ERROR                                                                                                 |
| Internal Server Error | scenario: INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR

template_adherence.title: We will use a secure token to validate InResponseTo
template_adherence.context:
A SAML relying party must check that responses it receives have an InResponseTo attribute that matches the ID of a request that the relying party sent for this user.

Since we're trying to keep the verify service provider as stateless as possible we don't want it to have to remember which IDs belong to which users. Instead we'd like to delegate this behaviour to the client of the service provider (i.e. the service itself), which will have its own session store.

If a relying party's session store was insecure (for example and unsigned session cookie) then an attacker could circumvent the InResponseTo check by setting the value in session to something else. To mitigate against this attack the verify service provider could pass the service back a HMAC of the ID (either alongside the ID or instead of it).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to validate InResponseTo attribute securely to prevent attacks.
- Desire to keep the verify service provider stateless.
- Concern about insecure session stores at relying parties.
- Initial confidence in relying parties' session security.
- Potential future need for extra security measures.
template_adherence.decision: We won't implement the secure token validation for now because initially we're happy that our relying parties will store the session securely. We may want to implement it later as an extra level of security.
template_adherence.consequences: We will defer implementing the "secure token" until later in the project.

alternatives.description: Implement a secure token (HMAC of the ID) to validate InResponseTo attribute, either alongside or instead of the ID.
pros: Provides an extra level of security against session store attacks.
Mitigates risk of attackers circumventing InResponseTo checks.
cons: Increases complexity of the system.
Requires changes to relying parties to handle the secure token.
May impact statelessness of the verify service provider.

template_adherence.title: Use of the "full" SAML profile for signing Responses and Assertions
template_adherence.context: Verify's SAML profile specifies that Responses and Assertions should be signed. Responses should be signed by the Verify Hub and Assertions should be signed by the Matching Service Adapter. This profile causes problems with some off-the-shelf SAML service providers, which can't handle multiple signatures from different keys in the same message. As a workaround, Verify introduced a "simple" profile where we do not sign Responses.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to comply with Verify's SAML profile requirements for signing Responses and Assertions; compatibility issues with some SAML service providers that cannot handle multiple signatures; security considerations favoring the "full" profile.
template_adherence.decision: We will use the "full" profile, not the "simple" profile. The hub will sign responses and the service provider will validate them against the hub's metadata.
template_adherence.consequences: The verify-service-provider will need to request metadata from the hub, requiring more configuration. Additional work is needed to handle responses correctly. Relying parties using the verify-service-provider will be more secure.

alternatives.description: Use the "simple" profile where Responses are not signed to avoid compatibility issues with some SAML service providers.
pros: Avoids problems with off-the-shelf SAML service providers that can't handle multiple signatures.
cons: Less secure as Responses are not signed.
Does not comply fully with Verify's SAML profile requirements.

Some of the libraries at higher levels of abstraction are of questionable value - although they make it easy to be consistent with the rest of verify they abstract away the exact nature of the SAML which makes the code hard to read.

template_adherence.title: 17. We will pass the request ID to the client

Verify will send the same request ID that it sees in the AuthnRequest to the MSA when it does matching. If the service is able to see the request ID in a convenient form then they are able to correlate MSA attribute query requests with AuthnRequests they've sent.

We also need to be able to validate that the InResponseTo attribute on the Response matches the ID we sent in the AuthnRequest. So long as the service is able to store the ID in a secure way (i.e. without the possibility of a malicious user changing it in their session) it should be fine for them to send this back to the service to validate directly.

- Security concerns about storing the request ID securely to prevent malicious changes.
- Consideration of using HMAC to mitigate attacks related to insecure storage.
template_adherence.decision: We'll return the request ID alongside the AuthnRequest when we generate it and ask for it when translating Responses.
template_adherence.consequences: Relying parties will need to store the request ID in session securely and send it back to the verify-service-provider when handling responses.

template_adherence.title: We will not validate the recipient
template_adherence.context:
The subject confirmation data on assertions has a recipient attribute, which the MSA sets to the assertion consumer service url. The assertions also have an audience restriction, which is set to the service entity id.

The verify service provider, conceptually, should not need to know the assertion consumer service url - as this ties somewhat to the relying party's infrastructure, and makes it difficult to change. Knowing it would also lead to more complicated configuration for relying parties as we introduce multi tenancy to the verify service provider.

In usual usages of SAML, the recipient should be validated, as should the audience restriction (if present), and these might be different and have slightly different meanings. However, since we control the production of this SAML (via the MSA), we know that the audience restriction will always be present and set to the service entity id, so validating this will mitigate any potential issues from not validating the recipient.
template_adherence.decision: The verify service provider will not validate the assertion consumer service url.
template_adherence.consequences:
We will not be performing a check that the SAML specification says should be performed (however, as above, we believe this is covered by the audience restriction check).
We will have to revert some commits already merged.

template_adherence.title: We will report the version in a saml extension
template_adherence.context: The verify-service-provider will be deployed to a number of relying parties. Which relying party is using which version could potentially become difficult to keep track of. To make it as easy as possible for us to manage this we'd like the verify-service-provider to report its version in some way. Because the verify-service-provider is not intended to be accessible to the internet we can't simply expose an endpoint that reports the version number. Also, since the SAML messages go via the browser we can't use a custom HTTP header. There's also a concern about the security implications of reporting a version number in cleartext. We considered a couple of options: - Requesting metadata from Verify with a custom user-agent string - Sending the version in an unencrypted saml extension - Sending the version in an encrypted saml extension
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to track which relying party is using which version of the verify-service-provider, the inability to expose a simple endpoint due to security and accessibility constraints, the limitation of not using custom HTTP headers because SAML messages go via the browser, and concerns about security implications of exposing version numbers in cleartext.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to send the version number in the SAML AuthnRequests as an encrypted SAML extension. This approach balances the need to report version information while maintaining security by encrypting the version data within the SAML message.
template_adherence.consequences: Verify will be able to monitor the versions of connected instances of the verify-service-provider. AuthnRequests sent by the verify-service-provider will be approximately 2,500 bytes longer than they would be without the version extension, but still short enough to avoid validation issues. Version numbers will not be visible to malicious third parties as the extension will be encrypted with Verify's public key.

alternatives.description: Requesting metadata from Verify with a custom user-agent string
pros: Could leverage existing metadata request mechanisms
Might be simpler to implement
cons: May not provide precise version tracking per relying party
Potentially less secure or reliable

alternatives.description: Sending the version in an unencrypted saml extension
pros: Simple to implement
Directly includes version information in SAML messages
cons: Version number exposed in cleartext, posing security risks

alternatives.description: Sending the version in an encrypted saml extension
pros: Version information is securely transmitted
Maintains confidentiality of version data
cons: Increases size of AuthnRequests by approximately 2,500 bytes
Requires encryption and decryption handling

template_adherence.title: 25. We will only release one configuration file
template_adherence.context:
Historically we have had "two ways" of configuring Verify Service Provider:

- Using environment variables
- Using a YAML file

When using environment variables the application used the verify-service-provider-env.yml
file from the resources directory (so inside the jar). When using the YAML file you would
pass the path to a different file as a command line parameter - usually people
would use the example one that's contained in the repo.

There were a couple of reasons for the extra complexity of managing two files, both due to
restrictions with the java buildpack used by cloudfoundry:

- It's not possible to specify command line arguments through the java buildpack,
so you can't specify a path to your config file
- We weren't confident in the way cloudfoundry manages static files, so we didn't want
to rely on one.

There was also a philosophical point that 12 factor applications should be configured through
their environment. This made the "hide the configuration in the .jar and do everything through
env vars" way appealing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify configuration management by removing dual configuration methods.
- Limitations of the java buildpack on Cloud Foundry preventing command line argument specification.
- Uncertainty about Cloud Foundry's static file management.
- Alignment with 12 factor app principles favoring environment variable configuration.
- Desire to reduce user confusion and maintenance overhead.
template_adherence.decision:
We will remove the verify-service-provider-env.yml file from src/main/resources.

The application will default to the verify-service-provider.yml file that's included in the .zip if no command line arguments are provided.

If the application is started without command line arguments specifying a yml file AND no environment variables have been set, startup should error gracefully and inform the user about missing configuration.

We will establish the path to verify-service-provider.yml by asking Java for the path to the .jar file containing the Application class and looking in the parent folder.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to implement a story to make the default configuration file work compatibly with the current environment variable based solution.
- Only one configuration file will need to be maintained going forward.
- Users will not have to learn about the dichotomy between "configure with env vars" and "configure with files".
- The application will still run on PaaS using the default java buildpack.

template_adherence.title: 26. Development mode for the Verify Service Provider
template_adherence.context: Interacting with the Compliance Tool (CT) is not a straightforward process and the API could be better. When a user is using the VSP for the first time it can be frustrating having to make sense of the CT API in order to make progress. In order to get the VSP running with the CT so that can start development they need to: 1. Create a set of private keys and certificates 2. Configure the VSP to interact with the CT and use the newly generated keys and certificates 3. Create a script that can initiate a session with the CT 4. Create a client that can interact with the VSP 5. Test the interaction between the client, VSP, and CT
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify the initial development experience for users of the Verify Service Provider (VSP) interacting with the Compliance Tool (CT).
- Reduce complexity in setting up keys, certificates, and sessions.
- Provide a development mode that is easy to start and configure.
- Support running on different platforms including Windows.
- Limit the scope to the 'non-matching' journey to simplify implementation.
template_adherence.decision: The VSP will provide a development mode initialized by a Dropwizard command. This mode will create in-memory keys and self-signed certificates, use a random UUID for an entity ID, configure itself to read the CT's metadata, run in non-matching mode, and initialize a new session with the compliance tool. Users can start this mode via a shell command with options to control host, port, SAML response location, and matching dataset contents. This mode is only available for the 'non-matching' journey.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Supersedes ADR-0008 which was never implemented.
- Introduces a dependency on bouncycastle for in-memory certificate creation.
- Simplifies development setup for VSP users.
- Limits development mode to non-matching journey, potentially restricting some use cases.

alternatives.description: Continue without a dedicated development mode, requiring users to manually set up keys, certificates, and sessions.
pros: No additional implementation effort required.
No new dependencies introduced.
cons: High complexity for new users.
Slower development and onboarding process.

alternatives.description: Implement a development mode but support both matching and non-matching journeys.
pros: More comprehensive development support.
Covers more use cases.
cons: Increased implementation complexity.
Longer development time.

template_adherence.title: 6. Puppet architecture
template_adherence.context:
For our initial iteration we should discuss whether we use a Puppetmaster architecture, or use a masterless Puppet approach.

Using the former approach, we would have to take the following into account:

- We would set up a Puppetmaster for the rest of the provisioned instances to connect to
- We would deploy new Puppet code to this machine only
- It matches our current architecture and approach
- We would need to take into account certificate management
- Each machine would "check in" to the Puppetmaster every 30 minutes, ensuring
a consistent state

If we used a masterless approach:

- We would need to deploy Puppet code and secrets to each instance that we provision
- We would run Puppet only when we deploy new code
- It differs from our current approach
- We would not have to manage a Puppetmaster which means no single point of failure
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly list decision drivers as a separate section or heading. However, the context section implicitly contains decision drivers such as the need to align with current architecture, manageability, certificate management, and deployment process considerations.
template_adherence.decision: Use a Puppetmaster to not diverge from current architecture in the initial iteration.
template_adherence.consequences:
We may suffer from having to manage two Puppetmasters while we run in two environments.

There is additional work around the management of a Puppetmaster.

However, this matches our current working architecture so it means that we're more in line of doing a straight "lift and shift". In theory deployments would be more straight forward to manage as we would not have to create a new deployment process, instead we could amend the current deployment process.

Machines check in regularly ensuring consistent state.
cons: Requires setting up and managing a Puppetmaster.

Potential single point of failure.

alternatives.description: Use a masterless Puppet approach.
pros: No need to manage a Puppetmaster, avoiding single point of failure.
Puppet runs only when deploying new code.
cons: Deploy Puppet code and secrets to each instance individually.
Differs from current approach, requiring new deployment processes.

template_adherence.title: 7. Puppet certificate management
template_adherence.context:
When machines connect to a Puppetmaster, they require a signed certificate to be present to allow interaction.

If we lose a Puppetmaster (or it is recreated by an Auto Scaling Group) then we would have to re-sign all the certificates to allow all machines in the environment to run Puppet again (ref: https://docs.puppet.com/puppet/3.8/ssl_regenerate_certificates.html).

This would involve manual intervention to allow machines to connect again and we would be unable to deploy new Puppet code during this period.

Ideally we should back up our signed certificates, and a new machine would be able to restore them when it is recreated.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to maintain Puppetmaster availability and minimize downtime.
- Avoid manual intervention for certificate re-signing.
- Focus on getting the stack up and running initially.
- Plan to revisit and implement a certificate backup solution later.
template_adherence.decision:
We will defer this until a later date while we're testing this with Integration to concentrate on getting the stack up and running and accept the loss of certificates.

At a later date we will re-visit this approach and implement a suitable solution.
template_adherence.consequences:
If we lose our Puppetmaster while we are not backing up our certificates it may delay us while we have to regenerate certificates.

We will be able to focus on bringing up the environment rather than working on a solution that is not currently present in our Puppet code.

alternatives.description: Implement immediate backup and restoration of signed certificates to avoid downtime.
pros: Minimizes downtime and manual intervention.
Ensures seamless Puppetmaster recovery.
cons: Requires additional implementation effort.
May delay initial stack deployment.

alternatives.description: Defer certificate backup implementation until after initial stack deployment.
pros: Allows focus on getting the stack up and running.
Accepts temporary risk of downtime.
cons: Potential delays if Puppetmaster is lost.
Manual intervention required during recovery.

template_adherence.title: 9. Environment bootstrapping process
template_adherence.context:

* Backups of our data can be retrieved (for the restore process)
template_adherence.decision:
The chosen process has a few, early bootstrap steps, that differ from normal operations. These aim to quickly provide the usual level of self-service to allow teams to independently restore services without a dependency on a central operations team. An early draft of this process, which will be updated as changes are required, will be:

1. Clone all the relevant repositories
2. Build the S3 bucket for Terraform state
3. Provision the new DNS zones for this environment
4. Build the Puppet master
5. Deploy the puppet code and secrets
6. Build the deploy Jenkins
7. Rebuild everything else in the usual deployment ways

This document will be written so that one of the non-infrastructure members of the team will be able to provision a complete environment within our allowed recovery time.
template_adherence.consequences:
Having a well defined, documented, bootstrap process will allow us to test our business continuity plans, build special environments for things like performance testing and prevent drift between our version controlled and deployed infrastructure.

Providing the ability for non-technical specialists to build an environment will help to reassure our management team and auditors that our BCP/DR plans are both actionable and current.

- We want to be able to encrypt sensitive data in the repository: we want to support sensitive data encryption as part of the same process, without having to manage secrets in a different repository, with different scripts, etc.
- We want to create Terraform modules to reuse code
- We want to separate Terraform code into different projects, each one managing an infrastructure tier or application stack. This is especially important to separate resources between GOV.UK applications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a consistent Terraform directory structure
- Separation of code and data for open sourcing and privacy
- Support for sensitive data encryption within the same repository
- Reusability of Terraform modules
- Separation of Terraform code into projects managing different infrastructure tiers or application stacks
template_adherence.decision:
The initial solution presents three directories: data, modules and projects:
- The data directory contains a subdirectory per Terraform project, to store variable values that can be customised per environment.
- The data directory also contains _secrets files with sensitive data encrypted with 'sops'
- The modules directory contains a subdirectory per Terraform provider
- The projects directory contains the Terraform stacks/tiers
- Projects will be named such that:
  + Those to deploy common infrastructure will have a `govuk` prefix (e.g. networking, DNS zones)
  + Those to deploy applications (or groups of applications) will have an `app` prefix (e.g. frontend, puppetmaster).
template_adherence.consequences:
- Secrets files need to be decrypted at run time and unencrypted files cleaned up after running Terraform commands.
- The setup requires relative paths to import modules in Terraform stacks depending on the directory from where the project is initialized.
- Future consideration to put modules on Github repositories to source them via URL once comfortable with modules.

template_adherence.title: 11. Migration Strategy
template_adherence.context:
Two strategies were considered for the "lift and shift" aspect of this work. This is to clarify what those two options were and what was considered in the process of making the decision.

1) Migrate an environment to AWS step-by-step in groups of applications at a time - eg. frontends, then backends or even finer groupings, and building the infrastructure as we go.

2) Provision and configure the entire environment, deploy all applications, restore all databases and other data and then switchover to using the new environment in one go - a small maintenance window is necessary to sync data and switch DNS.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for an atomic change to avoid complexity of running two platforms simultaneously, the risk of prolonged dual-platform operation without strict deadlines, flexibility to test infrastructure stacks without impacting live services, and the benefit of mirroring a disaster recovery (DR) situation to prepare and rehearse DR processes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to choose the second option: provision and configure the entire environment, deploy all applications, restore all databases and other data, and then switch over to the new environment in one go. This was chosen because it provides an atomic change, reduces complexity, allows flexible testing, and serves as DR preparation.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include less planning required as focus can be on core applications without affecting live service, the necessity of a maintenance window for switchover, and increased costs during testing due to maintaining full stacks on both current and AWS platforms.

alternatives.description: Migrate an environment to AWS step-by-step in groups of applications at a time - e.g., frontends, then backends or even finer groupings, building the infrastructure as we go.
pros: Allows incremental migration which might reduce risk by smaller changes at a time.
cons: Complexity of managing two environments simultaneously.
Requires multiple sets of monitoring, configuration management, and metrics.
Risk of prolonged dual-platform operation without strict deadlines.

alternatives.description: Provision and configure the entire environment, deploy all applications, restore all databases and other data, then switch over to the new environment in one go.
pros: Atomic change simplifies management.
Avoids running two platforms simultaneously.
Higher flexibility to test stacks without affecting live service.
Mirrors disaster recovery situation, aiding preparation and rehearsal.
cons: Requires a maintenance window for switchover.
Increased costs during testing phase due to maintaining full stacks on both platforms.

template_adherence.title: Security Groups in Terraform
template_adherence.context: There are two methods of defining security groups for AWS in Terraform and they are distinguished by how you add rules: in-line and separate. Using in-line rules keeps the definition close to the resource but when ever a rule is changed Terraform will re-generate the entire resource. Using separate rules Terraform will only make the single rule change but there is greater boilerplate and separation between the group resource and the rule resource.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated in the ADR text.
template_adherence.decision: Security groups will be defined separate to their rules. Additionally each security group will be defined, in its entirety, in a single file.
template_adherence.consequences: Terraform should only create the specific rules that have changed when run. There will be a larger 'distance' between the definition of a group and its rules. Separate files may be harder to follow if there is heavy cross-referencing of security groups. There may be a performance impact to Terraform depending on how it treats forward references.

pros: Keeps the definition close to the resource.
cons: When a rule is changed, Terraform will re-generate the entire resource.

alternatives.description: Define security groups with separate rules.
pros: Terraform will only make the single rule change.
cons: Greater boilerplate and separation between the group resource and the rule resource.

template_adherence.title: Userdata provisioning snippets
template_adherence.context:
Our provisioning process with Terraform uses a user_data script to customise the installation during the instance initialisation. Parts of this customisation will be common to most projects, for instance, install the puppet client, apply package updates, add external disks, etc.

At the moment, the node_group module takes a parameter for a default user_data script, and optionally accepts another parameter for an additional script that is appended to the default one. We've been adding common customisation to the default user_data script in the node_group module, and adding similar code in additional user_data scripts within the project modules.

This is a problem because the default user_data script in the node_group module is becoming very specific for GOV.UK use, and we are repeating a lot of code in the additional user_data scripts.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have common user_data script parts reusable across projects, avoid code duplication, keep the default user_data script generic, and maintainability of provisioning scripts.
template_adherence.decision: Add a userdata-snippets directory to the root Terraform directory with parts of scripts that can be concatenated to create the additional user_data script for each project. Use a variable that accepts a list of parts to concatenate so the final script can be customised per project. Keep the default user_data script in the node_group module very generic, probably just a header.
template_adherence.consequences: Adding logic to project code to evaluate the variable with the list of snippets and concatenate parts into the additional_user_data parameter passed to the node_group module. Snippet scripts need numeric prefixes to ensure correct concatenation order.

template_adherence.title: 14. Launch Config change propagation process
template_adherence.context:
An Auto-scaling Group's (ASG) instances are all created using a Launch Configuration (LC). The LC manages the image used to build instances as well as any user-data, security groups or tags.

When the LC of an ASG is changed those changes are only propagated to new instances. New instances are only created if the ASG scales-out or if an existing instance goes away (e.g. is terminated or fails).

Historically many of our instances are long lived (e.g. production puppetmaster, at time of writing, has an uptime of 79 days). This means that changes to the LC may take a long time to propagate fully. In the case of important changes to the LC (e.g. new security groups or tags that add Puppet facts) this is undesirable.

There are several possible ways to force propagation of LC changes within the existing Terraform code were considered ([issue](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/1552)):

* Manual termination of instances
* Embedding CloudFormation in Terraform to more tightly manage instance life-cycle ([e.g. see this comment](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/1552#issuecomment-191847434))
* Creating a new ASG for every LC ([e.g. see this post](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/terraform-tool/7Gdhv1OAc80/iNQ93riiLwAJ))
template_adherence.decision: In order to propagate LC changes we will manually terminate effected instances.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Dev time that involves changing the LC may slow slightly or require further automation to enable rapid work on instances
* Our Terraform will remain simple
* ASGs will persist between LCs
* LC deploys will need to manage instance life-cycles

alternatives.description: Manual termination of instances
pros: Simple to implement
Does not require changes to Terraform code
cons: Requires manual effort
May slow down deployment process

alternatives.description: Embedding CloudFormation in Terraform to more tightly manage instance life-cycle
pros: More automated management
Better lifecycle control
cons: Increased complexity
Requires learning and maintaining CloudFormation

alternatives.description: Creating a new ASG for every LC
pros: Ensures new instances with updated LC
cons: Potentially more resource usage
More complex management

template_adherence.title: 15. DNS infrastructure
template_adherence.context:
- All our instances will need to be able to resolve internal infrastructure services, such us Puppet, Graphite or Logstash
- Some services and application endpoints will need to be exposed to the Internet and be resolved by public DNS. For instance alerts.integration, deploy.integration, www-origin, etc
- We want to be able to create new pieces of infrastructure alongside the current piece of infrastructure with the ability to test direct access to each piece using DNS endpoints
- We want to control which stack is running the active version of a piece of infrastructure, and control how applications connect using DNS
- We want to ensure the site and all links works correctly when users browse using the publishing (publishing.service.gov.uk) domain.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for internal DNS resolution of infrastructure services
- Need for public DNS resolution of some services and application endpoints
- Ability to create and test new infrastructure pieces alongside existing ones
- Control over which stack is active and how applications connect via DNS
- Ensuring correct site and link functionality under the publishing domain
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use stack-specific internal and external DNS domains managed via Route53 zones. Each stack has its own internal and external DNS domain (e.g., green.<internalrootdomain> and green.<externalrootdomain>). Services add records to these zones. Root domain service records point to stack records and can be updated to switch active versions. External Route53 zones manage public root domains and stack subdomains. Internal Route53 zones cannot delegate overlapping subdomains in the same VPC, so a single internal zone is used with stack subdomains appended to records.
template_adherence.consequences: Initially, entries in the root domains need to be managed manually. The approach allows control over DNS resolution for internal and external services, supports multiple stacks, and enables switching active versions via DNS records. However, internal DNS delegation limitations require a single internal zone with appended stack subdomains.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text. The ADR focuses on the chosen approach without detailing other alternatives.

```
├── data
```

* `<project>/<environment>/common.tfvars`

template_adherence.title: Use RDS instead of provisioned EC2 databases
template_adherence.context: We use both MySQL and PostgreSQL in our stack for different applications. These have been traditionally provisioned as VM instances and managed with Puppet. Puppet manages every aspect of these instances: Server configuration and tuning, CRUD actions on databases, Users and permissions, Replication/clustering, Backups. AWS offers the Relational Database Service (RDS). Using RDS would remove the following away from being managed by Puppet: Server configuration and tuning, Replication/clustering, Backups. Terraform code would be required to ensure the above is configured correctly.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce Puppet management complexity and leverage AWS RDS features such as managed server configuration, replication, and backups. Desire to reduce operational overhead and improve maintainability by removing Puppet code related to database management.
template_adherence.decision: We are going to use RDS to remove a significant portion of our Puppet code that traditionally managed both PostgreSQL and MySQL. To manage databases, users, data loading and long-term offsite backups, we will create a new type of node class named "db_admin". This will be able to connect and configure each RDS instance in a stack.
template_adherence.consequences: New code will need to be written to create the "db_admin" class, and some rewriting of our logic will be required in Puppet. We will need to understand and create relevant monitoring for RDS instances. We will eventually be able to remove the large amount of Puppet code related to the management and provisioning of both MySQL and PostgreSQL servers.

pros: Full control over database server configuration and management.
No dependency on AWS RDS service.
cons: High operational overhead managing servers and backups.
More Puppet code to maintain.
Less scalability and resilience compared to managed services.

alternatives.description: Use other managed database services or third-party solutions instead of AWS RDS.
pros: Potentially better fit for specific use cases.

cons: Additional integration complexity.
Less standardization if multiple services are used.
Potentially less support and community knowledge.

template_adherence.context:

template_adherence.title: Use ACM for SSL purchases and terminate certificates on ELBs
template_adherence.context:
Traditionally to manage our SSL certificates, we did the following:

- Purchased SSL certificates from a third party company, and did manual renewals
- Set up monitoring so we were aware when a certificate needed to be renewed
- Terminated SSL using nginx on the frontend_lb and backend_lb machines

We have looked into using Amazon Certificate Manager (ACM) to purchase and manage
our SSL certificates, and using Elastic Load Balancers (ELBs) to terminate the
SSL in front of the instances.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to use ACM to manage our SSL certificates, and terminate SSL on
the ELBs.

This gives us the following advantages:

- Automatic renewal and notifications related to the SSL certificates we purchase
through ACM
- Multi-domain certificates; this helps us manage several stacks within an environment
eg *.blue.integration.govuk.digital, *.green.integration.govuk.digital
- Terminate SSL on ELBs means the deployment is managed through Terraform
- We reference the certificate by an ARN ID, rather than having the SSL private key
and certificate be present in encrypted hieradata
template_adherence.consequences:
Technically this may be considered vendor lock-in, but the advantages significantly
outweigh the cost.

We can only manually create certificates in ACM so are unable to automate this process,
but we accept the time cost of doing this step.

between the current environments and the new, AWS ones. This means we won't be
testing the exact same thing but will simplify the networking and application
data flow paths.

template_adherence.title: 24. AMI Lookups
template_adherence.context:
All of our launch configs require that an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) be specified. How the AMI ID is specified is the point of debate.

Currently we use the `aws_ami` data source to determine the newest AMI ID published by Ubuntu within a major version and use that in our launch configurations. This ensures we're always using newest version of Ubuntu when we spin up a new set of machines. On the downside, as this can change without our intervention, our terraform runs sometimes want to change more than we would expect:

```
image_id: "ami-2944as50" => "ami-10c9asa9" (forces new resource)
```

In some cases _this is fine_ but due to the legacy nature of our deployments it causes issues with machines that need a number of manual deployment steps applied to them. Examples of these include the app servers and the puppet master.

The other alternative is to specify a specific image name. This has the benefit that we know exactly which version we deploy and it cannot change without our intervention.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections: the need to control AMI versions to avoid unexpected changes during terraform runs, balancing between always using the newest AMI and stability for legacy deployments.
template_adherence.decision: We override the `instance_ami_filter_name` parameter of the `node_group` module in all the projects. In the data directory, there is a common variable that sets the default value of the parameter for an environment. This can be customised per project in the project tfvars file.
template_adherence.consequences: Moving away from the dynamic AMI lookup means we might deploy auto scaling groups with an older version of the AMI that could have more security issues present. We'd work around this in the same way we do our other environments; by using the overnight security patching we deploy via puppet.

alternatives.description: Use the `aws_ami` data source to always get the newest AMI ID published by Ubuntu within a major version.
pros: Always use the newest version of Ubuntu when spinning up new machines.
cons: Terraform runs sometimes want to change more than expected due to AMI changes.
Causes issues with machines needing manual deployment steps, such as app servers and puppet master.

alternatives.description: Specify a specific image name for the AMI.
pros: Know exactly which version is deployed.
Cannot change without intervention.
cons: Might deploy older AMI versions with potential security issues.

template_adherence.title: 27. Move PublicAPI away from frontend-lb
template_adherence.context:
Traffic flows for frontend applications in the following way:

![Frontend traffic flow](./0027-move-publicapi-away-from-frontend-lb-img01.jpg?raw=true "Frontend traffic flow")

Most frontend applications can go straight from the cache instances to the application instances, bypassing frontend-lb. They do this by creating a DNS entry for each application service ELB, and setting the appropriate upstream DNS entry for the nginx configuration on the cache machines.

The exception to this rule is the "publicapi" application ([reference](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-puppet/blob/34c587b76abee63d0c84b9f67212ac2f1c65ba2e/modules/govuk/manifests/apps/publicapi.pp)).

This is a set of nginx configuration that sits on frontend-lb, and forwards specific paths to applications upstream.

Router on the cache instances forwards all traffic bound for `/api` to frontend-lb, and then publicapi handles the forwarding from there.

The configuration for the paths is [relatively simple](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-puppet/blob/34c587b76abee63d0c84b9f67212ac2f1c65ba2e/modules/govuk/templates/publicapi_nginx_extra_config.erb).
template_adherence.decision: Move publicapi application to either the cache instances themselves, or replace the configuration with an Application Load Balancer.
template_adherence.consequences: The frontend-lb will be able to be removed from the stack.

template_adherence.title: 30. Change in architecture to Asset Master
template_adherence.context:
Traditionally we built an "asset-master-1" instance with a large disk, and exported that disk as an NFS share.

The "backend", "whitehall-backend" and "asset-slave" instances all mounted this NFS share for the tasks they needed to do (uploading files for the backend machines, and making backups on the asset-slave machines).

In AWS, we have the option to use Elastic File System (EFS). This is an autoscaling filesystem so we do not have to manage disk space, and is independent to any instance. Each instance would have to mount this filesystem in the same way as NFS, but it is not managed by us.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context implies drivers such as the need to avoid disk management, use autoscaling filesystem, and independence from instance management. These drivers are implicit but not explicitly stated in a dedicated section.
template_adherence.decision:
We will create an EFS resource and expose the mount using our internal Route 53 DNS. We will allow the required machines to mount the resource using Security Groups.

The backend and whitehall-backend instances will mount as usual, and the asset-master will also mount the disk like an external share.

The asset-master is required to mount because it moves files about the filesystem after running virus scans.

A decision has yet to be made on the role of the asset-slave, as we could potentially move these tasks onto the asset-master (pushing backups to an S3 bucket, for example).
template_adherence.consequences:
No more disk management on the asset-master.

Architecture has changed so there may be further work related to how do we backups of attachments.

template_adherence.title: 37. ALB Health Checks
template_adherence.context:
On our platform, application instances receive traffic routed from a load balancer. Typically, an application instance runs Nginx with a server_name based Vhost per application. Each application Vhost proxies the requests to the local port where the application listens.

Load balancers use a health check to determine which instances to send traffic to. Health checks depend on the type of load balancer and protocol in use. Usually we are going to configure health checks using TCP+PORT (ELBs) or HTTP+PORT+Request_path+Response_code (ALB). For more information on health checks, have a look at the following links:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/classic/elb-healthchecks.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html

When we configure HTTP health checks, the load balancer sends a request without a Host header. In this case, Nginx processes that request in the default Vhost. These requests have been configured in the default Vhost to serve an `200 OK` response code, which indicates to the load balancer that the instance is healthy and ready to receive traffic. This presents a problem when we are starting or redeploying applications in that instance, because the application port will be unavailable for a period of time, and Nginx will serve 5xx responses. The load balancer still sees the health check responses as `200 OK`, so it continues sending traffic to that instance, even though the application is not ready to receive traffic.

The current ALB health check is rudimentary and does only test for the basic Nginx configuration being in place, rather than testing whether all apps are properly deployed.  If an instance is terminated, this causes its replacement to be added to the target group pool prematurely which causes elevated 5xx rates.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to ensure load balancer health checks accurately reflect application readiness.
- Current health checks only test basic Nginx configuration, not application deployment status.
- Avoid sending traffic to instances where applications are not ready, to reduce 5xx errors.
- Support multiple applications per instance with dedicated target groups and health checks.
- Align health check paths with existing monitoring (Icinga) checks.
- Manage increased number of target groups and monitor health status closely.
template_adherence.decision:
When an instance is running more than one application, we are going to route traffic to the instance with an ALB. Each application has a dedicated target group, with a specific health check path, following the format `/_healthcheck_<app-name>`.

This health check path is configured in the default Vhost to proxy the request to the upstream application, and rewrites the request to match the application health check path that is also used in Icinga checks. This is configured in Puppet, in `govuk::app::config`, as the `health_check_path` parameter.

The ALB includes routing rules based on Host header, and redirects the traffic to the application target group when the Host header matches the value `<<app-name>.*`
template_adherence.consequences:
If an application health check is broken or hasn't been deployed properly, the load balancer will see that target as unhealthy and won't send traffic to.

We are going to have more target groups in the platform, we need to monitor closely the number of healthy hosts detected per target group and make sure we alert is we detect problems.

alternatives.description: Continue using the current rudimentary ALB health check that only tests basic Nginx configuration in the default Vhost.
pros: Simple to configure and maintain.
No changes required to existing infrastructure or configuration.
cons: Does not verify if applications are properly deployed and ready.
Causes load balancer to send traffic to instances that may not be ready, leading to elevated 5xx errors.
Prematurely adds replacement instances to target group pool, causing instability.

template_adherence.title: 38. Mongo Replacement by DocumentDB
template_adherence.context:
GOV.UK uses MongoDB as the backing database for a number of apps. In a generic GOV.UK environment, there are 5 MongoDB clusters: one for Licensify (a legacy service), one for performance monitoring, one for router and another per cloud provider (i.e. AWS and Carrenza) for all other apps (e.g. assets, imminence, maslow, content, publisher and short url manager).

One architectural strategy principle of TechOps is to make use as much as possible AWS managed services in order to reduce the burden on GOV.UK teams to manage Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) functionality/services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to migrate from MongoDB to AWS DocumentDB.
- Desire to leverage AWS managed services to reduce operational burden.
- Compatibility concerns between existing MongoDB versions and AWS DocumentDB.
- Authentication and security differences between MongoDB and DocumentDB.
- Impact on existing applications and migration prioritization.
- Backup and operational tooling adjustments required.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to evaluate new and already migrated apps for compatibility with AWS DocumentDB and decide on migration based on cost-benefit analysis. New apps migrating to AWS should be evaluated during migration, and existing apps on AWS MongoDB clusters should be prioritized for migration accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences:
- AWS DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB API 3.6, but GOV.UK uses older versions (3.2.7 and 2.4.9), which may cause compatibility issues.
- AWS DocumentDB does not support null characters in strings, requiring data amendments before migration.
- Authentication changes from IP-based to username/password, requiring apps to retrieve credentials and possibly code changes.
- DocumentDB users are effectively super users with access to all databases.
- TLS certificates are AWS provided and cannot be customized, affecting DNS and FQDN usage.
- Backup mechanisms need updating; govuk_env_sync tool supports DocumentDB but requires credentials configuration.

template_adherence.title: Coin Source Tracing
template_adherence.context: The specification for IBC cross-chain fungible token transfers (ICS20) requires awareness of the origin of any token denomination to relay a Packet containing sender and recipient addresses. The problem involves handling token denomination prefixes that grow with each transfer and contain special characters, conflicting with SDK coin denomination validation rules.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to maintain compatibility with SDK-based chains, handle denomination length limits, and ensure valid coin denominations without special characters or uppercase letters. The solution must not require changes to the ICS20 spec affecting other implementations.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen solution hashes the denomination prefix to produce a consistent-length, valid denomination string for internal storage and transfer. The format is 'ibc/' plus a SHA256 hash of the trace path and base denomination. A lookup table in the ibc-transfer module stores the mapping from hash to full trace information. Coin validation is updated accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clearer separation of source tracing from coin denomination, consistent coin validation, and cleaner denominations. Negative consequences include added storage requirements, client complexity to fetch base denominations, and slight gas usage increase. Neutral consequences include slight deviation from ICS20 spec and additional validation logic.

alternatives.description: Use the full denomination prefix with port and channel identifiers directly in the coin denomination without hashing.
pros: Directly follows ICS20 spec without modification.
No need for additional lookup tables or hashing logic.
cons: Denomination length can exceed SDK limits causing validation failures.
Special characters and uppercase letters in port/channel IDs violate SDK coin validation rules.
Leads to inconsistent and potentially invalid coin denominations.

alternatives.description: Modify the SDK coin validation rules to accept longer denominations and special characters.
pros: Allows full denomination prefixes without hashing.
Simplifies denomination handling by removing need for hashing and lookup.
cons: Requires changes to SDK coin validation, affecting all SDK-based chains.
May introduce security or UX issues due to special characters and long denominations.
Not backward compatible with existing SDK chains.

template_adherence.title: ADR 015: IBC Packet Receiver
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the implementation of the IBC packet receiving mechanism within the Cosmos SDK, focusing on routing packets to application modules using the existing baseapp.router, verification and execution separation via AnteHandler and Handler, and handling atomic multi-message transactions to prevent channel blocking due to state reverts.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is driven by the need to leverage existing routing infrastructure (baseapp.router), improve developer ergonomics by reducing boilerplate verification code, ensure atomic multi-message transaction state consistency, and prevent channel blocking by introducing a new CodeType (CodeTxBreak).
template_adherence.decision: The ADR decides to implement PortKeeper with capability keys for port-bound channel access, modify baseapp.runMsgs to break message loops on specific result codes including CodeTxBreak, introduce an AnteDecorator for IBC packet verification, extract side effects into separate functions called by application handlers, and provide a ChannelChecker mechanism for channel open validation. The ProofVerificationDecorator is inserted after the default sybil attack resistant layer in the AnteHandler chain. The Packet Data field is defined as []byte for application-specific deserialization.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include an intuitive interface for developers and embedded state change commitment logic in baseapp.runTx. Negative consequences include lack of support for dynamic ports due to routing tied to baseapp router. Neutral consequences include the introduction of a new AnteHandler decorator and potential support for dynamic ports via hierarchical port identifiers.

alternatives.description: Implement a separate routing module as defined in ICS 26 instead of using baseapp.router.
pros: Clear separation of routing logic from baseapp.
Potentially more modular and reusable routing component.
cons: Increased complexity by adding a new module.
Duplication of routing functionality already present in baseapp.router.

alternatives.description: Do not introduce CodeTxBreak and handle all state changes atomically, reverting on any failure.
pros: Simpler transaction model with all-or-nothing semantics.
Easier reasoning about transaction state.
cons: Risk of channel blocking if application side state changes revert.
Less flexibility in handling partial state changes in multi-message transactions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025: IBC Passive Channels
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to expand the naive IBC relayer strategy to a passive one that can detect and relay channel handshake messages and packets without prior knowledge of channels.
- Desire to expose comprehensive events to provide channel metadata for relayers.
- Allow application modules to control channel open attempts.
- Maintain compatibility with existing naive relayer implementations.
- Avoid constraining application modules to complete channel open handling within a single transaction or block.
template_adherence.decision:
- Expose events to allow "passive" connection relayers.
- Enable application-initiated channels via such passive relayers.
- Allow port modules to control how to handle open-try messages.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Makes channels into a complete application-level abstraction.
- Applications have full control over initiating and accepting channels, rather than expecting a relayer to tell them when to do so.
- A passive relayer does not have to know what kind of channel (version string, ordering constraints, firewalling logic) the application supports. These are negotiated directly between applications.

Negative:
- Increased event size for IBC messages.

Neutral:
- More IBC events are exposed.

alternatives.description: Continue using the naive relayer strategy that requires predetermined channels and watching specific events for those channels.
pros: Simplicity in relayer implementation.
Less event data emitted, potentially smaller event size.
cons: Relayer must know channels in advance.
Less flexible, cannot handle dynamic or application-initiated channels.

alternatives.description: Implement a fully active relayer that queries chain state extensively to discover channels and manage handshakes.
pros: Relayer has full control and knowledge of channels.
Can handle complex negotiation and channel management.
cons: Increased complexity in relayer implementation.
Higher resource usage due to querying chain state.
Potentially slower reaction to channel events.

template_adherence.title: Add support for Wasm based light client
template_adherence.context:
Currently in ibc-go light clients are defined as part of the codebase and are implemented as modules under `modules/light-clients`. Adding support for new light clients or updating an existing light client in the event of a security issue or consensus update is a multi-step process which is both time-consuming and error-prone. In order to enable new IBC light client implementations it is necessary to modify the codebase of ibc-go (if the light client is part of its codebase), re-build chains' binaries, pass a governance proposal and validators upgrade their nodes.

Another problem stemming from the above process is that if a chain wants to upgrade its own consensus, it will need to convince every chain or hub connected to it to upgrade its light client in order to stay connected. Due to the time consuming process required to upgrade a light client, a chain with lots of connections needs to be disconnected for quite some time after upgrading its consensus, which can be very expensive in terms of time and effort.

We are proposing simplifying this workflow by integrating a Wasm light client module that makes adding support for new light clients a simple governance-gated transaction. The light client bytecode, written in Wasm-compilable Rust, runs inside a Wasm VM. The Wasm light client submodule exposes a proxy light client interface that routes incoming messages to the appropriate handler function, inside the Wasm VM for execution.

With the Wasm light client module, anybody can add new IBC light client in the form of Wasm bytecode (provided they are able to submit the governance proposal transaction and that it passes) as well as instantiate clients using any created client type. This allows any chain to update its own light client in other chains without going through the steps outlined above.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to simplify and speed up the process of adding or upgrading IBC light clients.
- Avoid requiring codebase changes, binary rebuilds, and hard forks for light client updates.
- Enable governance-gated transactions to add or upgrade light clients.
- Maintain security and authority control over who can upload new light client bytecode.
- Support for Rust-based light clients compiled to Wasm.
- Maintain compatibility with existing IBC infrastructure and client interfaces.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to implement the Wasm light client module as a light client proxy that will interface with the actual light client uploaded as Wasm bytecode. Users add the Wasm light client module to the allowed clients list in the 02-client submodule. Adding new light client contracts is governance-gated via a proposal that submits the Wasm bytecode using `MsgStoreCode`. The Wasm VM stores the bytecode and executes light client logic. The light client proxy routes calls to the Wasm VM, serializing and deserializing data as needed. A global Wasm VM variable is maintained for access within client state functions.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Simplifies adding or upgrading light clients to a single transaction without hard forks.
- Improves maintainability by removing the need for codebase changes for new clients.
- Enables use of Rust dependencies not available in Go.

Negative:
- Light clients must be written in a Wasm-compilable subset of Rust.
- Introspection of light client code is difficult since only compiled bytecode is stored on-chain.

alternatives.description: Continue with the current approach where light clients are hardcoded in Go modules within the ibc-go codebase.
pros: No need to introduce Wasm VM or new module complexity.
Light clients are fully visible and auditable in source code form.
Existing tooling and processes remain unchanged.
cons: Upgrading or adding light clients requires code changes, binary rebuilds, governance proposals, and validator upgrades.
Process is time-consuming and error-prone.
Chains must coordinate upgrades to maintain connectivity, causing potential downtime.

alternatives.description: Implement light clients as plugins or dynamically loaded modules in Go without Wasm.
pros: Potentially simpler than introducing Wasm VM.
Keeps light clients in Go, avoiding cross-language complexity.
May allow dynamic updates without full codebase rebuilds.
cons: Go does not have strong support for safe dynamic loading, increasing risk.
Security and stability concerns with dynamically loaded code.
Less flexible than Wasm for supporting other languages like Rust.

- By deferring some features to the user of the library means that the user might need to write more code to use the component. - Code is smaller, less bloated and easier to maintain and test.
