The Cloud Platform team is working on a new Kubernetes-based hosting platform to replace Template Deploy. The LAA fee calculator is already live on that platform, and other teams are using it for development and pre-live services. This platform is MOJ D&T's strategic hosting choice. template_adherence.title: 4. Separate API and user-facing applications
template_adherence.context:
We are moving into beta on allocations, which is the first area of our work on Manage Offenders in Custody. The team is now also in discovery on handover, and there are more areas which we know very little about at this stage which we intend to look at in future.

We anticipate that we will build more than one product as part of this work, to meet different needs of different users. That means that we're very likely to build more than one application as part of this larger service area in future.

We need to decide now whether we should start out by building one application for allocations, or follow the common pattern of separating an API layer from presentation.

### Microservices

There are many advantages to a microservices architecture, but also some costs.

If we start off with more than one application, the decisions we make early on about their responsibilities may take more work to change later on, as we learn more.

On the other hand, if we start off with one application and decide later that we want to split it into several, that work is likely to be substantial. Given the timescales involved in OMiC, it may be hard to prioritise paying off that technical debt when it becomes a burden.

We anticipate that other services will need to use allocation data, and so we are likely to need to make it accessible via APIs at some stage anyway. Those services may need to access allocation data in different ways from our frontend, so more work may be needed then to support them even if we do have an API from the start.

### Operating microservices

Microservices can introduce more operational complexity by moving function calls to network calls and by introducing more moving parts which need to be deployed. However we expect the number of microservices to remain relatively small so do not anticipate this complexity to be significant for us.

Our choice of the Kubernetes-based Cloud Platform for hosting (see [ADR 0002](0002-use-cloud-platform-for-hosting.md)) should make it easier to scale small services efficiently and independently. It also gives us easy access to tooling designed to support many small services.

We expect our decision on how far we should follow a microservices approach to have minimal impact on our hosting costs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decide between building one application or separating API and presentation layers.
- Anticipation of multiple products to meet different user needs.
- Consideration of microservices advantages and costs.
- Operational complexity concerns with microservices.
- Hosting platform capabilities (Kubernetes-based Cloud Platform).
- Timescales and technical debt management.
template_adherence.decision:
We will start off with two applications for allocation:

- an allocation API which will call other APIs (to read data from NOMIS, and in future Delius and OASys)
- an allocation frontend which will call the allocation API and serve progressively enhanced HTML to users (see [ADR 0003](0003-use-progressive-enhancement.md))
template_adherence.consequences:

template_adherence.title: 5. Allocation API owns allocation data
template_adherence.context:
Allocation of Prison Offender Managers is a new process being introduced by OMiC, and it's different from Offender Supervisor allocation (data for which is mostly stored in per-prison spreadsheets). The data which will be created by this process does not live anywhere yet.

We've heard that some prisons are starting to use the new terminology and have started to store staff names as POMs against prisoners in NOMIS (although they are not actually using the OMiC model yet). There is no support in NOMIS for the tiering data or anything else needed to support the allocation process.

We have learned from our allocation discovery that staff around the prison need to know who is responsible for a prisoner, but there's no indication that storing that data in NOMIS is a good way of meeting that need.

We don't know much yet about the user needs around handover of responsibility from prison to probation. It's possible that there will be a stronger need to store some allocation data in Delius (for example) so we may need to revisit this decision in future.

HMPPS needs to reduce its dependence on NOMIS over time, and building an ecosystem of APIs around new datastores will enable data to be used in other services without it all needing to be in one central database. The keyworker API is an existing example of this pattern.
template_adherence.decision:
The allocation API will store all data created by the allocation process in its own database.

We will not also write allocation data back to NOMIS or any other system.
template_adherence.consequences:
It will be clear where responsibility for this data lies.

We will be responsible for a critical data set, and need to operate the service appropriately for that context.

This is a high-level principle, so as we begin development we'll need to consider how far the scope of this decision extends in practice.

We will need to ensure that any POM contacts which have been added to NOMIS are removed when those prisons move to the OMiC model and start using the allocation manager.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use the Custody API to access NOMIS data
template_adherence.context:
Our main source of data on prisoners and prison staff which we need for allocations is NOMIS.

There are now four APIs into NOMIS providing general data access, with varying approaches to presenting the data and authentication. We do not want to add to this duplication.

The APIs which have been developed more recently are more under the control of HMPPS than the earlier ones (which were developed by a supplier). That gives us more flexibility around how we work with them and makes it possible to get changes into production more quickly. Using one of the newer APIs should mean that we are less blocked by delays around API changes than we have been on our work on Visit someone in prison.

It has been agreed by the HMPPS technical community that we would like to move all clients to use the Custody API in preference to the other APIs over time. Although that work has not yet been prioritised, using the Custody API for new applications will reduce the work needed in future to align our API usage.

The Custody API has been designed to give a more direct view of the data in NOMIS than the previous APIs have been - earlier approaches have favoured implementing specific endpoints to meet the needs of service teams rather than giving a more comprehensive view of all the data.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce duplication of APIs accessing NOMIS data.
- Desire to use APIs more under HMPPS control for flexibility and faster changes.
- Agreement by HMPPS technical community to move clients to Custody API over time.
- Need to reduce dependencies and improve speed of development.
- Desire to use system-to-system authentication rather than user-based authentication.
- Potential need for API to support filtering and specific field requests.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use the Custody API to access the NOMIS data we need.

We will work with the team in Sheffield on development of the Custody API to add support for accessing the data we need.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Alignment with agreed HMPPS API approach.
- Reduced dependencies between teams by taking on API development work.
- Need to learn Java development and established Custody API patterns.
- Ongoing support needed from Sheffield team for reviews and deployments.
- Reduced pressure on Sheffield API developers over time.
- Ability to use system-to-system authentication.
- Potential efficiency gains by requesting exact data needed.
- May require expanding Custody API scope to support filtering or specific fields, to be discussed with Sheffield team if needed.

alternatives.description: Continue using existing multiple NOMIS APIs without consolidating to Custody API.
pros: No immediate need to learn new API or Java development.

cons: Continued duplication and fragmentation of API usage.

More complex integration and maintenance overhead.
Not aligned with HMPPS technical community agreement.

template_adherence.title: 10. Allocation API has less responsibility
template_adherence.context:
When we decided to start off with separate API and user-facing applications (see [ADR 0004](0004-separate-api-and-user-facing-applications.md)) we thought that we would need to build more than one service as part of this work, to meet different needs of different users. That may still be true in general, but from what we've learned in the Handover discovery it's looking more likely at the moment that the Handover phase of our work will involve expanding on Allocations rather than being an entirely separate journey and service.

We were also intending that the allocation manager would be a fairly minimal user-facing application, which would fetch all the data it needed from the allocation API and then render pages based directly on it.

We've been looking at how we should set up authentication on our two applications and have realised that that split of responsibilities between the allocation manager and API could lead to some confusions:

- Calling the Custody API from the allocation API means that the allocation API can be seen as sitting in two different layers depending on the context: either above the Custody API from the point of view of the allocation manager, but on the same level as the Custody API from the point of view of other services which need to use allocation data. This lack of clarity raises questions around which OAuth2 grant type to use for authentication on the allocation API.
- Responsibility for access control may be split between the allocation manager and API. The user-facing application would need to know what the user should have access to in order to show the right options, but the API may also need to know what the user should have access to in order to fetch the right data from other APIs.

We still think there's value in having a separate allocation API, but it would be easier to understand if it were a more RESTful interface to the data it stores.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to clarify responsibilities between allocation API and allocation manager to avoid confusion in authentication and access control.
- Desire to keep allocation API as a RESTful interface to its own data.
- Avoid splitting access control responsibilities between API and user-facing application.
- Maintain clear layering and relationships between APIs.
- Anticipate future needs and potential splitting of responsibilities if allocation manager grows too complex.
template_adherence.decision:
The allocation API will be a simpler interface to the data held in its database.

The allocation API will not call other APIs to return data from them to the allocation manager.

The allocation manager will call the allocation API and other APIs (Custody, Delius etc) directly.

The allocation manager will be entirely responsible for access control for its users.
template_adherence.consequences:
The relationships between the various APIs become easier to understand, because they are all providing data from only their own databases.

The allocation API clearly sits at the same level as the other APIs in this space.

The allocation manager will now be responsible for both fetching and combining data from various sources, and displaying it to users.

There's a risk that the allocation manager will acquire more responsibilities to the point where it needs to be split up in future. We don't know enough at this stage to decide where its boundaries should be, so will need to keep an eye on this as we continue to work on Manage Offenders in Custody.

We haven't yet built anything which needs to be moved between applications as a result of this decision - this only affects future work.

alternatives.description: Keep the allocation API calling other APIs to aggregate data and handle access control responsibilities.
pros: Simplifies the allocation manager by offloading data aggregation and access control to the API.

template_adherence.title: 11. Use NOMIS OAuth2 server for allocation API authentication
template_adherence.context:
We need to protect the allocation API with authentication, but we'd rather not have to come up with an approach to do that ourselves from scratch.

The new NOMIS OAuth2 server is already being used in production for authentication on almost all of the NOMIS APIs and some other APIs built in Sheffield. We will need to use it to authenticate with the Custody API, and the other services which may need to use the allocation API are very likely to already be using this authentication method for the other APIs they use.

Clients can use one token (of a particular grant type) to authenticate with all APIs which use the NOMIS OAuth2 server, which makes things simpler for all those services - they don't have to work with multiple different authentication approaches.

The NOMIS OAuth2 server uses JWTs signed with a private key, so relying services can verify the integrity and authenticity of tokens presented by clients using the corresponding public key.

We've decided that the allocation manager will be entirely responsible for user access control and will call other APIs directly, and the allocation API will be a smaller interface onto its data (see ADR 0010). That means that the allocation API doesn't need to know which user it's returning data for, and we can use a system-to-system approach to authentication.

We don't know of any other shared approaches to API authentication which are used in the prison space.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to protect the allocation API with authentication.
- Desire to avoid creating a new authentication approach from scratch.
- Existing use of NOMIS OAuth2 server in production for other APIs.
- Simplification for clients using a single token across multiple APIs.
- Use of JWTs signed with private keys for token verification.
- Allocation manager responsible for user access control, allowing system-to-system authentication.
- Lack of other shared API authentication approaches in the domain.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use the NOMIS OAuth2 server for authentication on the allocation API.

We will use the client credentials OAuth2 grant type for authentication on the allocation API.

We will verify signatures on presented tokens in the allocation API.

We will respect expiration times on presented tokens in the allocation API.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to develop our own approach to modeling permissions for the API using roles and/or scopes in the NOMIS OAuth2 server.
- Need to build support for restricting access based on permissions into the allocation API.
- Future need to account for clients with more limited read access than the allocation manager.
- Allocation manager and other clients can use the same client credentials token for multiple APIs.
- Clients of the allocation API are responsible for implementing appropriate access control around their use of data from the API.

template_adherence.title: 12. Start out with one environment which uses T3 NOMIS
template_adherence.context: We want to run the smallest number of pre-production environments which give us useful feedback on changes to our applications before we deploy them to production. We think that as we integrate with more systems (NOMIS, Delius, OASys etc) we are likely to need more pre-production environments of our own in order to test against pre-production environments of those systems. It's unlikely that data will match up well across systems in these environments so we may need to create matching data in them ourselves in order to test our applications. We don't know yet how many pre-production environments would be useful for us to have in this context. We suspect that challenges around data quality and how quickly records are matched will only be clear in production data, so we're keen to start working with production systems as soon as we can. However only NOMIS has available APIs in production, and working with only one system is less likely to reveal the scale of those challenges. So far we've set up one environment for our new applications on the new cloud platform, called Staging. It's straightforward and quick to set up further environments as we need them, but there's no way at the moment to share config between cloud platform environments so there is a code maintenance cost to having many environments. We still need to finish setting up authentication on our applications as a minimum before we start using production APIs to other systems. There's little benefit in us having a Production environment ourselves until we can do that - we're a long way from having real users. Setting up authentication means that we need to pick a NOMIS pre-production environment to use from our Staging environment, because we're going to use the NOMIS OAuth2 server (see ADR 0011). Our team already have comprehensive access to the T3 NOMIS environment from our work on Visit someone in prison. That environment contains anonymised data, which is sufficient for our needs at this stage. All the NOMIS-based services we need are running there. It's commonly used as a development environment (rather than staging) by other services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to minimize the number of pre-production environments while still getting useful feedback.
- Integration with multiple systems (NOMIS, Delius, OASys) requiring testing environments.
- Data quality and record matching challenges best revealed with production data.
- Only NOMIS has production APIs available currently.
- Ease and cost of setting up and maintaining multiple environments.
- Requirement to set up authentication using NOMIS OAuth2 server.
- Existing access to T3 NOMIS environment with anonymised data sufficient for current needs.
template_adherence.decision: We will start out with one shared Staging environment for our new applications. We will use the T3 NOMIS environment from that environment to start with.

template_adherence.title: Manage short-lived access tokens in tests
template_adherence.context:
We have implemented the VCR gem as part of our testing suite; this gem allows you to "record your test suite's HTTP interactions and replay them during future test runs for fast, deterministic, accurate tests.". The interactions are saved into yaml files (cassettes) as part of the spec/fixtures folder and committed to the repository.

VCR allows you to filter out sensitive information, but this does not cover any data returned in the body.  We get a short-lived access token returned in the body as part of the OAuth flow and need to find a way of ensuring that these are not exposed and used to get access to sensitive data.  Whilst the tests are run against T3, which is an anonymised dataset, we don't want to risk the possibility of someone being able to engineer a way of undoing that and seeing real data.

The main options:

- making the github repository private
- git-crypting the VCR cassettes folder
- adding the VCR cassettes folder to .gitignore
- not using VCR and instead using other ways of mocking external calls in tests

Making the github repository private contradicts our commitment to coding in the open, and eventually opening a previously closed repository is often risky and hard to prioritise.

Encrypting the VCR cassettes folder would effectively mean making a portion of the repository private.  There are three criteria for keeping code closed and they are: not publishing keys and credentials; algorithms related to detecting fraud; and anything around unreleased policy.  This situation does not meet any of these criteria.  Full documentation related to open source code guidance can be found [here](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-source-guidance/when-code-should-be-open-or-closed).

Adding the VCR cassettes folder to gitignore would mean that we could continue to make use of the gem in local development and during the CircleCi workflow.  The APIs that we are using are being actively developed against and it's important that we catch any changes as early as possible. Therefore a developer can re-record all cassettes at the start of a feature to check for changes, and then just reuse them to speed up the tests.  The cassettes then don't get committed to Github and access tokens are not exposed. CircleCi can continue to run the tests as normal and whilst anyone can access the project, cannot see the contents of the cassettes.

Lastly, there is an option to not use the VCR gem at all and use something like WebMock to mock every API call in the test suite. However, if there were any issues with API documentation being out of date we wouldn't necessarily know what to expect in the response.  Also, if we mock the calls there might have been changes we weren't aware of and find out late in to the development process, whereas actually making the calls will cause the tests to fail and let us investigate.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to prevent exposure of short-lived access tokens in test recordings.
- Desire to keep the repository open and avoid making parts private.
- Importance of catching API changes early during development.
- Maintaining test speed and reliability.
- Balancing security with development and CI/CD workflow needs.
template_adherence.decision:
We will add the VCR cassettes folder to gitignore.

We will change the VCR config to allow a recording mode to be added i.e. "all" -> re-record all cassettes, "new_episodes" -> append the cassette(s) with any new calls made, "once" -> just record them once and reuse.
template_adherence.consequences:
We remove the risk of short-lived access tokens being exposed publicly, we can continue to use VCR in local development to keep our test speeds as low as possible, and we will also continue to use VCR during our CI/CD workflow in CircleCi.

In regards to CircleCi it does mean that our CircleCI project environment variables need to include credentials for authenticating against T3.

It's important to note that our tests will be making external network calls, which may increase build times and flakiness. We are likely to need to address these concerns later, but this decision is a pragmatic approach to help us move forward now.

alternatives.description: Making the github repository private
pros: Keeps the VCR cassettes and sensitive data private.
cons: Contradicts commitment to coding in the open.

template_adherence.title: 16. Use the Elite2 API to access NOMIS data
template_adherence.context: Our main source of data on prisoners and prison staff is NOMIS. The allocation tool currently uses the Custody API, as decided in ADR 0006, to retrieve data on both offenders and staff. There are still four APIs into NOMIS providing general data access, with varying approaches to presenting the data and authentication. We still do not want to add to this duplication. Although it has been agreed by the HMPPS technical community that we would like to move all clients to use the Custody API in preference to the other APIs, initial use of the Custody API has raised some issues. Problems exist with the locality of data, N+1 API requests, and data that is unavailable through the currently published endpoints. These issues are intrinsic to the current design of the Custody API, and it is unlikely that they will be resolved or mitigated in the short to medium term. The scale of the work required makes it unrealistic that we would be able to deliver this in a realistic timescale. The Elite2 API, is under more active development, is entirely owned by the Sheffield team and provides endpoints more focused on the need of clients. Most of the endpoints available work on the caseload of the connecting client token, but also support the provision of more specific parameters to handle alternate needs. Although we will not be authenticating with the token of the eventual end user, enough flexibility exists for us to obtain the data we require from Elite2. Elite2 provides functionality closer to what we currently require and its design encompasses the need for extra API endpoints for specific services. Moving to Elite2 is a pragmatic, and tactical approach to resolving the issues around the Custody API to allow us to deliver the allocation component of MOiC. This decision doesn't invalidate the overall agreed strategy of moving HMPPS services to the Custody API over time, but it highlights that more coordinated work is needed to achieve that than we are able to take on ourselves.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to access NOMIS data effectively for prisoners and prison staff.
- Existing use of Custody API has issues: data locality, N+1 API requests, unavailable data.
- Custody API issues unlikely to be resolved in short to medium term.
- Desire to avoid duplication of APIs.
- Elite2 API is under active development and owned by Sheffield team.
- Elite2 API provides endpoints more focused on client needs and flexibility.
- Pragmatic and tactical approach to deliver allocation component of MOiC.
- Overall strategy still favors Custody API long term, but immediate needs require alternative.
template_adherence.decision: We will use the Elite2 API for access to the data we require from NOMIS. We will work with the team in Sheffield on development of the Elite2 API to add support for accessing the data we need, in the structure that we need it.

template_adherence.title: 17. Use blue-green deployments to manage database migrations
template_adherence.context: We have reached a point where we are going to start reading and writing data to our Allocation API application database and will need to manage database migrations when adding tables, columns and so forth. This ADR decision outlines the agreed upon approach that the team will take for managing these migrations.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use blue-green deployments split into the following steps (using adding column as an example):

* Add a database migration that inserts the new column
* Update the application so that all new data gets written to new column
* Run a task to copy all the data from the old column to the new column
* Update the application so that it reads from the new column
* Add a database migration that removes the old column

We will also ensure that any migrations include 'up' and 'down' methods, rather than just 'change' to avoid any situations where Rails doesn't know how to handle the inverse of the up or down.
template_adherence.consequences:
This will reduce downtime, and reduce the risk of losing data as we can more granularly control individual tasks rather than it happening in one big bang type event that you can't recover from.

Another ADR will be required once we have researched, discussed and decided on how we will manage situations involving rollbacks.

template_adherence.title: 19. Manage runtime secrets with git-crypt
template_adherence.context:
The recommended way of managing application config needed at runtime on the cloud platform is to use Kubernetes secrets. These can be created manually using kubectl on the command line to apply config files, or as part of a deployment process.

We want to manage as much of our application config as possible in version-controlled code, so that we can see when config was changed and so that we can easily reproduce changes and rebuild environments.

The team are used to using git-crypt to encrypt files containing secrets from their work on Visit someone in prison, but that service is hosted on a different platform which means that the secrets are in a private repo, separate from the application. It's easy to forget to update config at the right time when it's managed separately from the application, and that has resulted in production outages in the past on that service.

If we use git-crypt to encrypt secrets files in public repos rather than private ones, the risk associated with accidentally pushing secrets in unencrypted files is increased. If we take this approach, we would want to make it easier to avoid doing that rather than relying only on people being careful.

We are using kubectl for deploying. Some other teams are using helm, which has support for templating so that values for config files can be kept separately from the structure of the configuration. Unless we start using templating of some kind in our config files, we will need to keep the whole files containing Kubernetes secrets definitions private instead of just the secret values.

Other options

Alternatives to using git-crypt in public repos include:

- separating out secrets into a private repo, using git-crypt there instead. This would increase the likelihood of us not updating the config when it's needed, leading to production outages.

- creating Kubernetes secrets manually from the command line, using config files committed in the application repo without secret values or encryption - so the secret values would be generated as needed and only stored in the relevant namespace. This would mean that our Kubernetes secrets could not be deployed as part of our automated pipeline but would need to be manually updated, and the manual workflow for updating a single value in a secret with multiple data values would be more complex. We would need to be careful to not accidentally commit the values in the secrets files after deploying them.

- storing secret values in CircleCI envvars, to be used when creating Kubernetes secrets during deployment, using templating in our secrets files. CircleCI has no concept of environments (all envvars for a project are available to all jobs) so all of our test and build steps would have access to production secrets, and we would need to define an approach to namespacing CircleCI envvars for different environments. Even so, envvars needed for running tests, building and pushing images, running deployments and running applications in different environments would all live together in one list, which would make that list more confusing than it already is.

- using another secrets store to manage our secrets, probably instead of using Kubernetes secrets. This would add another external dependency for our applications and would have the same challenges around either managing secrets values manually (thereby losing the ability to automate processes) or finding somewhere to manage version-controlled secrets from, and having another place to coordinate changes to required config with application deploys. It could also introduce another system for the team to authenticate with in order to manage secrets.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage application config needed at runtime on the cloud platform.
- Desire to keep config in version-controlled code for traceability and reproducibility.
- Existing team familiarity with git-crypt.
- Risks of managing secrets in public repos and accidental exposure.
- Deployment tooling constraints (kubectl vs helm).
- Alternatives have drawbacks such as manual updates, complexity, or additional dependencies.
- Need to reduce production outages caused by config mismanagement.
- Desire to automate deployment processes as much as possible.
- Security concerns around access control and secret rotation.
template_adherence.decision:
We will keep the Kubernetes secrets definitions which are related to our applications in the public application repos, encrypted with git-crypt.

We will only add team members who need access to production secrets to the git-crypt setup. The only exception to this is our CircleCI deployment jobs which need to decrypt the secrets to deploy them.

We will define a standard for creating and managing GPG keys and only use keys with the git-crypt setup which meet that standard.

We will set up pre-commit hooks on our repos which contain encrypted secrets to help us use git-crypt well.

We will agree processes for revoking credentials with other relevant teams in case they are accidentally exposed.

If another standard way of managing secrets for applications running on the cloud platform is developed, we will consider using that instead.
template_adherence.consequences:
We will have fewer places to manage config needed by our applications in production, making it less likely that we forget to make or apply a required config change and so reducing the likelihood of breaking production.

Our production config will be entirely managed in code, making it easier to rebuild environments if we need to. Our only manually-created config will be CircleCI envvars.

We will still need to be careful to not commit secrets in unencrypted files in our application repos, or to rename files containing secrets without also updating the corresponding git-crypt config (although pre-commit hooks can help us with this).

We need to remain aware that git-crypt does not fully support removing users who no longer need access, and that in any case secrets should be rotated if possible after someone has left the team.

pros: Reduces risk of secrets exposure in public repos.
cons: Increases likelihood of not updating config when needed, leading to production outages.

No concept of environments in CircleCI envvars; requires namespacing approach.

template_adherence.title: 20. Unify API and Presentation layers
template_adherence.context: Previously, it was decided in ADR 0004 that we would separate data and presentation concerns. This however was reversed by ADR 0010 which meant there was an overlap of data concerns with some data access from the presentation layer, and some via the Allocation API. It was envisioned that starting off with more than one application would mean that we would be able to structure the responsibilities early in the process and reduce later efforts, but in practice this has not happened. With more exposure to some of the APIs we are dependent on which service should access them has become less clear over time. For instance, it was discovered that it was better for the Allocation API to retrieve staff data from Elite2, rather than the presentation layer. There was concern that later migration from a monolith to separate services would be technical debt that we would be unable to pay off in future, due to other competing pressures. The cost of managing two different services, sharing contexts and overlapping boundaries has however increased the development complexity and cognitive load. There was a requirement that other services are likely to require access to the allocation information that we have stored. This made sense when there was a clean separation of concerns (with all data access via the Allocation API) but currently provides little benefit. Whether the API is a separate service or a modular component of a monolith is currently a deployment strategy as architecturally it provides few benefits over a modular application. It is entirely possible to provide an API via a modular monolith. As we have progressed with development, we have encountered issues with our approach of enriching API sourced data with locally acquired data. Processes where we retrieve data, enrich it with data from external APIs and then enrich it with data from local APIs result in the movement of lots of data which has performance costs. template_adherence.title: Event Subscription
template_adherence.context: In the light client (or any other client), the user may want to subscribe to a subset of transactions (rather than all of them) using `/subscribe?event=X`. For example, I want to subscribe for all transactions associated with a particular account. Same for fetching. The user may want to fetch transactions based on some filter (rather than fetching all the blocks). For example, I want to get all transactions for a particular account in the last two weeks (`tx's block time >= '2017-06-05'`). Now you can't even subscribe to "all txs" in Tendermint. The goal is a simple and easy to use API for doing that.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for users to subscribe to a subset of transactions rather than all.
- Desire for a simple and easy to use API.
- Support for filtering and fetching transactions based on queries.
- Performance considerations with many queries/subscribers.
- Compatibility with different indexers for historic queries.
template_adherence.decision: ABCI app returns tags with a `DeliverTx` response inside the `data` field (for now). Tags are a list of key-value pairs, protobuf encoded. These tags are parsed and matched with current queries (subscribers). If the query matches the tags, the subscriber receives the transaction event. A new package will replace the current `events` package to allow clients to subscribe to different types of events. For fetching transactions, an indexing storage (Postgres, SQLite, etc.) will be needed for historic queries.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Same format for event notifications and search APIs.
- Powerful enough query capabilities.

Negative:
- Performance issues with the `match` function when there are too many queries/subscribers.
- Potential issues with too many transactions in the database.

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implied alternatives include not supporting filtered subscriptions or using existing event subscription mechanisms without tags.
pros: Simplicity by not adding new tagging and querying mechanisms.
cons: Lack of flexibility for users to subscribe to subsets of transactions.
Inability to fetch transactions based on filters efficiently.

template_adherence.title: Must an ABCI-app have an RPC server?
template_adherence.context:
ABCI-server could expose its own RPC-server and act as a proxy to Tendermint.

The idea was for the Tendermint RPC to just be a transparent proxy to the app.
Clients need to talk to Tendermint for proofs, unless we burden all app devs

server than two, but granted it makes querying a bit more kludgy since it needs
to be passed as a `Query`. Also, **having a very standard rpc interface means
the light-client can work with all apps and handle proofs**. The only
app-specific logic is decoding the binary data to a more readable form (eg.
json). This is a huge advantage for code-reuse and standardization.

- Desire to avoid burdening app developers with exposing Tendermint proof logic.
- Complexity considerations in managing one server versus two.
- Importance of code reuse and standardization for light-client compatibility.
template_adherence.decision: We dont expose an RPC server on any of our ABCI-apps.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Unified interface for all apps

Negative:
- `Query` interface

Neutral:
- (No content provided)

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Historical Validators
template_adherence.context:
Right now, we can query the present validator set, but there is no history.
If you were offline for a long time, there is no way to reconstruct past validators. This is needed for the light client and we agreed needs enhancement of the API.
template_adherence.decision:
For every block, store a new structure that contains either the latest validator set,
or the height of the last block for which the validator set changed. Note this is not
the height of the block which returned the validator set change itself, but the next block,
ie. the first block it comes into effect for.

Storing the validators will be handled by the `state` package.

At some point in the future, we may consider more efficient storage in the case where the validators
are updated frequently - for instance by only saving the diffs, rather than the whole set.

An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Can query old validator sets, with proof.

### Negative

- Writes an extra structure to disk with every block.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: Keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
pros: Might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed.
cons: More complex.
Likely less efficient.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Consensus Params
template_adherence.context: Consensus critical parameters controlling blockchain capacity have until now been hard coded, loaded from a local config, or neglected. Since they may be need to be different in different networks, and potentially to evolve over time within networks, we seek to initialize them in a genesis file, and expose them through the ABCI. While we have some specific parameters now, like maximum block and transaction size, we expect to have more in the future, such as a period over which evidence is valid, or the frequency of checkpoints.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to have consensus critical parameters configurable per network and evolvable over time; parameters should not be hardcoded or only in local config; parameters must be exposed through ABCI; maintain backward compatibility and sane defaults; allow for future extensibility.
template_adherence.decision: Consensus critical parameters should not be in config.toml but optionally included in genesis.json and loaded into State. Parameters not included get default values; 0 means undefined, -1 means not applicable. Parameters determine block and transaction validity. ConsensusParams struct defined with BlockSize, TxSize, BlockGossip. Parameters can evolve by adding new structs. Certain parameters must be >0 for sanity. ABCI's InitChain and EndBlock extended to handle ConsensusParams appropriately.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Allows specifying alternative capacity limits and consensus parameters without recompiling; parameters can change over time under app control. Negative: More exposed parameters increase complexity; different rules at different blockchain heights complicate fast sync. Neutral: Potential conflicts between TxSize validity checks and config's max_block_size_tx proposal sizes.

alternatives.description: Keep consensus parameters hardcoded or only in local config files.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need to extend genesis or ABCI interfaces.
cons: Parameters cannot vary per network easily.
Cannot evolve parameters over time without software changes.
Less flexibility and adaptability.

alternatives.description: Include all consensus parameters directly in the ABCI InitChain call.
pros: Centralizes all parameters in one place.
Potentially simpler for the application to access all parameters.
cons: May expose parameters that the application shouldn't know about.
Could complicate the ABCI interface.
Less modular and flexible.

template_adherence.title: ADR 006: Trust Metric Design
template_adherence.context: The proposed trust metric will allow Tendermint to maintain local trust rankings for peers it has directly interacted with, which can then be used to implement soft security controls. The calculations were obtained from the TrustGuard project. Background information explains the need for tracking peer trustworthiness to improve security and reliability, and discusses challenges such as strategic oscillation by malicious nodes and the use of fading memories to maintain history data efficiently.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve Tendermint security and reliability by tracking peer behavior over time, the challenge of malicious nodes adapting behavior to circumvent trust metrics, the desire to maintain a history of trust data efficiently, and the requirement to have a flexible and resilient trust metric that can be queried at any time.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a trust metric that counts good and bad events over intervals, calculates a trust value using a PID-controller-like equation combining proportional, integral, and derivative components, and maintains history data using fading memories. A trust metric store will manage trust metrics for peers, saving history data across node executions. An interface is defined for recording events, querying trust values, and managing the metric lifecycle. Configuration options are provided for weights and time intervals.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling non-binary security decisions, providing soft security controls, and useful profiling information. Negative consequences include the requirement to save trust metric history data across node executions. Neutral notes emphasize the need to record both good and bad events.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implied alternatives include not using a trust metric or using simpler metrics without history or PID-like calculations.
pros: Simpler implementation
Less storage overhead
cons: Less resilient to strategic malicious behavior
Less adaptive to recent events
Potentially less accurate trust assessments

template_adherence.title: ADR 009: ABCI UX Improvements
template_adherence.context: The ABCI was first introduced in late 2015 as a generic interface between state machines and their replication engines, designed to be language- and replication-engine-agnostic. It uses Protocol Buffers (proto3) for message types, with a dominant Go implementation. Recent community discussions identified pain points including Amino encoded types, managing validator sets, and protobuf imports.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include improving developer experience by addressing issues with Amino encoding, protobuf imports, validator set management, and compatibility between ABCI and Tendermint headers. Desired qualities include ease of use, cross-language compatibility, performance considerations, and maintenance overhead.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to move away from gogoproto annotations in protobuf files, remove Amino encoding requirements in the short term, and improve Amino for future use. PubKey encoding will use a type string and bytes data without enums or oneof. Addresses computation is simplified. Validator messages include addresses. RequestBeginBlock includes full validator sets with voting info but excludes public keys. ResponseEndBlock includes validator addresses. RequestInitChain and ResponseInitChain are extended to include full genesis info and allow app control over initial validator set and consensus parameters. Headers in ABCI and Tendermint will match exactly.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier development on ABCI and identical serialization of ABCI and Tendermint headers. Negative consequences include maintenance overhead of alternative encoding schemes and performance overhead of passing validator info every block. Neutral consequence is that developers must understand validator addresses.

alternatives.description: Continue using gogoproto with its annotations and dependencies.
pros: Leverages existing gogoproto features improving developer experience.
No immediate need to maintain duplicate protobuf files.
cons: Creates additional dependencies.
Complicates cross-language protobuf compilation.
Reported failures in compiling protobuf types for other languages.

alternatives.description: Keep Amino encoding as required for PubKey and address computations.
pros: Maintains current encoding scheme.
Leverages Amino's design improvements over protobuf.
cons: Frustration due to incompatibility with protobuf.
Adds complexity for developers.
Limits cross-language compatibility.

alternatives.description: Use protobuf oneof or enum for PubKey interface types.
pros: Utilizes protobuf native features for union types.
Potentially clearer type definitions.
cons: Not fitting for PubKey as interface type with unknown implementations.
Reduces flexibility.
Does not align with desired opaque bytes approach.

After nearly 4 years of development, Tendermint has recently undergone multiple security reviews to search for vulnerabilities and to assess the the use and composition of cryptographic primitives. The ADR details the current use of cryptographic primitives such as RIPEMD160 in hash functions, Merkle trees, addresses, and authenticated encryption, and discusses concerns and considerations for changes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for more secure and modern cryptographic primitives, wider adoption and hardware acceleration, concerns about the use of outdated or less widely used algorithms (e.g., RIPEMD160, Salsa20), and the desire to align with cryptographic community standards and best practices.

template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include adoption of more modern and standard cryptographic functions with wider adoption and hardware acceleration. Negative consequences include that the exact authenticated encryption construction is not already provided in a well-used library. Neutral consequences are not specified.

Potential security concerns remain.

alternatives.description: Adopt SHA256 and xChaCha20 with HKDF as decided.
pros: More modern and standard cryptographic functions.

cons: Authenticated encryption construction not provided in a well-used library.
Requires code changes and testing.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: PeerTransport
template_adherence.context: One of the more apparent problems with the current architecture in the p2p package is that there is no clear separation of concerns between different components. Most notably the `Switch` is currently doing physical connection handling. An artifact is the dependency of the Switch on `config.P2PConfig`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate concerns between components, reduce dependencies of Switch on configuration, simplify implementation and testing, and allow pluggable transport implementations.
template_adherence.decision: Transport concerns will be handled by a new component (`PeerTransport`) which will provide Peers at its boundary to the caller. The Switch will use this new component to accept new Peers and dial them based on NetAddress. This removes transport concerns from Switch and its dependency on P2PConfig.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Frees Switch from transport concerns, simpler implementation, pluggable transport implementations, easier testing. Negative: More setup required for tests depending on Switch. Neutral: Multiplexed transport will be the default implementation.

template_adherence.title: ADR 013: Need for symmetric cryptography
template_adherence.context:
We require symmetric ciphers to handle how we encrypt keys in the sdk, and to potentially encrypt `priv_validator.json` in tendermint.

Currently we use AEAD's to support symmetric encryption, which is great since we want data integrity in addition to privacy and authenticity. We don't currently have a scenario where we want to encrypt without data integrity, so it is fine to optimize our code to just use AEAD's. Currently there is not a way to switch out AEAD's easily, this ADR outlines a way to easily swap these out.

How do we encrypt with AEAD's

AEAD's typically require a nonce in addition to the key. For the purposes we require symmetric cryptography for, we need encryption to be stateless. Because of this we use random nonces. (Thus the AEAD must support random nonces)

We currently construct a random nonce, and encrypt the data with it. The returned value is `nonce || encrypted data`. The limitation of this is that does not provide a way to identify which algorithm was used in encryption. Consequently decryption with multiple algoritms is sub-optimal. (You have to try them all)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for symmetric ciphers to encrypt keys and potentially `priv_validator.json`.
- Desire to use AEADs for data integrity, privacy, and authenticity.
- Current lack of easy way to switch AEAD algorithms.
- Requirement for stateless encryption using random nonces.
- Need to identify encryption algorithm in ciphertext to optimize decryption.
- Ease of use for downstream applications.
- Security concerns to prevent malicious modification of AEAD registrations.
template_adherence.decision:
We should create the following two methods in a new `crypto/encoding/symmetric` package:

```golang
func Encrypt(aead cipher.AEAD, plaintext []byte) (ciphertext []byte, err error)
func Decrypt(key []byte, ciphertext []byte) (plaintext []byte, err error)
func Register(aead cipher.AEAD, algo_name string, NewAead func(key []byte) (cipher.Cipher, error)) error
```

This allows specifying the algorithm in encryption but not in decryption, improving ease of use. Encrypt returns `algo_name || nonce || aead_ciphertext` with `algo_name` length-prefixed. A mapping from AEAD type to name is maintained via reflection. Decryption reads `algo_name`, instantiates the AEAD, and decrypts accordingly. Register allows downstream users to add AEADs safely, preventing runtime modification.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Supports new AEADs and simplifies decryption.
- Allows downstream users to add AEADs.

Negative:
- Requires breaking all private keys stored on disk, though recoverable via seed words and upgrade scripts.

Neutral:
- Caller must instantiate AEAD with private key, which enforces awareness of signing algorithm.

alternatives.description: Continue using AEADs without a way to switch or identify algorithms in ciphertext.
pros: Simplicity in current implementation.
No changes to existing code or keys.
cons: Decryption requires trying all algorithms, which is inefficient.
No flexibility to add new AEADs easily.
No way to identify which algorithm was used in encryption.

alternatives.description: Use a different encryption scheme that does not require AEAD or random nonces.
pros: Potentially simpler nonce management.
Might avoid some complexity with AEADs.
cons: Loses benefits of AEAD like data integrity and authenticity.
May not meet security requirements.
Requires significant redesign.

template_adherence.title: Secp256k1 Signature Malleability
template_adherence.context:
Secp256k1 has two layers of malleability. The signer has a random nonce, and thus can produce many different valid signatures. This ADR is not concerned with that. The second layer of malleability basically allows one who is given a signature to produce exactly one more valid signature for the same message from the same public key. (They don't even have to know the message!) The math behind this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Note that in many downstream applications, signatures will appear in a transaction, and therefore in the tx hash. This means that if someone broadcasts a transaction with secp256k1 signature, the signature can be altered into the other form by anyone in the p2p network. Thus the tx hash will change, and this altered tx hash may be committed instead. This breaks the assumption that you can broadcast a valid transaction and just wait for its hash to be included on chain. One example is if you are broadcasting a tx in cosmos, and you wait for it to appear on chain before incrementing your sequence number. You may never increment your sequence number if a different tx hash got committed. Removing this second layer of signature malleability concerns could ease downstream development.

### ECDSA context

Secp256k1 is ECDSA over a particular curve. The signature is of the form `(r, s)`, where `s` is a field element. (The particular field is the `Z_n`, where the elliptic curve has order `n`) However `(r, -s)` is also another valid solution. Note that anyone can negate a group element, and therefore can get this second signature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to remove the second layer of signature malleability to ease downstream development.
- Desire to maintain the ability to expect a transaction hash to appear in the blockchain.
- Simplicity and ease of checking the canonical form.
- Alignment with existing solutions such as Ethereum's approach.
- Consideration of implementation effort and maintenance overhead.
template_adherence.decision:
We can just distinguish a canonical form for the ECDSA signatures. Then we require that all ECDSA signatures be in the form which we defined as canonical. We reject signatures in non-canonical form.

A canonical form is rather easy to define and check. It would just be the smaller of the two values for `s`, defined lexicographically. This is a simple check, instead of checking if `s < n`, instead check `s <= (n - 1)/2`. An example of another cryptosystem using this is the parity definition here https://github.com/zkcrypto/pairing/pull/30#issuecomment-372910663.

This is the same solution Ethereum has chosen for solving secp malleability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Lets us maintain the ability to expect a tx hash to appear in the blockchain.

Negative:
- More work in all future implementations (Though this is a very simple check)
- Requires us to maintain another fork

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated)

template_adherence.title: Protocol Versions ADR 016
template_adherence.context: The ADR focuses on software-agnostic protocol versions, distinguishing them from software versions (covered by SemVer). It addresses the need to version components of the blockchain that may be independently upgraded, such as BlockVersion, P2PVersion, and AppVersion, to facilitate upgrades and compatibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for scalable and maintainable versioning of blockchain components, the ability to support independent upgrades of BlockVersion, P2PVersion, and AppVersion, compatibility with older versions for syncing, clear communication of versions through ABCI, and minimizing complexity in supporting multiple versions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to represent each of BlockVersion, AppVersion, and P2PVersion as monotonically increasing uint64 values included in key data structures: the block Header, NodeInfo, and ABCI messages. The Header includes a Version struct with Block and App versions; NodeInfo includes P2P, Block, and App versions; and ABCI messages (Info and EndBlock) are extended to communicate version information. Peer compatibility is currently unrestricted by version, relying on ChainID, with future plans for more restrictive rules.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clearer communication of versions, distinction between protocol and software versions, and inclusion of versions in key data structures. Neutral consequences include unresolved versioning of the initial P2P handshake and lack of current use of versions for peer compatibility restrictions. Negative consequences include added fields to ABCI and the implication that a single codebase must handle multiple versions.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated as alternatives, but the ADR mentions considerations such as restricting peer compatibility based on versions, using tags for version updates in ABCI, and different ways to version the authenticated encryption handshake.
pros: Allows gradual upgrades and compatibility with older versions.
Clear separation of versioning concerns (Block, P2P, App).
cons: Adds complexity to ABCI and data structures.
Does not currently restrict peer compatibility by version, which may cause issues.

template_adherence.title: ADR 018: ABCI Validator Improvements
template_adherence.context: ADR 009 introduced major improvements to the ABCI around validators and the use of Amino. Here we follow up with some additional changes to improve the naming and expected use of Validator messages.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to clarify the distinction between different uses of validator information, optimize message contents by separating Validator and ValidatorUpdate, and reduce unnecessary data transmission (e.g., large quantum public keys) over ABCI.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to separate the Validator message into two distinct messages: Validator (containing just the address and power) used for RequestBeginBlock, and ValidatorUpdate (containing pubkey and power) used for ResponseEndBlock and InitChain. Additionally, rename SigningValidator to VoteInfo in LastCommitInfo to better reflect its purpose. This approach reduces data redundancy and clarifies message semantics.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Clarifies the distinction between different uses of validator information.
Negative: Applications must still store public keys in state to utilize RequestBeginBlock info.
Neutral: ResponseEndBlock does not require an address.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing Validator message containing both address and pub_key, sending one or the other optionally depending on use case.
pros: Simplicity in having a single Validator message type.
No need to change existing message structures significantly.
cons: Inefficient data transmission as large pubkeys are sent unnecessarily.
Confusing semantics as one or the other field is optional depending on context.

alternatives.description: Require Validator message to always contain both address and pub_key.
pros: Clear and consistent Validator message structure.
No ambiguity about presence of fields.
cons: Inefficient due to large pubkeys being sent with every block.
Increased bandwidth and processing overhead.

template_adherence.title: Limiting txs size inside a block
template_adherence.context: We currently use MaxTxs to reap txs from the mempool when proposing a block, but enforce MaxBytes when unmarshaling a block, so we could easily propose a block thats too large to be valid. We should just remove MaxTxs all together and stick with MaxBytes, and have a `mempool.ReapMaxBytes`. But we can't just reap BlockSize.MaxBytes, since MaxBytes is for the entire block, not for the txs inside the block. There's extra amino overhead + the actual headers on top of the actual transactions + evidence + last commit. We could also consider using a MaxDataBytes instead of or in addition to MaxBytes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid proposing blocks that are too large to be valid.
- Desire to simplify configuration by removing MaxTxs.
- Need to account for overhead beyond just transaction bytes (headers, evidence, last commit).
- Consideration of MaxBytes vs MaxDataBytes for bounding block size.
- Maintainability concerns regarding constants if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove MaxTxs entirely and rely on MaxBytes as the main limit for block size. MaxTxsBytes is renamed to MaxBytes. When reaping transactions from the mempool, the upper bound is calculated by subtracting known overheads (amino overhead, last commit bytes, evidence bytes, header bytes) from MaxBytes. Constants for overhead sizes are defined and used in the calculation. ChainID length is bounded to 50 symbols. A test should be written to ensure constants remain accurate if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a clear and singular way to limit block size.
- Reduces the number of configuration variables.
Negative:
- Requires maintenance of constants that represent overhead sizes; these must be updated if underlying data structures change.
Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Keep using MaxTxs and MaxBytes separately, with MaxTxs limiting the number of transactions and MaxBytes limiting the block size during unmarshaling.
pros: Allows separate control over transaction count and block size.
May be simpler to reason about transaction limits.
cons: Can lead to proposing blocks that are too large to be valid.
More configuration variables to manage.
Complexity in ensuring consistency between MaxTxs and MaxBytes.

alternatives.description: Use both MaxBytes and MaxDataBytes to separately limit total block size and transaction data size.
pros: More fine-grained control over block size components.
Can optimize resource usage more precisely.
cons: Adds complexity with two size limits to manage.
Requires additional calculations and understanding.
Potential confusion about which limit applies when.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: ABCI Events
template_adherence.context: ABCI tags were first described in ADR 002. They are key-value pairs used to index transactions. Currently, ABCI messages return a list of tags describing an event during Check/DeliverTx/Begin/EndBlock, with each tag referring to a property of the event. Since there is only one list of tags, recording data for multiple events in a single message must be done using prefixes in the key space. Alternatively, groups of tags can be separated by a special tag to denote breaks between events, allowing encoding of multiple events without prefixing, at the cost of special tags.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to represent multiple distinct events within a single ABCI message and improve the clarity and structure of event tagging and indexing.
template_adherence.decision: Instead of returning a list of tags, return a list of events, where each event is a list of tags, naturally capturing multiple events during a single ABCI message.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to track distinct events separate from ABCI calls and more powerful query abilities. Negative consequences include more complex query syntax and more complex search implementation. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using a single list of tags with prefixes to distinguish multiple events.
pros: Simple to implement with existing system.
No change to current indexing and querying mechanisms.
cons: Requires prefixing keys which can be error-prone and less clear.
Does not naturally represent multiple distinct events.

alternatives.description: Use special tags to separate groups of tags constituting different events within a single list.
pros: Allows encoding multiple events without prefixing.
Somewhat clearer separation of events than prefixing.
cons: Requires special tags which add complexity.
Less natural representation compared to a list of events.
May complicate indexing and querying.

template_adherence.title: ADR 024: SignBytes and validator types in privval
template_adherence.context: Currently, the messages exchanged between tendermint and a (potentially remote) signer/validator, namely votes, proposals, and heartbeats, are encoded as a JSON string and then signed. JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and ethereum smart contracts. There are no differences between sign-request and -replies, and no possibility for a remote signer to include error codes or messages. The messages currently live in privval/socket.go and encapsulate corresponding types in types.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a binary encoding format easily parseable by hardware devices and smart contracts; need to separate sign-requests and responses; need to include error types in responses; compatibility with existing code and interfaces.
template_adherence.decision: Restructure vote, proposal, and heartbeat encoding to use a binary format (amino); split messages into requests and responses; include error types in responses; keep SignBytes interface without ChainID parameter; explore design alternatives for signature inclusion; further thoughts needed for PubKey handling.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: easier parsing by hardware and smart contracts, clearer request/response separation, better error handling. Negative: large refactoring, changes to interfaces expecting Vote with signature. Neutral: none noted.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSON encoding for messages exchanged between tendermint and remote signers.
pros: No changes required to existing codebase.
Maintains current compatibility with existing hardware wallets and smart contracts.
cons: JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and smart contracts.
No separation between sign-requests and replies.
No error codes/messages in responses.

alternatives.description: Use a different binary encoding format other than amino for message encoding.
pros: Potentially better performance or features depending on chosen format.

template_adherence.title: Commit structure optimization by introducing CommitSig to deduplicate data
template_adherence.context: Currently the Commit structure contains a lot of potentially redundant or unnecessary data. It contains a list of precommits from every validator, where the precommit includes the whole Vote structure. Thus each of the commit height, round, type, and blockID are repeated for every validator, and could be deduplicated, leading to very significant savings in block size. The original tracking issue is #1648. There are concerns about what should be included in the new CommitSig type, including timestamp, validator address, absent votes, and handling other block IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce block size by deduplicating repeated data in Commit precommits, maintain necessary information for BFT time calculation, ergonomic and debugging advantages of including validator address, handling absent votes properly for serialization, and protocol correctness regarding block IDs in commits.
template_adherence.decision: Deduplicate the fields by introducing a new CommitSig type that replaces Vote in Commit.Precommits. CommitSig includes BlockIDFlag, ValidatorAddress, Timestamp, and Signature. Timestamp is kept for now to maintain BFT time calculation. ValidatorAddress is included for ergonomic and debugging benefits despite increasing block size. Absent votes are explicitly included with no signature or timestamp but with validator address. Only three BlockIDFlag values are allowed (Absent, Commit, Nil), disallowing other block IDs in commits. Future changes may reconsider these decisions.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Significant block size savings (up to 8kB per block for 100 validators) by removing redundant fields. Negative: Large breaking change to block and commit structure; added complexity in code to differentiate Vote and CommitSig objects. Neutral: Commit.Precommits no longer contains nil values, improving serialization.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing Commit structure with Vote objects for each precommit without deduplication.
pros: No breaking changes to block and commit structure.
No added complexity in code to differentiate Vote and CommitSig.
cons: Large block size due to repeated data.
Inefficient serialization and bandwidth usage.

alternatives.description: Remove timestamp from CommitSig to further reduce size and switch to proposer based time for BFT time calculation.
pros: Further reduction in block size.
Simplifies CommitSig structure.
cons: Requires more analysis and work.
Potentially breaks BFT time calculation assumptions.
Deferred to future breaking change.

alternatives.description: Exclude ValidatorAddress from CommitSig to reduce block size.
pros: Reduces block size by 20 bytes per validator.
Simplifies CommitSig.
cons: Loses ergonomic and debugging advantages.
Lite clients cannot verify validators without downloading validator set.
Commit cannot reconstruct []Vote without external data.

template_adherence.title: ADR 026: General Merkle Proof
template_adherence.context:
We are using raw `[]byte` for merkle proofs in `abci.ResponseQuery`. It makes hard to handle multilayer merkle proofs and general cases. Here, new interface `ProofOperator` is defined. The users can defines their own Merkle proof format and layer them easily.

Goals:
- Layer Merkle proofs without decoding/reencoding
- Provide general way to chain proofs
- Make the proof format extensible, allowing thirdparty proof types
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle multilayer Merkle proofs and general cases more easily, to layer proofs without decoding/reencoding, to provide a general way to chain proofs, and to make the proof format extensible for thirdparty proof types.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to define a new interface `ProofOperator` for Merkle proofs, allowing users to define their own Merkle proof format and layer them easily. The interface and related protobuf message `ProofOp` are introduced to support this extensibility and layering.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include easier layering without encoding/decoding at each step and availability of thirdparty proof formats. Negative consequences include larger size for abci.ResponseQuery, unintuitive proof chaining (unclear what `Run()` does), and additional code for registering `OpDecoder`s.

alternatives.description: Continue using raw `[]byte` for Merkle proofs in `abci.ResponseQuery` without introducing the `ProofOperator` interface.
pros: No changes to existing codebase.
Simplicity in current implementation.
cons: Hard to handle multilayer Merkle proofs and general cases.
No extensibility for thirdparty proof types.
Requires decoding/reencoding at each step, which is inefficient.

alternatives.description: Use a fixed, non-extensible Merkle proof format with explicit layering support.
pros: Clear proof format and chaining semantics.
Potentially simpler implementation than fully extensible interface.
cons: Less flexible, cannot easily support thirdparty proof types.
May require more complex encoding/decoding logic.
Less adaptable to future proof types.

template_adherence.title: ADR 029: Check block txs before prevote
template_adherence.context:
We currently check a tx's validity through 2 ways.

1. Through checkTx in mempool connection.
2. Through deliverTx in consensus connection.

The 1st is called when external tx comes in, so the node should be a proposer this time. The 2nd is called when external block comes in and reach the commit phase, the node doesn't need to be the proposer of the block, however it should check the txs in that block.

In the 2nd situation, if there are many invalid txs in the block, it would be too late for all nodes to discover that most txs in the block are invalid, and we'd better not record invalid txs in the blockchain too.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to validate transactions earlier in the consensus process to avoid committing invalid transactions.
- Desire to prevent blocks full of invalid transactions from being proposed and committed.
- Performance concerns about adding additional validation steps.
- Impact on application interface and logic due to new method requirements.
- Potential redundancy in validation steps and increased network load.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to reject the proposed solution of adding a CheckBlock method to the application interface to validate all transactions before prevote, due to the performance impact being too great. This is supported by the linked issue #2384.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- More robust defense against adversaries proposing blocks full of invalid transactions.

Negative:
- Requires adding a new interface method, necessitating changes in application logic.
- Increases network load by sending all transaction data twice over ABCI.
- Potentially redundant validations, such as signature checks in both CheckBlock and DeliverTx.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Implement the CheckBlock method in the application interface to validate all transactions in a block before sending a prevote.
pros: Allows early detection of invalid transactions in a block before consensus prevote phase.
Prevents committing blocks with many invalid transactions.
Improves robustness against adversarial block proposals.
cons: Adds a new interface method, requiring application logic changes.
Increases network traffic by sending transaction data twice over ABCI.
May cause redundant validations, impacting performance.

template_adherence.title: ADR 030: Consensus Refactor
template_adherence.context:
One of the biggest challenges this project faces is to proof that the implementations of the specifications are correct, much like we strive to formaly verify our alogrithms and protocols we should work towards high confidence about the correctness of our program code. One of those is the core of Tendermint - Consensus - which currently resides in the `consensus` package. Over time there has been high friction making changes to the package due to the algorithm being scattered in a side-effectful container (the current `ConsensusState`). In order to test the algorithm a large object-graph needs to be set up and even than the non-deterministic parts of the container makes will prevent high certainty. Where ideally we have a 1-to-1 representation of the [spec](https://github.com/tendermint/spec), ready and easy to test for domain experts.

Addresses:

- [#1495](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1495)
- [#1692](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1692)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to increase confidence in correctness of the consensus algorithm implementation.
- Current implementation is scattered and side-effectful, making testing and reasoning difficult.
- Desire for a 1-to-1 representation of the specification for easier testing and verification.
- Need to improve separation of concerns and testability.
- Minimize invasive changes to existing codebase initially.
template_adherence.decision: To remedy these issues we plan a gradual, non-invasive refactoring of the `consensus` package. Starting off by isolating the consensus algorithm into a pure function and a finite state machine to address the most pressuring issue of lack of confidence. Doing so while leaving the rest of the package intact and have follow-up optional changes to improve the separation of concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Isolated implementation of the algorithm.
- Improved testability - simpler to prove correctness.
- Clearer separation of concerns - easier to reason.

Negative:
- None explicitly stated.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Keep the current implementation without refactoring.
pros: No immediate development effort required.
No risk of introducing new bugs due to refactoring.
cons: Continued difficulty in testing and reasoning about the consensus algorithm.
High friction in making changes to the consensus package.
Low confidence in correctness of implementation.

alternatives.description: Rewrite the consensus package entirely from scratch.
pros: Opportunity to design a clean, well-structured implementation from the ground up.
Potentially better long-term maintainability.
cons: High development effort and risk.
Potentially disruptive to existing codebase and users.
Longer time before benefits are realized.
