template_adherence.title: ADR 033: pubsub 2.0
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses issues with the initial pubsub design, including problems with synchronous vs asynchronous message publishing, blocking vs non-blocking sends, and the choice between channels and callbacks for message transmission. It highlights the need for strict ordering of events and addresses the "slow client problem" where slow subscribers can block the system.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include ensuring strict ordering of events, avoiding deadlocks caused by slow subscribers, providing subscribers with information about message tags, and improving the interface to be more idiomatic and informative about subscription cancellation reasons.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a MsgAndTags struct for messages, change Subscribe() to return a Subscription struct with methods Out(), Canceled(), and Err(), make Out() channel buffered by default with capacity 1, provide a separate SubscribeUnbuffered() function for unbuffered channels, and treat buffered and unbuffered channels differently in the publisher to avoid blocking on buffered channels. Slow subscribers on buffered channels are terminated to prevent blocking.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a more idiomatic interface, subscribers knowing message tags, and awareness of subscription cancellation reasons. Negative consequences include no concurrency in publishing messages since version 1. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use synchronous publishing with goroutines per subscriber or per message.
pros: Allows concurrency in message publishing.
Avoids slow client problem by using goroutines.
cons: Difficult to maintain strict ordering of events.
Potential uncontrolled memory growth due to many goroutines.
Complex implementation and unclear benefits.

alternatives.description: Use non-blocking sends with select default case to avoid blocking on slow subscribers.
pros: Prevents system from halting due to slow or unresponsive clients.
Simplifies handling of slow clients.
cons: Slow clients may miss messages without notification.
Requires developers to ensure subscriber handling code does not block, which is difficult.

alternatives.description: Use callback functions instead of channels for message transmission.
pros: Gives subscribers more flexibility in handling messages.
Allows use of mutexes, channels, goroutines as needed.
cons: Callbacks carry local scope, which can cause memory leaks or increased memory usage.
Less idiomatic in Go compared to channels.

template_adherence.title: ADR 034: PrivValidator file structure
template_adherence.context:
For now, the PrivValidator file `priv_validator.json` contains mutable and immutable parts. Even in an insecure mode which does not encrypt private key on disk, it is reasonable to separate the mutable part and immutable part.

References:
[#1181](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1181)
[#2657](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2657)
[#2313](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2313)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate mutable and immutable parts of the PrivValidator file to improve structure and security, and to specify file paths in configuration.
template_adherence.decision: Split the PrivValidator file into two structs representing mutable and immutable parts (`FilePVKey` and `FilePVLastSignState`), then combine them into `FilePV`. Store `FilePV` in `config` and `FilePVLastSignState` in `data`, with file paths specified in `config.yml`.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Separation of mutable and immutable parts of PrivValidator.
Negative:
- Additional configuration needed for file paths.
Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Keep the PrivValidator file as a single structure without separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Simpler file structure.
No need to change existing methods or add configuration.
cons: Less clear separation of concerns.
Potential security and maintainability issues.

alternatives.description: Encrypt the private key on disk instead of separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Improves security by encrypting sensitive data.
cons: Does not address separation of mutable and immutable data.
May add complexity in encryption management.

template_adherence.title: ADR 039: Peer Behaviour Interface
template_adherence.context: The responsibility for signaling and acting upon peer behaviour lacks a single owning component and is heavily coupled with the network stack. Reactors maintain a reference to the `p2p.Switch` which they use to call `switch.StopPeerForError(...)` when a peer misbehaves and `switch.MarkAsGood(...)` when a peer contributes in some meaningful way. While the switch handles `StopPeerForError` internally, the `MarkAsGood` method delegates to another component, `p2p.AddrBook`. This scheme of delegation across Switch obscures the responsibility for handling peer behaviour and ties up the reactors in a larger dependency graph when testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decouple signaling peer behaviour from acting upon it.
- Reduce coupling between reactors and the network stack.
- Improve testability by reducing dependencies.
- Centralize responsibility for managing peer behaviour.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a `PeerBehaviour` interface and concrete implementations which provide methods for reactors to signal peer behaviour without direct coupling to `p2p.Switch`. Introduce `ErrorBehaviourPeer` and `GoodBehaviourPeer` types to provide concrete reasons for stopping peers and ways peers contribute, respectively. Provide a concrete implementation wrapping the switch and another for testing purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Decouples signaling from acting upon peer behaviour.
- Reduces coupling of reactors and the Switch and the network stack.
- Centralizes responsibility for managing peer behaviour.

Negative:
- Initial iteration adds a level of indirection by wrapping the Switch.

Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing approach where reactors directly call methods on `p2p.Switch` and `p2p.AddrBook` to signal peer behaviour.
pros: No additional abstraction or interface needed.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: High coupling between reactors and network stack.
Responsibility for peer behaviour is split and unclear.
Difficult to unit test reactors due to dependencies.

alternatives.description: Introduce a monolithic component that handles all peer behaviour without interfaces, tightly integrated with the network stack.
pros: Centralizes peer behaviour management.
Potentially simpler implementation without interfaces.
cons: Tight coupling with network stack remains.
Less flexible and harder to mock or replace in tests.
Violates separation of concerns.

template_adherence.title: ADR 044: Lite Client with Weak Subjectivity
template_adherence.context:
The concept of light clients was introduced in the Bitcoin white paper. It describes a watcher of distributed consensus process that only validates the consensus algorithm and not the state machine transactions within.

Tendermint light clients allow bandwidth & compute-constrained devices, such as smartphones, low-power embedded chips, or other blockchains to efficiently verify the consensus of a Tendermint blockchain. This forms the basis of safe and efficient state synchronization for new network nodes and inter-blockchain communication (where a light client of one Tendermint instance runs in another chain's state machine).

In a network that is expected to reliably punish validators for misbehavior by slashing bonded stake and where the validator set changes infrequently, clients can take advantage of this assumption to safely synchronize a lite client without downloading the intervening headers.

Light clients (and full nodes) operating in the Proof Of Stake context need a trusted block height from a trusted source that is no older than 1 unbonding window plus a configurable evidence submission synchrony bound. This is called “weak subjectivity”.

Weak subjectivity is required in Proof of Stake blockchains because it is costless for an attacker to buy up voting keys that are no longer bonded and fork the network at some point in its prior history. See Vitalik’s post at Proof of Stake: How I Learned to Love Weak Subjectivity.

Currently, Tendermint provides a lite client implementation in the light package. This lite client implements a bisection algorithm that tries to use a binary search to find the minimum number of block headers where the validator set voting power changes are less than < 1/3rd. This interface does not support weak subjectivity at this time. The Cosmos SDK also does not support counterfactual slashing, nor does the lite client have any capacity to report evidence making these systems theoretically unsafe.

NOTE: Tendermint provides a somewhat different (stronger) light client model than Bitcoin under eclipse, since the eclipsing node(s) can only fool the light client if they have two-thirds of the private keys from the last root-of-trust.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support light clients in a Proof of Stake blockchain context with weak subjectivity.
- Desire to allow bandwidth and compute-constrained devices to verify consensus efficiently.
- Requirement to safely synchronize light clients without downloading all headers.
- Need to handle clients that have been offline longer than the unbonding period.
- Desire to implement a safe and efficient verification algorithm (linear and bisecting).
- Need to provide a trust interface for initializing light clients.
- Consideration of user experience and trust sources.
- Handling of forged headers and evidence submission.
- Balancing complexity and safety in the verification algorithms.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to add a weak subjectivity interface for new or offline light clients, requiring initialization of a TrustOptions structure with trust period, trust height, and trust hash or a callback for confirmation.

Implement two verification algorithms:
- Linear Verification: download all headers between TrustHeight and LatestHeight and verify each.
- Bisecting Verification: a more bandwidth and compute efficient method using a bisection algorithm to verify headers recursively, minimizing downloads.

The client should submit evidence of misbehavior if forged headers are encountered and retry verification with other full nodes.

This approach balances safety, efficiency, and usability for light clients in Tendermint.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a safe light client that can go offline but not for too long.

Negative:
- Adds complexity due to the bisection verification algorithm.

Neutral:
- Social consensus can be prone to errors when new light clients join or have been offline for too long.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing light client implementation without weak subjectivity support.
pros: Simplicity: no additional complexity added to the current system.
No changes required to existing clients or protocols.
cons: The system remains theoretically unsafe due to lack of weak subjectivity.
Cannot safely handle clients that have been offline for long periods.
No mechanism to report evidence of misbehavior.

alternatives.description: Implement only linear verification without bisecting verification.
pros: Simpler implementation compared to bisecting verification.

alternatives.description: Develop a stronger light client model similar to Bitcoin's under eclipse attack assumptions.
pros: Potentially stronger security guarantees under eclipse attacks.
May provide better protection against certain attack vectors.
cons: More complex to implement and understand.

Not aligned with Tendermint's current consensus and trust assumptions.

template_adherence.title: ABCI Evidence Handling
template_adherence.context:
Evidence is a distinct component in a Tendermint block and has its own reactor for high priority gossipping. Currently, Tendermint supports only a single form of evidence, an explicit equivocation, where a validator signs conflicting blocks at the same height/round. It is detected in real-time in the consensus reactor, and gossiped through the evidence reactor. Evidence can also be submitted through the RPC.

Currently, Tendermint does not gracefully handle a fork on the main chain. If a fork is detected, the node panics. At this point manual intervention and social consensus are required to reconfigure. We'd like to do something more graceful here, but that's for another day.

It's possible to fool lite clients without there being a fork on the main chain - so called Fork-Lite. See the fork accountability document for more details. For a sequential lite client, this can happen via equivocation or amnesia attacks. For a skipping lite client this can also happen via lunatic validator attacks. There must be some way for applications to punish all forms of misbehaviour.

The essential question is whether Tendermint should manage the evidence verification, or whether it should treat evidence more like a transaction (ie. arbitrary bytes) and let the application handle it (including all the signature checking).

Currently, evidence verification is handled by Tendermint. Once committed, evidence is passed over ABCI in BeginBlock in a reduced form that includes only the type of evidence, its height and timestamp, the validator it's from, and the total voting power of the validator set at the height. The app trusts Tendermint to perform the evidence verification, as the ABCI evidence does not contain the signatures and additional data for the app to verify itself.

Arguments in favor of leaving evidence handling in Tendermint:
1) Attacks on full nodes must be detectable by full nodes in real time, ie. within the consensus reactor. So at the very least, any evidence involved in something that could fool a full node must be handled natively by Tendermint as there would otherwise be no way for the ABCI app to detect it (ie. we don't send all votes we receive during consensus to the app ... ).
2) Amensia attacks can not be easily detected - they require an interactive protocol among all the validators to submit justification for their past votes. Our best notion of how to do this currently is via a centralized monitor service that is trusted for liveness to aggregate data from current and past validators, but which produces a proof of misbehaviour (ie. via amnesia) that can be verified by anyone, including the blockchain. Validators must submit all the votes they saw for the relevant consensus height to justify their precommits. This is quite specific to the Tendermint protocol and may change if the protocol is upgraded. Hence it would be awkward to co-ordinate this from the app.
3) Evidence gossipping is similar to tx gossipping, but it should be higher priority. Since the mempool does not support any notion of priority yet, evidence is gossipped through a distinct Evidence reactor. If we just treated evidence like any other transaction, leaving it entirely to the application, Tendermint would have no way to know how to prioritize it, unless/until we significantly upgrade the mempool. Thus we would need to continue to treat evidence distinctly and update the ABCI to either support sending Evidence through CheckTx/DeliverTx, or to introduce new CheckEvidence/DeliverEvidence methods. In either case we'd need to make more changes to ABCI then if Tendermint handled things and we just added support for another evidence type that could be included in BeginBlock.
4) All ABCI application frameworks will benefit from most of the heavy lifting being handled by Tendermint, rather than each of them needing to re-implement all the evidence verification logic in each language.

Arguments in favor of moving evidence handling to the application:
5) Skipping lite clients require us to track the set of all validators that were bonded over some period in case validators that are unbonding but still slashable sign invalid headers to fool lite clients. The Cosmos-SDK staking/slashing modules track this, as it's used for slashing. Tendermint does not currently track this, though it does keep track of the validator set at every height. This leans in favour of managing evidence in the app to avoid redundantly managing the historical validator set data in Tendermint
6) Applications supporting cross-chain validation will be required to process evidence from other chains. This data will come in the form of a transaction, but it means the app will be required to have all the functionality to process evidence, even if the evidence for its own chain is handled directly by Tendermint.
7) Evidence from lite clients may be large and constitute some form of DoS vector against full nodes. Putting it in transactions allows it to engage the application's fee mechanism to pay for cost of executions in the event the evidence is false. This means the evidence submitter must be able to afford the fees for the submission, but of course it should be refunded if the evidence is valid. That said, the burden is mostly on full nodes, which don't necessarily benefit from fees.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for real-time detection of attacks on full nodes, the complexity of detecting amnesia attacks requiring interactive protocols, the priority handling of evidence gossiping, the benefit of centralized evidence verification logic in Tendermint, the need to track historical validator sets for skipping lite clients, cross-chain validation requirements, and concerns about denial of service (DoS) vectors from large evidence submissions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is that evidence detection belongs in Tendermint. Arguments (5) and (6) do not impose large obligations on Tendermint and can be handled by the app using Tendermint libraries. Although (7) raises concerns about DoS attacks, these can be mitigated out of band, for example by full nodes offering light client services via payment channels or banning client IPs sending bad data. The burden is on the client to send large amounts of data. A separate ADR will describe how Tendermint will handle new forms of evidence, including monitoring protocols, tracking past validators, and managing DoS issues.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- No real changes to ABCI
- Tendermint handles evidence for all apps

Neutral:
- Need to be careful about denial of service on the Tendermint RPC

Negative:
- Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period

pros: Attacks on full nodes can be detected in real time within the consensus reactor.
Amnesia attacks detection is tightly integrated with Tendermint's protocol specifics.

cons: Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period.

alternatives.description: Move evidence handling to the application, treating evidence as arbitrary bytes and letting the application handle verification and processing.

template_adherence.title: Lite Client Implementation
template_adherence.context: A `Client` struct represents a light client, connected to a single blockchain. The user has an option to verify headers using `VerifyHeader` or `VerifyHeaderAtHeight` or `Update` methods. The light client can be created from scratch or from a trusted store. The light client uses a bisection algorithm for header verification and interacts with providers and a trusted store. The `Verify` function is exposed for header verification, handling both adjacent and non-adjacent headers. A non-recursive bisection algorithm was chosen for constant memory consumption and faster finality.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Security by default (requiring at least one witness), performance considerations (non-recursive bisection algorithm), flexibility in interfaces for providers and storage, and alignment with the Tendermint specification.

template_adherence.title: ADR 50: Improved Trusted Peering
template_adherence.context:
When `max-num-inbound-peers` or `max-num-outbound-peers` of a node is reached, the node cannot spare more slots to any peer by inbound or outbound. Therefore, after a certain period of disconnection, any important peering can be lost indefinitely because all slots are consumed by other peers, and the node stops trying to dial the peer anymore.

This is happening because of two reasons, exponential backoff and absence of unconditional peering feature for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain stable and persistent peering connections despite limits on inbound and outbound peer slots, and to overcome issues caused by exponential backoff and lack of unconditional peering for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce two new parameters in `config.toml`: `unconditional-peer-ids` to allow certain peers to connect regardless of peer limits, and `persistent-peers-max-dial-period` to limit the maximum dial period during exponential backoff for persistent peers. This approach was chosen over modifying existing persistent-peers due to complexity and to cover both inbound and outbound connections.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Allows node operators to ensure stable connections with trusted peers by configuring new parameters, leading to more persistent peering.

Negative: Introduces two new configuration parameters that require explanation and understanding by node operators.

Neutral: None specified.

alternatives.description: Use only the existing `persistent-peers` parameter and handle id-only items as unconditional peers.
pros: Reuses existing configuration structure without adding new parameters.
cons: Requires complicated structural exceptions due to different item structures.
Does not cover inbound connections, limiting utility.

template_adherence.title: ADR 051: Double Signing Risk Reduction
template_adherence.context:
To provide a risk reduction method for double signing incidents mistakenly executed by validators
- Validators often mistakenly run duplicated validators to cause double-signing incident
- This proposed feature is to reduce the risk of mistaken double-signing incident by checking recent N blocks before voting begins
- When we think of such serious impact on double-signing incident, it is very reasonable to have multiple risk reduction algorithm built in node daemon
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce risk of double signing incidents caused by validator mistakes
- Validators mistakenly running duplicated validators causing double-signing
- Serious impact of double-signing incidents requires robust risk reduction
- Desire to have multiple risk reduction algorithms built into the node daemon
template_adherence.decision: We would like to suggest a double signing risk reduction method. - Methodology : query recent consensus results to find out whether node's consensus key is used on consensus recently or not - When to check - When the state machine starts `ConsensusReactor` after fully synced - When the node is validator ( with privValidator ) - When `cs.config.DoubleSignCheckHeight > 0` - How to check 1. When a validator is transformed from syncing status to fully synced status, the state machine check recent N blocks (`latest_height - double_sign_check_height`) to find out whether there exists consensus votes using the validator's consensus key 2. If there exists votes from the validator's consensus key, exit state machine program - Configuration - We would like to suggest by introducing `double_sign_check_height` parameter in `config.toml` and cli, how many blocks state machine looks back to check votes - `double_sign_check_height = {{ .Consensus.DoubleSignCheckHeight }}` in `config.toml` - `tendermint node --consensus.double_sign_check_height` in cli - State machine ignore checking procedure when `double_sign_check_height == 0`
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Validators can avoid double signing incident by mistakes. (eg. If another validator node is voting on consensus, starting new validator node with same consensus key will cause panic stop of the state machine because consensus votes with the consensus key are found in recent blocks)
- We expect this method will prevent majority of double signing incident by mistakes.

### Negative

- When the risk reduction method is on, restarting a validator node will panic because the node itself voted on consensus with the same consensus key. So, validators should stop the state machine, wait for some blocks, and then restart the state machine to avoid panic stop.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: Separate the ADR into two ADRs: one for Double Signing Protection and another for Tendermint Mode, as indicated in the changelog.
pros: Clear separation of concerns between different features.
Easier to manage and understand each ADR individually.
cons: May cause fragmentation of related decisions.
Requires cross-referencing between ADRs.

alternatives.description: Not implementing any double signing risk reduction method and relying on existing mechanisms.
pros: Simpler system without added complexity.
No risk of panic stops due to the new check.
cons: Higher risk of double signing incidents due to validator mistakes.
Potentially serious impact on network consensus and security.

template_adherence.title: ADR 052: Tendermint Mode
template_adherence.context:
- Full mode: full mode does not have the capability to become a validator.
- Validator mode : this mode is exactly same as existing state machine behavior. sync without voting on consensus, and participate consensus when fully synced
- Seed mode : lightweight seed node maintaining an address book, p2p like TenderSeed
template_adherence.decision:
We would like to suggest a simple Tendermint mode abstraction. These modes will live under one binary, and when initializing a node the user will be able to specify which node they would like to create.

- Which reactor, component to include for each node
- full
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- *~~no privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)~~*
- validator
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- with privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)
- seed
- switch, transport
- reactor
- p2p/pex
- Configuration, cli command
- We would like to suggest by introducing `mode` parameter in `config.toml` and cli
- `mode = "{{ .BaseConfig.Mode }}"` in `config.toml`
- `tendermint start --mode validator`  in cli
- full | validator | seednode
- There will be no default. Users will need to specify when they run `tendermint init`
- RPC modification
- `host:26657/status`
- return empty `validator_info` when in full mode
- no rpc server in seednode
- Where to modify in codebase
- Add  switch for `config.Mode` on `node/node.go:DefaultNewNode`
- If `config.Mode==validator`, call default `NewNode` (current logic)
- If `config.Mode==full`, call `NewNode` with `nil` `privValidator` (do not load or generation)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `privValidator` to related functions
- If `config.Mode==seed`, call `NewSeedNode` (seed node version of `node/node.go:NewNode`)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `reactor`, `component` to related functions
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Node operators can choose mode when they run state machine according to the purpose of the node.
- Mode can prevent mistakes because users have to specify which mode they want to run via flag. (eg. If a user want to run a validator node, she/he should explicitly write down validator as mode)
- Different mode needs different reactors, resulting in efficient resource usage.

### Negative

- Users need to study how each mode operate and which capability it has.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 053: State Sync Prototype
template_adherence.context:
State sync will allow a new node to receive a snapshot of the application state without downloading blocks or going through consensus. This bootstraps the node significantly faster than the current fast sync system, which replays all historical blocks.

Background discussions and justifications are detailed in [ADR-042](./adr-042-state-sync.md). Its recommendations can be summarized as:

* The application periodically takes full state snapshots (i.e. eager snapshots).

* The application splits snapshots into smaller chunks that can be individually verified against a chain app hash.

* Tendermint uses the light client to obtain a trusted chain app hash for verification.

* Tendermint discovers and downloads snapshot chunks in parallel from multiple peers, and passes them to the application via ABCI to be applied and verified against the chain app hash.

* Historical blocks are not backfilled, so state synced nodes will have a truncated block history.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for faster node bootstrap compared to existing fast sync.
- Requirement for deterministic, consistent, and asynchronous snapshots.
- Necessity to split snapshots into verifiable chunks for parallel download and application.
- Desire to keep the ABCI interface minimal and general for application flexibility.
- Need to handle snapshot discovery, selection, and application robustly.
- Considerations for snapshot metadata, chunk format, scheduling, and garbage collection.
- Addressing open questions about snapshot validity, punishment of invalid nodes, and interface design.
template_adherence.decision:
The ADR proposes a state sync prototype with the following key decisions:

- Use periodic, deterministic, consistent, asynchronous, chunked, and garbage collected snapshots.
- Define a Snapshot data structure with height, format, chunks, hash, and metadata.
- Use a minimal ABCI interface for listing snapshots, offering snapshots, loading chunks, and applying chunks.
- Tendermint remains unaware of snapshotting internals; the application manages snapshot creation.
- Nodes restore snapshots by discovering peers, verifying trusted headers, selecting suitable snapshots, downloading and applying chunks, and then switching to fast sync and normal consensus.
- Gaia-specific snapshot format and scheduling details are provided as an example.
- Open questions are resolved with pragmatic choices favoring simplicity and extensibility.

This approach balances flexibility, performance, and security for state sync implementation.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Enables significantly faster node bootstrap.
- Provides a clear, extensible ABCI interface for snapshot management.
- Allows parallel chunk downloads and application for efficiency.
- Supports multiple snapshot formats and versions.
- Addresses consistency and determinism requirements.

Negative consequences:
- Introduces complexity in snapshot management and verification.
- Requires applications to implement snapshot creation and application logic.
- Initial prototype lacks incremental chunk verification.
- Potential for DoS attacks mitigated by peer selection heuristics but not fully eliminated.
- Breaking ABCI interface change required, delaying release.

alternatives.description: Do not implement state sync and continue using existing fast sync methods.
pros: Simpler implementation with no new interface changes.
No breaking changes to ABCI.
cons: Slower node bootstrap times.
Does not address scalability and performance improvements.
Misses opportunity for improved user experience.

alternatives.description: Implement state sync with a separate optional ABCI service for snapshot management.
pros: Keeps existing ABCI interface unchanged for applications not using state sync.
Allows incremental adoption.
cons: Increases complexity by having multiple ABCI services.
May complicate application implementation and maintenance.
Potentially delays adoption due to optional nature.

alternatives.description: Implement state sync with mandatory ABCI interface changes as proposed.
pros: Simplifies interface by having a single mandatory snapshot interface.
Ensures all applications support state sync uniformly.
Enables default implementations for non-supporting apps.
cons: Breaking change to ABCI, delaying release.
Requires all applications to implement or handle the new interface.
Potentially increases initial development effort.

template_adherence.title: ADR 054: Crypto encoding (part 2)
template_adherence.context:
Amino has been a pain point of many users in the ecosystem. While Tendermint does not suffer greatly from the performance degradation introduced by amino, we are making an effort in moving the encoding format to a widely adopted format, Protocol Buffers. With this migration a new standard is needed for the encoding of keys. This will cause ecosystem wide breaking changes.

Currently amino encodes keys as <PrefixBytes> <Length> <ByteArray>.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Amino encoding has performance and usability issues.
- Need to adopt a widely used and supported encoding format (Protocol Buffers).
- Desire to minimize user impact and headaches during migration.
- Backwards compatibility concerns where amino encoding is still relied upon.
- Need to define key types appropriately in protobuf.
- Hardfork upgrade is required due to ecosystem-wide breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to shift all encoding of keys to protobuf. Cosmos-SDK will define its own protobuf type for keys, allowing Tendermint to define only the keys used in its codebase (ed25519). Where amino encoding is still relied upon, custom marshal and unmarshal functions will be used to maintain compatibility. The migration will be done in stages via multiple PRs merged into a proto-breakage branch. A hardfork upgrade will be required to adopt these changes.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Keys will be encoded using protobuf, improving performance and ecosystem compatibility.
- Amino marshal and unmarshal functions will be used where backwards compatibility is needed.
- A hardfork upgrade is necessary to integrate these changes into running chains.
- Positive impacts include stable protobuf encoding, reduced amino overhead, and access to a large ecosystem of supported languages.
- Negative impact includes the need for a hardfork.
- Neutral consequences are not explicitly detailed.

alternatives.description: Continue using amino encoding for keys without migrating to protobuf.
pros: No breaking changes or hardfork needed.
No immediate migration effort required.
cons: Continued performance degradation and user pain points.
Lack of adoption of a widely supported encoding format.
Missed opportunity to improve ecosystem compatibility.

alternatives.description: Define all key types in Tendermint protobuf definitions instead of Cosmos-SDK defining its own.
pros: Centralized key type definitions in Tendermint.
Potentially simpler for Tendermint codebase.
cons: Less flexibility for Cosmos-SDK to define keys as needed.
May complicate Tendermint protobuf definitions.
Not aligned with the decision to let Cosmos-SDK define its own protobuf types.

alternatives.description: Use protobuf 'oneof' type for keys to allow multiple key types.
pros: Supports multiple key types in protobuf.
Flexible and extensible design.
cons: Requires manual switching over possible key types.
Adds complexity to interface handling.
May postpone complexity rather than eliminate it.

template_adherence.title: Protobuf Design
template_adherence.context: Currently we use go-amino throughout Tendermint. Amino is not being maintained anymore (April 15, 2020) by the Tendermint team and has been found to have issues. Amino enables quick prototyping and development of features but does not provide the performance and developer convenience expected. For Tendermint to see wider adoption as a BFT protocol engine a transition to an adopted encoding format is needed. Several options are considered including Protobuf, FlatBuffers, and CapnProto, with pros and cons discussed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for better performance, developer convenience, wider adoption, and support for multiple languages. The current solution (Amino) is unmaintained and has known issues. The ecosystem and tooling support of the serialization format are important factors.
template_adherence.decision: Transition Tendermint to Protobuf because of its performance and tooling. The ecosystem behind Protobuf is vast and has outstanding support for many languages. The approach includes keeping current handwritten types and creating a /proto directory for .proto files, with utility functions to transition between handwritten Go types and protobuf generated types, following recommended file structure from buf.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling modular types in the future, less refactoring, ability to pull proto files into the spec repo, improved performance, and tooling support in multiple languages. Negative consequence is the need for developers to update proto types when updating types. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Use FlatBuffers as the serialization format.
pros: More efficient than Protobuf due to no parsing/unpacking to a second representation.
Tested and used in production.
cons: Not widely adopted.

alternatives.description: Use CapnProto as the serialization format.
pros: Insanely fast data interchange format and capability-based RPC system.
No encoding/decoding step.
Supports random access to process huge messages without loading into memory.
Has an opt-in canonical form useful for determinism.
cons: Has not seen wide adoption throughout the industry.
Despite technical advantages, Protobuf is preferred due to wider adoption.

template_adherence.title: ADR 056: Light client amnesia attacks
template_adherence.context: Whilst most created evidence of malicious behavior is self evident such that any individual can verify them independently there are types of evidence, known collectively as global evidence, that require further collaboration from the network in order to accumulate enough information to create evidence that is individually verifiable and can therefore be processed through consensus. Fork Accountability has been coined to describe the entire process of detection, proving and punishing of malicious behavior. This ADR addresses specifically what a light client amnesia attack is and how it can be proven and the current decision around handling light client amnesia attacks. For information on evidence handling by the light client, it is recommended to read ADR 47.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision surrounding amnesia attacks has both a short term and long term component. The need for a sturdy protocol to handle amnesia attacks, the complexity of implementing accountability protocols, the limited time frame before version 0.34, and the difficulty and unlikelihood of the attack occurring. Also, the desire to detect attacks without punishing malicious validators in the short term, and the hope to implement a secure protocol in the long term.
template_adherence.decision: The short term decision is to identify when the attack has occurred and implement the detector algorithm highlighted in ADR 47 but to not implement any accountability protocol that would identify malicious validators and allow applications to punish them. The long term goal is to develop a concrete and secure protocol to identify and deal with these attacks.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Light clients are still able to prevent falsely validating a block and this is already implemented.
Negative: Light clients where all witnesses are faulty can be subject to an amnesia attack and verify a forged block that is not part of the chain.
Neutral: No evidence will be passed to the application indicting any malicious validators, thus meaning that no malicious validators will be punished for performing the attack.

alternatives.description: Completely remove the protocol handling amnesia attacks before version 0.34.
pros: Simplifies the system by removing complex logic.
Avoids temporary and possibly incomplete implementations.
cons: Light clients would not detect amnesia attacks.
Potentially allows attacks to go unnoticed and unmitigated.

alternatives.description: Store a record of all votes in any height with more than one round and allow applications to perform off-chain verification and punishment.
pros: Enables accountability and punishment of malicious validators.
Provides more comprehensive evidence handling.
cons: Too much to ask of the application to implement temporarily.
Applications may lack domain specific knowledge.
Complexity may be high for a temporary solution.

template_adherence.title: ADR 057: RPC
template_adherence.context:
Currently the RPC layer of Tendermint is using a variant of the JSON-RPC protocol. This ADR is meant to serve as a pro/con list for possible alternatives and JSON-RPC.

There are currently two options being discussed: gRPC & JSON-RPC.

### JSON-RPC

JSON-RPC is a JSON-based RPC protocol. Tendermint has implemented its own variant of JSON-RPC which is not compatible with the JSON-RPC 2.0 specification.

**Pros:**

- Easy to use & implement (by default)
- Well-known and well-understood by users and integrators
- Integrates reasonably well with web infrastructure (proxies, API gateways, service meshes, caches, etc)
- human readable encoding (by default)

**Cons:**

- No schema support
- RPC clients must be hand-written
- Streaming not built into protocol
- Underspecified types (e.g. numbers and timestamps)
- Tendermint has its own implementation (not standards compliant, maintenance overhead)
- High maintenance cost associated to this
- Stdlib `jsonrpc` package only supports JSON-RPC 1.0, no dominant package for JSON-RPC 2.0
- Tooling around documentation/specification (e.g. Swagger) could be better
- JSON data is larger (offset by HTTP compression)
- Serializing is slow ([~100% marshal, ~400% unmarshal](https://github.com/alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks)); insignificant in absolute terms
- Specification was last updated in 2013 and is way behind Swagger/OpenAPI

### gRPC + gRPC-gateway (REST + Swagger)

gRPC is a high performant RPC framework. It has been battle tested by a large number of users and is heavily relied on and maintained by countless large corporations.

**Pros:**

- Efficient data retrieval for users, lite clients and other protocols
- Easily implemented in supported languages (Go, Dart, JS, TS, rust, Elixir, Haskell, ...)
- Defined schema with richer type system (Protocol Buffers)
- Can use common schemas and types across all protocols and data stores (RPC, ABCI, blocks, etc)
- Established conventions for forwards- and backwards-compatibility
- Bi-directional streaming
- Servers and clients are be autogenerated in many languages (e.g. Tendermint-rs)
- Auto-generated swagger documentation for REST API
- Backwards and forwards compatibility guarantees enforced at the protocol level.
- Can be used with different codecs (JSON, CBOR, ...)

**Cons:**

- Complex system involving cross-language schemas, code generation, and custom protocols
- Type system does not always map cleanly to native language type system; integration woes
- Many common types require Protobuf plugins (e.g. timestamps and duration)
- Generated code may be non-idiomatic and hard to use
- Migration will be disruptive and laborious
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to evaluate alternatives to the current JSON-RPC variant used by Tendermint.
- Consider pros and cons of JSON-RPC and gRPC.
- Desire for better schema support, tooling, performance, and maintainability.
- Consideration of migration complexity and disruption.

template_adherence.title: ADR 058: Event hashing
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the problem of proving that certain events are part of the result in Tendermint's consensus process. Before PR#4845, only certain fields were included in the Merkle tree for DeliverTx results, excluding non-deterministic fields and events. PR#4845 introduced hashing of events from BeginBlock, EndBlock, and DeliverTx results into the LastResultsHash, but this approach makes adding or removing events difficult as it requires a hard-fork, which is undesirable for evolving applications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers include the need to prove event inclusion in results, the desire to avoid hard-forks when adding/removing events, and the need for a stable and explicit mechanism to manage which events are hashed into the LastResultsHash.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add a new consensus parameter Block#LastResultsEvents, a list of event types to be hashed into the LastResultsHash. This list can be updated via InitChain or EndBlock, allowing networks to change it through parameter change proposals without hard-forks. Initially, the list is empty, and applications must explicitly include events they want hashed by adding their types to this list.

template_adherence.title: ADR 061: P2P Refactor Scope
template_adherence.context:
The `p2p` package responsible for peer-to-peer networking is rather old and has a number of weaknesses, including tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilites, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior. A refactor has been discussed for several years ([#2067](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2067)).

Informal Systems are also building a Rust implementation of Tendermint, [Tendermint-rs](https://github.com/informalsystems/tendermint-rs), and plan to implement P2P networking support over the next year. As part of this work, they have requested adopting e.g. [QUIC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-transport/) as a transport protocol instead of implementing the custom application-level `MConnection` stream multiplexing protocol that Tendermint currently uses.

This ADR summarizes recent discussion with stakeholders on the scope of a P2P refactor. Specific designs and implementations will be submitted as separate ADRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to address multiple weaknesses in the current P2P package such as tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilities, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior.
- Desire to maintain protocol compatibility as far as possible initially.
- Interest from Informal Systems to adopt modern transport protocols like QUIC.
- Concerns about breaking protocol changes and the complexity of adopting external libraries like LibP2P.
- Need for incremental improvements and phased refactoring.
- Desire for improved testability, observability, performance, security, and resilience.
- Balancing disruptive changes with backward compatibility and user impact.
template_adherence.decision:
The P2P stack will be refactored and improved iteratively, in several phases:

* Phase 1: code and API refactoring, maintaining protocol compatibility as far as possible.

* Phase 2: additional transports and incremental protocol improvements.

* Phase 3: disruptive protocol changes.

The scope of phases 2 and 3 is still uncertain, and will be revisited once the preceding phases have been completed as we'll have a better sense of requirements and challenges.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:

* Cleaner, simpler architecture that's easier to reason about and test, and thus hopefully less buggy.

* Improved performance and robustness.

* Reduced maintenance burden and increased interoperability by the possible adoption of standardized protocols such as QUIC and Noise.

* Improved usability, with better observability, simpler configuration, and more automation (e.g. peer/service/address discovery, rate-limiting, and backpressure).

Negative:

* Maintaining our own P2P networking stack is resource-intensive.

* Abstracting away the underlying transport may prevent usage of advanced transport features.

* Breaking changes to APIs and protocols are disruptive to users.

alternatives.description: Adopt LibP2P instead of maintaining our own P2P networking stack.
pros: Good idea in principle, potentially leveraging a mature P2P stack.
cons: Highly breaking protocol change.
Might require forking and modifying LibP2P.
Concerns about the abstractions used.

alternatives.description: Incremental improvements to the current P2P stack, add support for pluggable transports, and gradually experiment with LibP2P as a transport layer.
pros: Allows gradual adoption and testing of new technologies.
Maintains backward compatibility initially.
Reduces risk of disruptive changes.
cons: Longer timeline for full adoption.
Requires maintaining current stack during transition.

template_adherence.title: ADR 063: Privval gRPC
template_adherence.context:
Validators use remote signers to help secure their keys. This system is Tendermint's recommended way to secure validators, but the path to integration with Tendermint's private validator client is plagued with custom protocols.

Tendermint uses its own custom secure connection protocol (`SecretConnection`) and a raw tcp/unix socket connection protocol. The secure connection protocol until recently was exposed to man in the middle attacks and can take longer to integrate if not using Golang. The raw tcp connection protocol is less custom, but has been causing minute issues with users.

Migrating Tendermint's private validator client to a widely adopted protocol, gRPC, will ease the current maintenance and integration burden experienced with the current protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve security and integration ease of the private validator client protocol.
- Desire to use a widely adopted, language-agnostic protocol.
- Existing use of protobuf in Tendermint making gRPC a natural fit.
- Need to simplify the protocol and improve maintainability.
- Support for metrics and security features like TLS.
- Consideration of upgrade path and impact on users.
template_adherence.decision: After discussing with multiple stake holders, gRPC was decided on to replace the current private validator protocol. gRPC is a widely adopted protocol in the micro-service and cloud infrastructure world. gRPC uses protocol-buffers to describe its services, providing a language agnostic implementation. Tendermint uses protobuf for on disk and over the wire encoding already making the integration with gRPC simpler.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Use of an adopted standard for secure communication (TLS).
- Use of an adopted communication protocol (gRPC).
- Requests multiplexed onto the TCP connection (HTTP/2).
- Language agnostic service definition.

Negative:
- Users need to generate certificates to use TLS (added step).
- Users need to find a supported gRPC key management system.

Neutral:
- Not explicitly detailed in the ADR.

Overall, the decision simplifies integration, improves security, and aligns with modern protocols but introduces some user overhead in certificate management and migration.

alternatives.description: Use JSON-RPC as the protocol for the private validator client.
pros: JSON-RPC is a simpler, widely known protocol.
Might be easier to implement in some languages.
cons: Tendermint uses protobuf extensively, making JSON-RPC less natural.
Less efficient and less feature rich compared to gRPC.
Not chosen due to protobuf usage making gRPC a better fit.

template_adherence.title: ADR 064: Batch Verification
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint uses public private key cryptography for validator signing. When a block is proposed and voted on validators sign a message representing acceptance of a block, rejection is signaled via a nil vote. These signatures are also used to verify previous blocks are correct if a node is syncing. Currently, Tendermint requires each signature to be verified individually, this leads to a slow down of block times.

Batch Verification is the process of taking many messages, keys, and signatures adding them together and verifying them all at once. The public key can be the same in which case it would mean a single user is signing many messages. In our case each public key is unique, each validator has their own and contribute a unique message. The algorithm can vary from curve to curve but the performance benefit, over single verifying messages, public keys and signatures is shared.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve verification speed of signatures in Tendermint.
- Current individual signature verification slows down block times.
- Desire to leverage batch verification benefits where possible.
- Signature aggregation is an alternative but not suitable due to unique messages per validator.
- Maintain compatibility with existing verification methods.
- Minimize user errors in verification API usage.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt Batch Verification as the method to improve signature verification performance in Tendermint. Introduce a new interface with methods to add entries and verify them in batch. Use batch verification where supported (starting with ed25519), otherwise fall back to single signature verification.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Faster verification times if the cryptographic curve supports batch verification.
- Negative: No way to identify which specific key failed verification in batch mode.
- Negative: On batch verification failure, must revert to single signature verification, potentially impacting performance.
- Neutral: No impact on users other than improved verification speed.
- Implementation complexity added by new interface and fallback logic.

alternatives.description: Signature aggregation as an alternative to batch verification.
pros: Leads to fast verification and smaller block sizes.
cons: Not suitable currently because every validator signs a unique message, preventing aggregation before verification.
Potential slow down of 10x-100x in verification speeds if implemented with BLS in current context.

template_adherence.title: ADR 66: End-to-End Testing
template_adherence.context:
The current set of end-to-end tests under `test/` are very limited, mostly focusing on P2P testing in a standard configuration. They do not test various configurations (e.g. fast sync reactor versions, state sync, block pruning, genesis vs InitChain setup), nor do they test various network topologies (e.g. sentry node architecture). This leads to poor test coverage, which has caused several serious bugs to go unnoticed.

We need an end-to-end test suite that can run a large number of combinations of configuration options, genesis settings, network topologies, ABCI interactions, and failure scenarios and check that the network is still functional. This ADR outlines the basic requirements and design for such a system.

This ADR will not cover comprehensive chaos testing, only a few simple scenarios (e.g. abrupt process termination and network partitioning). Chaos testing of the core consensus algorithm should be implemented e.g. via Jepsen tests or a similar framework, or alternatively be added to these end-to-end tests at a later time. Similarly, malicious or adversarial behavior is out of scope for the first implementation, but may be added later.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for comprehensive end-to-end test coverage beyond current limited P2P tests.
- Ability to test various configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios.
- Feasibility constraints due to combinatorial explosion of test cases.
- Desire to run tests reproducibly both locally and in CI.
- Limitations on scope: excluding comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing initially.
- Preference for black-box testing via RPC rather than internal implementation details.
- Use of Docker Compose for testnet deployment.
- Resource constraints and engineering effort required to build custom test framework.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a custom end-to-end test suite that covers a broad range of configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios by grouping functionality into global, local, and temporal classes to manage combinatorial complexity. The testnets will be run using Docker Compose, configured via YAML files, and tests will be black-box RPC tests against individual nodes. The test runner will execute stages including setup, initialization, perturbation, and testing. The existing `testnet` command may be extended to support these tests. Comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing are out of scope for the initial implementation.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Comprehensive end-to-end test coverage of basic Tendermint functionality.
- Test environments reproducible locally and debuggable with standard tooling.

Negative:
- Limited coverage of consensus correctness and adversarial behavior initially.
- Need to develop and maintain a custom test framework, requiring engineering resources.
- Potentially slower CI times depending on tests run.
- Operational costs and overhead for infrastructure and maintenance.

Neutral:
- No support for alternative infrastructure platforms like Kubernetes or VMs initially.

alternatives.description: Continue with the existing limited end-to-end tests focusing on P2P in standard configurations.
pros: No additional engineering effort required.
Existing tests are already in place and understood.
cons: Poor test coverage leading to serious bugs going unnoticed.
Does not test various configurations, network topologies, or failure scenarios.

pros: Potentially faster to implement if suitable tools exist.

Less flexibility to cover specific configurations and scenarios.

template_adherence.title: ADR 067: Mempool Refactor
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the current design and challenges of the Tendermint Core mempool, which is a FIFO queue lacking transaction prioritization. It outlines the need for a priority-based, flexible, and performant mempool to allow application-determined transaction priority, efficient concurrent operations, prioritized transaction selection, eviction policies, and future extensibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to support transaction prioritization by applications, maintain or improve concurrency and performance, allow efficient transaction selection and gossiping by priority, support eviction of lower priority transactions, and enable future extensions such as replace-by-priority and multiple pending transactions per sender.

template_adherence.title: ADR 068: Reverse Sync
template_adherence.context:
The advent of state sync and block pruning gave rise to the opportunity for full nodes to participate in consensus without needing complete block history. This also introduced a problem with respect to evidence handling. Nodes that didn't have all the blocks within the evidence age were incapable of validating evidence, thus halting if that evidence was committed on chain.

[ADR 068](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/master/docs/architecture/adr-068-reverse-sync.md) was published in response to this problem and modified the spec to add a minimum block history invariant. This predominantly sought to extend state sync so that it was capable of fetching and storing the `Header`, `Commit` and `ValidatorSet` (essentially a `LightBlock`) of the last `n` heights, where `n` was calculated based from the evidence age.

This ADR sets out to describe the design of this state sync extension as well as modifications to the light client provider and the merging of tm store.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle evidence validation despite state sync and block pruning.
- Requirement for nodes to have sufficient block history to validate evidence.
- Desire to extend state sync to fetch and store recent light blocks.
- Integration with P2P messaging and light client providers.
- Maintainability and code complexity concerns.
- Future extensibility for pruning and reverse sync improvements.
template_adherence.decision:
The state sync reactor will be extended by introducing 2 new P2P messages (and a new channel) for LightBlockRequest and LightBlockResponse to implement a "reverse sync" protocol that fetches, verifies, and stores prior light blocks. This enables nodes to safely participate in consensus and validate evidence.

Additionally, a new light client provider will be created to use the underlying P2P stack instead of RPC.

The reverse sync process will run after state sync and before fast sync or consensus, with access to StateStore and BlockStore for persistence.

The design includes components like Dispatcher and BlockQueue to manage concurrent requests and serialization.

Pruning will be restricted for blocks within the evidence age.

Future work includes better P2P integration, store consolidation, and exploring opportunistic or full reverse sync.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Nodes have sufficient history to validate all types of evidence.
- State syncing nodes can use P2P for light client verification, potentially improving UX and speed.

Negative:
- Increased code complexity and maintenance burden.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implicitly alternatives include not extending state sync with reverse sync, or relying solely on RPC for light client verification.
pros: Simplicity, less code to maintain.
cons: Nodes may halt due to inability to validate evidence.
Less efficient or slower light client verification.

template_adherence.title: ADR 069: Flexible Node Initialization
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to support Go-API-Stability and reduce the API surface area by internalizing interfaces in the `node` package, which currently limits operational patterns such as introspection and component replacement. The problem is that the current node initialization tightly couples components, making it difficult to maintain and extend, especially for users who want to customize or replace components without vendoring the code.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to reduce coupling between components, improve maintainability, support future extensibility for component replacement, and avoid breaking existing user-facing APIs. The solution should be opaque to users, avoid premature complexity such as full dependency injection frameworks, and prioritize maintainability and minimal scope changes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to refactor the node initialization to factor code so packages handle their own initialization, minimize code in the `node` package, reduce direct coupling, and iterate on a flexible internal framework for node initialization. Reactors should not expose interfaces within the node implementation. The refactoring should be opaque to users and not require reevaluation of the `service.Service` framework. template_adherence.title: Restore Requests for Comments
template_adherence.context:
In the past, we kept a collection of Request for Comments (RFC) documents in `docs/rfc`. Prior to the creation of the ADR process, these documents were used to document design and implementation decisions about Tendermint Core. The RFC directory was removed in favor of ADRs, in commit 3761aa69 (PR #6345).

For issues where an explicit design decision or implementation change is required, an ADR is generally preferable to an open-ended RFC: An ADR is relatively narrowly-focused, identifies a specific design or implementation question, and documents the consensus answer to that question.

Some discussions are more open-ended, however, or don't require a specific decision to be made (yet). Such conversations are still valuable to document, and several members of the Tendermint team have been doing so by writing gists or Google docs to share them around. That works well enough in the moment, but gists do not support any kind of collaborative editing, and both gists and docs are hard to discover after the fact. Google docs have much better collaborative editing, but are worse for discoverability, especially when contributors span different Google accounts.

Discoverability is important, because these kinds of open-ended discussions are useful to people who come later -- either as new team members or as outside contributors seeking to use and understand the thoughts behind our designs and the architectural decisions that arose from those discussion.

With these in mind, I propose that:

-  We re-create a new, initially empty `docs/rfc` directory in the repository, and use it to capture these kinds of open-ended discussions in supplement to ADRs.

-  Unlike in the previous RFC scheme, documents in this new directory will _not_ be used directly for decision-making. This is the key difference between an RFC and an ADR.

Instead, an RFC will exist to document background, articulate general principles, and serve as a historical record of discussion and motivation.

In this system, an RFC may _only_ result in a decision indirectly, via ADR documents created in response to the RFC.

**In short:** If a decision is required, write an ADR; otherwise if a sufficiently broad discussion is needed, write an RFC.

Just so that there is a consistent format, I also propose that:

-  RFC files are named `rfc-XXX-title.{md,rst,txt}` and are written in plain text, Markdown, or ReStructured Text.

-  Like an ADR, an RFC should include a high-level change log at the top of the document, and sections for:

* Abstract: A brief, high-level synopsis of the topic.
* Background: Any background necessary to understand the topic.
* Discussion: Detailed discussion of the issue being considered.

-  Unlike an ADR, an RFC does _not_ include sections for Decisions, Detailed Design, or evaluation of proposed solutions. If an RFC leads to a proposal for an actual architectural change, that must be recorded in an ADR in the usual way, and may refer back to the RFC in its References section.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to document open-ended discussions that do not immediately result in a design change.
- Improve discoverability of such discussions compared to current informal methods (gists, Google docs).
- Maintain clear distinction between ADRs (for decisions) and RFCs (for discussions).
- Provide consistent format and naming conventions for RFCs.
- Avoid confusion between RFCs and ADRs.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to restore the RFC process alongside ADRs by creating a new `docs/rfc` directory to capture open-ended discussions that supplement ADRs. RFCs will not be used directly for decision-making but serve as background and historical records. ADRs remain the source for architectural decisions. RFCs will follow a consistent format and naming convention, distinct from ADRs.

Positive:

alternatives.description: Leave things as they are, with ADRs as the only log of record and other discussions held informally in various mediums.
pros: No additional process or documentation overhead.

cons: Open-ended discussions remain hard to discover and collaborate on.

template_adherence.title: 7. Use roles to authorise users to use certain data
template_adherence.context:
We need a way to authorise users in the MOLGENIS "Armadillo" service to use data. We want this to be as straightforward as possible.

Other techniques are ACL's for fine grained permissions on resources and ID-based.

**ACL's**
It is more time consuming to implement ACL's. With roles the you are less flexible, but we believe this is sufficient to use DataSHIELD.

**ID-based**
The ID-based approach was suggested as a first solution to make the service secure. A big disadvantage is that anyone with the link can
share the data. That means that there has to be a lot of trust between the data manager and the researcher. In practices, this is not feasible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a straightforward authorization method for users in the MOLGENIS "Armadillo" service; consideration of alternatives like ACLs and ID-based approaches; trade-offs between flexibility, implementation effort, and security.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use roles as a basic principle to give users permission on the data they need to have access to. Within the MOLGENIS "Armadillo" service there are at least these 2 types of roles:
- Researcher
*Implicit permissions*
- READ --> on data in the shared folder(s) to which they have access
- ADMIN --> on data in their own (user)folder
- Data manager
*Implicit permissions*
- ADMIN --> on all that lives
Each researcher role will have corresponding folder. The data manager is able to do anything anywhere.
template_adherence.consequences:
- In the file storage you need to be aware of the fact that you are using roles as an authorisation mechanism
- It is not possible to have fine grained permissions within a role

alternatives.description: ACL's (Access Control Lists) for fine grained permissions on resources.
pros: More flexible and fine grained control over permissions.
cons: More time consuming to implement.

alternatives.description: ID-based approach where access is controlled by possession of a link.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
cons: Anyone with the link can share the data, requiring a lot of trust between data manager and researcher, which is not feasible in practice.

This brings significant effort to rebuild a cluster as all servers would need to be manually deleted and recreated. The new OpenStack infrastructure is supposed to be available in a matter of months and we need to decide whether we want to invest effort in automating server creation.

template_adherence.title: 9. Bastion for cluster access
template_adherence.context: It will be necessary to access the servers that form the Datalabs network but we do not want to expose any services outside of the JASMIN tenancy that we do not have to.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided that all access to the cluster will be via a Bastion server over an SSH connection on port 22. We will restrict access through the firewall to known IP address ranges including the development workstations, the STFC VPN and the Tessella public IP address.

This excludes public facing services that should be available over HTTPS on port 443 via a different route.
template_adherence.consequences:
All communication with the servers in the cluster will have to be over an SSH tunnel. This will be straight forward to set up on Linux environments with first class SSH implementations but will cause problems on Windows machines.

On Linux, use [SSH config](https://linux.die.net/man/5/ssh_config) and [autossh](http://www.harding.motd.ca/autossh/).
On MacOS, use [SSH Tunnel](https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/ssh-tunnel/id734418810?mt=12).

template_adherence.title: 16. Glusterfs for storage
template_adherence.context: Containers running on Kubernetes only provide ephemeral storage. We need to provide persistent storage that allows volumes to be mounted into multiple containers. This restricts us to Kubernetes Volume Types that support "Read Write Many". Specifically, we are selecting between NFS, GlusterFS and Rook.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for persistent storage that supports multi-container mounts (Read Write Many). Desire for data resilience and disaster recovery capabilities. Concerns about production readiness of Rook. Limitations of simple NFS storage in terms of data resilience. Requirement for isolated storage cluster separate from Kubernetes cluster.
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to use GlusterFS to provide distributed persistent storage. We opted not to use Rook due to its perceived lack of production readiness and the need for a second Kubernetes cluster for isolated storage. We rejected simple NFS storage because it lacks data resilience and disaster recovery capabilities.
template_adherence.consequences: Potential uncertainty about Kubernetes integration via Heketi and possible inability to use Kubernetes storage abstractions later. Positive consequence is improved data resilience through replication. Negative consequence is the risk related to integration and abstraction compatibility.

alternatives.description: Use Rook for storage.
pros: Easy to deploy hyper-converged storage.
cons: Not yet ready for production usage.
Requires a second Kubernetes cluster to run isolated storage.

alternatives.description: Use simple NFS storage.
pros: Simplicity.
cons: No data resilience.
No disaster recovery capability due to lack of backups.

template_adherence.title: 36. Replace Kong with Nginx Ingress Controller
template_adherence.context:
We have reached a point where we need to secure third party web applications that provide no security of their own. The Kong proxy does not offer a mechanism for this in the open source version and we haven't had and response from our efforts to contact them.

We believe that the Nginx Ingress controller that has been available since Kubernetes 1.7 was released provides a Kubernetes native route for the same functionality.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to secure third party web applications lacking security; Kong proxy open source version lacks required security mechanisms; lack of response from Kong; availability of Nginx Ingress controller as a Kubernetes native solution providing similar functionality.
template_adherence.decision: We have decided the replace the Kong proxy with an Nginx Ingress Controller in the Kubernetes cluster and an Nginx load balancer running on the proxy servers. This should provide all of the same functionality as Kong and in addition should provide a mechanism for token and cookie authentication using the `auth_url` annotation that wraps the underlying Nginx `auth_request` module.
template_adherence.consequences:
We need to create the Ingress controller in the cluster.

The existing proxies need to be replaced with load balancers (or simple pass through proxy if single Ingress Controller).

The existing rules need to be migrated.

The Infrastructure Service needs to be updated to create Ingress Rules rather than Kong API rules.

We need to build a default backend service.

We need to build an authentication service to redirect inbound requests to.

alternatives.description: Continue using Kong as the reverse proxy solution.
pros: Already in use, so existing infrastructure and rules are in place.
Familiarity with Kong among the team.
cons: Kong open source version lacks required security mechanisms for third party apps.
No response from Kong for support or feature requests.
Does not meet current security needs.

alternatives.description: Replace Kong with Nginx Ingress Controller.
pros: Provides Kubernetes native routing functionality.
Supports token and cookie authentication via `auth_url` annotation.
Better integration with Kubernetes environment.
cons: Requires migration of existing rules and infrastructure changes.
Need to build additional services like default backend and authentication service.
Operational overhead of managing new components.

template_adherence.title: 37. Single Ingress Controller for Kubernetes Cluster
template_adherence.context:
Currently we have an Nginx Ingress controller deployed in the same namespace as the Datalabs application. This means that when multiple instances of Datalabs are deployed to a single cluster (such as prod and test), ingress controllers are deployed to each of these namespaces.

As we are in the process of implementing multiple project functionality within Datlabs, there is now a need for an ingress controller than can fulfill ingress rules across all namespaces. This also will move control of ingress to be a platform service and not part of the deployment of the application itself, which will aid to decouple Datalabs into being more of a standalone application.
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to deploy a single Nginx Ingress Controller into the kube-system namespace that will handle the ingress rules for the entire cluster.
template_adherence.consequences:
We need to edit the deployment process to deploy a single ingress controller in the kube-system namespace.

Minor configuration of the ingress controller will be required to use a default SSL certificate in order for ingresses in all namespaces to make use of it.

Without further configuration of the URL scheme to distinguish between Datalabs instances, only one can be deployed in a Kubernetes cluster at any time. This is due to the need for different wildcard certificates and the fact they do not support subdomains.

template_adherence.title: 38. Yarn Workspaces for package management and resolution across services
template_adherence.context:
We are using a mono-repository structure for the Datalabs project, this permits sharing of components across independent services. In NodeJS sharing of code without duplication requires linking of modules to the dependant service.

There are a few libraries to manages code-sharing:

* NPM Link
* Yarn Workspaces
* Learna
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to use Yarn Workspaces as is very lightweight and offers management of the links required for module share, including auto discovery of other services.

We have ruled out using straight NPM Links as they are difficult to set-up and share between development team. We have used Learna on other project and found it to be very heavyweight and requires that is adds git commits to releasing new versions.
template_adherence.consequences: We need to restructure our services to work with Yarn Workspaces. This will require splitting of the Datalabs Web-App, API and Shared module into independent services. As we are using Babel and ES-Modules rather than straight NodeJs and CommonJS modules, we will need to add and maintain scripts to handle the build process.

alternatives.description: NPM Link
cons: Difficult to set-up and share between development team

alternatives.description: Learna
cons: Very heavyweight
Requires that it adds git commits to releasing new versions
