template_adherence.title: 47. Remove need for wildcard certificates
template_adherence.context: DataLabs makes extensive use of reverse proxying, to give users access to resources (such as Minio or JupyterLabs). These resources need individually from an external URL to an internal service URL. There are four design options for reverse proxying (http://sawers.com/blog/reverse-proxying-with-nginx/): 1. Subdomain - this allows the external path and internal path to be the same, probably with a default root base path (/). Different services are identified by the external URL's hostname. This has some disadvantages - multiple hostnames require a wildcard certificate, or multiple certificates if a wildcard certificate can not be acquired; and it makes the development environment more difficult, because you can not just use localhost. 2. Port - this also allows the external path and internal path to be the same, probably with a default root base path (/). Different services are identified by the external URL's port. This has the disadvantage that some organisational firewalls restrict http traffic to unusual hosts. 3. Symmetric Path - this allows the external path and internal path to be the same, but with that path configured. Different services are identified by the path. This is the best option, but the internal service must allow the path to be configurable. 4. Asymmetric Path - here the external and internal paths are different. Different services are identifiable by the external path. This requires a search-and-replace of the path on the rendered HTML and JavaScript, so unless these are simple, then this is too fragile. Historically DataLabs has used Subdomain proxying.
template_adherence.decision: Where possible, Symmetric Path or Asymmetric Path proxying should be used. If this is not possible, a ConfigMap option should determine whether the remaining proxying strategy should be Subdomain or Port proxying.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Developer effort is required to develop the different proxying strategies.
* Portability will be improved and local development will be simplified.

alternatives.description: Subdomain proxying: external path and internal path are the same, identified by hostname.
pros: Allows external and internal paths to be the same with a default root base path.
cons: Requires wildcard certificates or multiple certificates.
Makes development environment more difficult (cannot just use localhost).

alternatives.description: Port proxying: external path and internal path are the same, identified by port.
pros: Allows external and internal paths to be the same with a default root base path.
cons: Some organizational firewalls restrict HTTP traffic to unusual ports.

alternatives.description: Symmetric Path proxying: external and internal paths are the same but configurable.
pros: Best option.
Internal service must allow path to be configurable.
cons: Requires internal service to support configurable path.

alternatives.description: Asymmetric Path proxying: external and internal paths differ.
pros: Different services identifiable by external path.
cons: Requires search-and-replace of path on rendered HTML and JavaScript, which can be fragile if complex.

template_adherence.title: Align technology, practice and process across the Libero Suite where appropriate
template_adherence.context:
The Libero suite of products currently contains four products: Reviewer, Producer, Publisher and Data Hub. All have different problems to solve where different technologies, frameworks, libraries, concepts and practices help in different ways. For example, Publisher takes a large amount of traffic from a globally diverse population who generally drop in quickly to read content and then disappear. In contrast, Reviewer serves users that are committed to filling forms and uploading content, and has a fraction of the traffic compared to Publisher. Striking the right balance between addressing these different needs while promoting a good experience for developers and service providers is the key to our alignment strategy.

There are a number of personas that we need to balance:

- Web site / app end users (readers, authors, editors and peer reviewers)
- Publishing staff (staff at organisations using the software)
- Community developers who wish to extend and configure the products
- Core developers (all at eLife currently) who may want to work across products and share services but also retain autonomy for a given product by reducing coupling
- Service providers who want to configure and deploy instances of the products
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include balancing different user needs across multiple products with different usage patterns, promoting a good experience for developers and service providers, avoiding undesirable coupling and synchronization overheads, and considering the experiences of end users, developers, and publishing staff in an open source, community-driven context.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to align technology, practice, and process across the Libero Suite where appropriate by exploring every reasonable opportunity for strong alignment and pursuing it when it does not harm the end user experience. Strong alignment is not mandatory if it negatively impacts product-specific needs or creates undesirable coupling. The decision process involves a time-boxed discovery session addressing key questions about value, feasibility, and consequences of alignment, with decisions made by consensus and recorded in ADRs.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include a better defined process for assessing alignment opportunities considering impacts on all stakeholders, faster and better-informed decision making, evidence-based documentation of decisions, and a balance between user experience, developer experience, and publishing staff experience.

alternatives.description: Strong alignment across all products regardless of differing needs.
pros: Simplifies technology stack and processes.
Easier to share services and components across products.
cons: May harm product-specific user experiences.
Could create undesirable coupling and synchronization overheads.
Reduces autonomy of product teams.

alternatives.description: No alignment, allowing each product to choose its own technologies and processes independently.
pros: Maximizes autonomy for each product team.
Allows optimization for specific product needs.
cons: Increases complexity for developers working across products.
Reduces ability to share services and components.
May increase maintenance overhead.

template_adherence.title: 5. Use Discovery Documents for requirements and technical choices
template_adherence.context: Libero product features and architectural choices benefit from the standardization of *discovery documents* that enable collaboration by being shared between team members, across teams, and outside of eLife.
template_adherence.decision:
- Always track discovery work in at least one dedicated Github issue.
- If using Google Docs prefix documents titles with `Discovery document:`
- If using Google Docs move them into the single [`Libero` shared drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/u/1/folders/0AC6f8fXdeXmMUk9PVA).
- Link them from the relevant Github issue.
- Establish a timebox in calendar time at the start of the discovery activity.
- Capture questions and answers, and document any assumptions that have been made.
- Link to a [Github milestone](https://github.com/libero/publisher/milestone/20) if applicable.
- Add a `TL;DR` section at the top before closing the document at the end of the timebox.
template_adherence.consequences:
A timebox helps limiting analysis time to favor prototyping and actual implementation.

Replenishment meetings are a possibility for choosing the length of the timeboxes.

Timeboxes are measured in calendar time so they need to take into account the percentage of time that is allocated to other tasks from the people that work on the discovery.

Github milestones may not exist if the discovery is related to an aspect of the product or to architecture rather than to a particular feature.

There is no explicit way to track the closure of a document on the document itself.

template_adherence.title: Convention for tagging of container images
template_adherence.context:
Libero's products are assembled from product specific, general libero and external container images.

Integration testing and reproducible deploys require uniquely identifiable image tags.

As a starting point for users each product has an umbrella repo. This is not only used to collect product issues and documents. I also contains e.g. docker-compose files, helm charts that combine various components to a useable whole.

To automatically update images in these files tools like dependabot, renovate and flux. These tools need way to determine which images to update, when to do so and whether human interaction is required. Semantic Versioning is ideally suited for this, but not all projects/components have/will implement automated semver from the start.

Therefor  this ADR also defines branch name, git hash and timestamp based tags. Branch names let us track specific branches. Hashes allow for unique identification. Timestamps are needed by tools like renovate that require some form of numeric versioning.

Container images always have a digest hash that uniquely identifies their build and is independent from git hashes, git tags and image tags.

The image associated with an image tag is allowed to change. This is useful for tracking semver image tags in deploys, but results in the image digest being required for pinning etc.

This ADR does not define how the image tags are used for integration tests or deploys. Nor does it define the consequences of their test results. But by defining a tagging convention is allows us to develop these strategies.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for uniquely identifiable image tags for integration testing and reproducible deploys.
- Requirement for tools like dependabot, renovate, and flux to determine image updates.
- Not all projects/components have automated semver tagging initially.
- Necessity to track specific branches, unique builds, and provide numeric versioning.
- Container image digest uniqueness and its relation to tags.
- Desire to define a tagging convention to enable further strategies for testing and deployment.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt a tagging convention for libero container images that includes always tagging images with both `${branch}-${short_git_hash}-${timestamp}` and `${branch}-${short_git_hash}` formats, using a timestamp format `%Y%m%d.%H%M`. Semver tags are applied when the git repo receives them, with semver tagging creating three tags (e.g., `1.2.43`, `1.2`, and `1`). Git tags must be prefixed with `v` (e.g., `refs/tags/v1.2.43`). Only images from the `master` branch are pushed as `latest`. This convention supports tracking images by branch or semver and facilitates automated tooling.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The tagging scheme will be rolled out to all Libero products as capacity and roadmap allow.
- Reviewer will be the first product to implement and validate this proposal.
- Libero deploys and integration tests can track image changes per branch or semver, reducing reliance on the `latest` tag for continuous deploys.
- Teams are encouraged to adopt automated semver tagging using tools that utilize conventional commits to ensure compliance.

alternatives.description:
Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly alternatives could be:
- Using only semver tagging without branch or timestamp tags.
- Using only branch and git hash tags without timestamps or semver.
- Relying solely on the `latest` tag.

These alternatives are not detailed in the ADR but can be inferred as less desirable due to the problems stated in the context.
pros: Simpler tagging scheme.
Less complexity in tag management.
cons: Does not support uniquely identifiable image tags for integration testing and reproducible deploys.
Does not support automated tools that require numeric versioning or branch tracking.
Increases risk of ambiguity and deployment errors.

template_adherence.title: Init Containers for dependency management
template_adherence.context:
Certain dependencies between the Kyma components impact the order in which components should be created. The controller pattern in Kubernetes allows you to disregard many dependencies and rely on the Kubernetes reconciliation process. However, there are still a few cases in which strict dependency management is necessary. The most significant example is when Kubernetes **Kind** should be defined before it is used, as in the CustomResourceDefinitions.

The default dependency management solution in Kubernetes uses Init Containers coupled with readiness probes.
Init Containers allow the delay of the Pod's creation until certain conditions are met. When the conditions are fulfilled, the container succeeds.

Currently, the concept of Kyma core and extensions is at an early stage of development. Our API is unstable at best, and undefined at worst. An investment in any complex dependency management solution is fraught with high risks.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage dependencies between Kyma components, especially for Kubernetes Kind definitions.
- Desire to keep the solution simple and aligned with Kubernetes core features.
- Avoid investment in complex dependency management due to unstable API and early development stage.
- Need for a solution that reduces entry cost for developers and users.
- Awareness of future needs for more advanced dependency management (e.g., DAGs).
- Concern about flexibility leading to inconsistency and maintenance challenges.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Kubernetes Init Containers together with the readiness probes for dependency management. There are no plans to invest further in more complex solutions.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Simplicity.
- Integration with Kubernetes core.
- No external components required.
- Low investment and reduced entry cost for developers and users.

Negative consequences:
- Lack of support for proper dependency management (e.g., DAGs).
- Potential inconsistency due to flexibility.
- Need to establish best practices to avoid maintenance difficulties.
- Future need to support more advanced dependency management solutions.

template_adherence.title: DR 008: (INVALID) DEX as an OIDC authenticator
template_adherence.context:
Although Kubernetes manages service accounts, the solution leaves the management of regular users to an independent, outside service.
For this reason, Kyma needs an authentication provider for end-users.

Kubernetes has the following requirements for authentication providers:

- The authentication provider must support the OpenID connect discovery.
- The authentication provider must run in TLS with non-obsolete ciphers.
- The authentication provider must support CA-signed certificates, even for commercial and self-signed CAs.

The solution must also fulfill the general platform requirements:

- It must be a cloud-native solution.
- It must be lightweight, preferably written in Go.
- It must be open-source, with the ability to contribute to the project development.

Additionally, the solution must allow to delegate authentication to SAML2-compliant Identity Providers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Must support OpenID Connect discovery.
- Must run in TLS with secure ciphers.
- Must support CA-signed certificates.
- Must be cloud-native.
- Must be lightweight and preferably written in Go.
- Must be open-source and allow contributions.
- Must allow delegation to SAML2-compliant Identity Providers.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Dex as an authentication provider for end-users in Kyma.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Dex is lightweight and written in Go.
- Supports OIDC and SAML2-compliant Identity Providers via connectors.
- Does not have its own user database; requires connectors.
- Static users supported but recommended only for testing.
- Multiple connectors require user selection; no automatic default.
- Kyma team contributed to Dex project despite some rejected PRs.
- Dex is designed to work with Kubernetes and recommended by Kubernetes documentation.

template_adherence.title: DR 009: ServiceBinding in Kyma
template_adherence.context:
The Service Catalog in Kubernetes implements the Open Service Broker API. The main goal of the Service Catalog is to provide a way for Kubernetes users to consume services managed by the brokers, and to easily configure their applications with no need for the detailed knowledge of how those services are created or managed. To learn more about the Service Catalog, see this documentation.

The workflow is as follows:
- The administrator creates a ServiceInstance in a given Namespace.
- The administrator creates a binding to the ServiceInstance, to allow the application access the provisioned service.

The binding operation results in creating Kubernetes Secret in a given Namespace.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to enable multiple applications to access the same ServiceInstance securely.
- Different brokers may return different credentials per binding or reuse credentials.
- The asynchronous binding specification is still in Alpha stage, so synchronous binding is preferred.
- Security considerations regarding Kubernetes Namespaces and Secrets.
template_adherence.decision:
When the administrator wants to enable the same ServiceInstance (i.e. the same database instance) to two different applications, it is necessary to create two separate bindings, one for each application. The broker returns a new set of credentials every time, if supported by a given ServiceClass.

It is recommended to use the synchronous binding, as the specification for the asynchronous binding is still in Alpha stage.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The service detects the interactions from different applications using separate credentials.
- Namespace acts as a security boundary; Secrets can be injected into any deployment within the Namespace.
- The Service Broker cannot prevent other applications from consuming a created Secret.
- For stronger isolation, use a dedicated Namespace.

alternatives.description: Use asynchronous binding instead of synchronous binding.
pros: Allows non-blocking binding operations.
cons: Specification is still in Alpha stage, potentially unstable or unsupported.

alternatives.description: Use a single binding shared among multiple applications.
pros: Simplifies credential management.
cons: May reduce security isolation between applications.
Not supported by brokers that return new credentials per binding.

template_adherence.title: Prettier as a JavaScript code formatter
template_adherence.context:
The Code Style Guide is a set of conventions on how to write the source code. It covers many areas, including the use of `camelCase` vs `PascalCase` for variable identifiers, whether or not to use a semicolon as a statement terminator, or the use of tabs or spaces for indentation.

It is obvious that an enforced, unified code style in a project is beneficial. Not only does it improve the readability, but it also saves you from a lot of noise while looking at diffs, caused by unadjusted whitespaces, different break line settings, and other issues. It also ends discussions around the style itself. Once applied, everyone can write code the way they want, and let the formatter do the work. In the end, it saves time and energy.

[Prettier](https://prettier.io) is one of the solutions dedicated to code formatting. It does not enforce such code quality rules as the use of globally scoped variables or naming. It only enforces the formatting rules. It can be used as a plugin for selected IDEs, as a pre-commit `git` hook, or as a standalone CLI tool. No matter which option you choose, it produces the same output given its configuration.

It was chosen because of its simplicity, ease of configuration, small amount of available options, and support for JavaScript, TypeScript, GraphQL, CSS, SCSS, and JSON, all of which are used in Kyma projects.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a unified, enforced code style to improve readability and reduce noise in diffs.
- Desire to end style discussions by automating formatting.
- Requirement for a tool supporting multiple relevant languages (JavaScript, TypeScript, GraphQL, CSS, SCSS, JSON).
- Preference for simplicity and ease of configuration.
- Compatibility with various integration options (IDE plugins, git hooks, CLI).
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Prettier as the only code formatter for JavaScript-based projects.
template_adherence.consequences: Every team working on a JavaScript-based project within Kyma has to incorporate Prettier into their workflow to ensure that the codebase is clean and unified across all projects.

template_adherence.title: DR 014: Certificate validation against remote environment
template_adherence.context:
Every remote environment in the cluster should be accessible only for clients authorized to this particular remote environment.
This requirement raises a need for a mechanism that will differentiate between clients' permissions.

Multiple server certificates

Having separate server certificate per remote environment would make it hard to manage all those certificates.

Single certificate

Having only one certificate creates the problem that the client who obtained signed certificate for accessing one of the existing remote environments can access all of them using this particular certificate.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to restrict access to remote environments only to authorized clients.
Desire to avoid managing multiple server certificates.
Avoid custom Common Name validation mechanisms.
Prefer handling validation within Ingress-Nginx configuration.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to check the Distinguished Name of the client's certificate in Ingress-Nginx configuration using `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet` in individual ingresses and grant permissions only in case the client certificate's Common Name matches the required one.
template_adherence.consequences:
The solution achieves the desired results with the single server certificate.
It does not require a custom Common Name validation mechanism.
It is handled in Ingress-Nginx configuration, which is the preferred solution.

alternatives.description: Multiple server certificates, one per remote environment.
pros: Clear separation of certificates per environment.
Fine-grained control over access.
cons: Hard to manage many certificates.
Increased operational overhead.

alternatives.description: Single certificate for all environments.
pros: Simpler certificate management.
cons: Client with one certificate can access all environments.
Lacks fine-grained access control.

template_adherence.title: DR 016: Decomposition of the Application Connector
template_adherence.context:
The Application Connector has three main areas of responsibility:

- Delivery of Events from the external solution to Kyma.
- Registration of Event Catalog and APIs exposed by the integrated solution.
- Proxying calls from Kyma to the external solution.

One big microservice, called the Gateway, implements all these three functionalities. The architecture introduced a technical debt. All functionalities require a different approach to scaling. Proxying the whole traffic over a single component is the introduction to a single point of failure.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to address technical debt caused by a monolithic Gateway service handling multiple responsibilities.
Different functionalities require different scaling approaches.
Avoiding a single point of failure by splitting the monolithic service.
Maintaining security aspects and integration with existing infrastructure like Nginx-Ingress and Service Catalog.
template_adherence.decision:
The Gateway service will be split into three independent services: Event service, Metadata service, and Proxy service.
Each service will handle a specific responsibility, with details on exposure and security handled by Nginx-Ingress or integration with Service Catalog.
This decomposition aims to improve scalability and reduce single points of failure.
template_adherence.consequences:
The Proxy service will require integration with the Service Catalog.
The security concept remains unchanged.
The architecture will be more modular, allowing independent scaling and deployment of services.
Potential complexity in managing multiple services instead of one monolith.

alternatives.description: Keep the Gateway as a single monolithic service handling all responsibilities.
pros: Simpler deployment and management as only one service is involved.
No need to change existing infrastructure or integration points.
cons: Technical debt remains due to monolithic design.
Scaling is inefficient as all functionalities scale together regardless of need.
Single point of failure risk remains.

alternatives.description: Split the Gateway into multiple services based on functionality.
pros: Improved scalability by allowing independent scaling of services.
Reduces single point of failure risk.
Better separation of concerns and maintainability.
cons: Increased complexity in deployment and management.
Requires integration with existing infrastructure like Nginx-Ingress and Service Catalog.

template_adherence.title: Knative-based Kyma Eventing
template_adherence.context:
Based on the decision of building Kyma on top of Knative, and along the effort to reuse as much of Knative functionality as possible, the eventing area shines as a good area for alignment. That is why a decision was made to have Kyma leverage as much of Knative Eventing as possible. This is a an architecture decision on how to achieve that target.

The assumptions are as follows:
1. Base Kyma on Knative.
2. Favor a smooth, gradual migration of the Kyma components to Knative Eventing.
3. Consider areas of contribution to Knative Eventing.
4. Event Bus public integration: Publish RESTful API, EventActivation and Subscriptions CRDs are still needed.
5. Leveraging Knative Eventing is a requirement.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
1. Need to build Kyma on top of Knative.
2. Desire to reuse as much Knative functionality as possible.
3. Requirement to leverage Knative Eventing.
4. Need for smooth, gradual migration of Kyma components.
5. Consideration of contribution areas to Knative Eventing.
6. Event Bus public integration requirements.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to provide a solution that abstracts the Knative Eventing concepts for the rest of Kyma as a short- or medium-term solution, making the transition transparent to other Kyma components. Specifically:
- Implement a production-ready Knative Bus using NATS Streaming.
- Provide a NATS Streaming operator for production-ready clusters.
- Implement Knative Bus Azure Service Bus Messaging as a fallback plan.
- Contribute both implementations to Knative Eventing.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Refactor Event Bus Publish application.
- Merge Event Bus Push and Sub Validator applications into a single Event Bus Controller application.

template_adherence.title: Remove components proxying requests to the Kubernetes API server
template_adherence.context: Proxying the API server calls was initiated in the early days of Kyma in order to introduce a unified authentication and authorization model for Kubernetes clusters coming from different vendors (Google Kubernetes Engine, Azure Kubernetes Service, Amazon EKS, etc). Whereas unification has some value for teams that need multi-cloud support, the solution has several drawbacks that should be addressed. In the meantime, the Kyma project picked Gardener as a managed Kubernetes platform to provide multi-cloud capabilities, and since then the additional layer of proxies does not add any value. The main reason for the decision to remove components proxying requests to the Kubernetes API server is the simplification of the authorization concept in Kyma. The proxies together with the custom dex connector for UAA are hard to explain and introduce additional security vulnerabilities. This decision is fundamental for changes coming in the Kyma 2.0 release.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to simplify the authorization concept in Kyma, reduce security vulnerabilities introduced by proxy components and custom connectors, improve maintainability and development speed, reduce resource consumption, and align with the adoption of Gardener as a managed Kubernetes platform providing multi-cloud capabilities.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove the following components from Kyma: apiserver-proxy, console-backend, iam-kubeconfig-service, permission-controller, uaa-activator, and dex. These components proxy requests to the Kubernetes API server. Instead, the Kubernetes API server and its native features for authentication and authorization, such as OpenId Connect Tokens and Role-based access control (RBAC), will be used directly.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include no pre-configured authentication model for Grafana, Kiali, or Jaeger exposure, which is addressed by using an OAuth2 Proxy in front of these UIs with default configuration pointing to documentation. Benefits include faster installation, lower resource consumption, reduced complexity of authentication and authorization flows, improved security by removing powerful service accounts, and easier maintenance and faster development of the Console UI. Additionally, some previous decisions (DR 007, DR 015, DR 008) become invalid as a result of this change.

alternatives.description: Keep the proxy components and continue using the unified authentication and authorization model with custom connectors.
pros: Maintains existing multi-cloud support with unified auth model.
No immediate changes required to existing components and flows.
cons: Continues complexity and security vulnerabilities associated with proxies and custom connectors.
Higher resource consumption and maintenance overhead.
Harder to explain and maintain authorization concepts.

alternatives.description: Replace proxy components with a different custom solution for multi-cloud authentication and authorization.
pros: Potentially tailored solution for multi-cloud needs.
Could address some current drawbacks of existing proxies.
cons: Requires development and maintenance of new custom components.
May introduce new complexity and security risks.
Delays simplification and alignment with Kubernetes native features.

template_adherence.title: use-pull-request-templates
template_adherence.context:
The quality of information included in our pull requests varies greatly which can lead to code reviews which take longer and are harder for the person to understand the considerations, outcomes and consquences of a series of changes.

A couple of recent projects have found a GitHub pull request template to have been a positive change. Prompting what pull request descriptions should include has lead to better documented changes that have been easier to review on the whole.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but can be inferred from the context and consequences sections: the need for better quality and consistency in pull request information to improve review efficiency and understanding.
template_adherence.decision: Include a basic pull request template for GitHub so that every pull request prompts every author to fill it out.
template_adherence.consequences:
- a small overhead to every pull request which may prompt us to spend more time in creating a pull request. We accept the cost of this to gain the benefits of easier reviews, and better documented changes
- writing good pull request descriptions is not to be done instead of commit messages, they are the primary source of storing rationale that will persist. Commit messages may be duplicated into the pull request description.
- prompting authors to articulate their thought process and decision making can improve the quality of code before a reviewer becomes involved. Essentially you are following the process of rubber ducking which gives you the final opportunity to amend your proposal
- this is not compatible when source code is hosted on other services eg. GitLab requires a file of a different name, as all of our Rails projects are on GitHub this should be a minor issue
- asking for screenshots doesn't always make sense especially when production deployments are facilitated by pull requests from develop into master. We accept that in these cases the cost of editing the template is small enough to not be a problem. The first header that prompts to describe changes does still apply
- not all pull requests result in a frontend change that requires screenshots, we believe that these prompts can be removed quickly with a minor cost to the author

template_adherence.title: Use DotEnv for Managing Environment Variables
template_adherence.context: Accessing ENV directly without a wrapper is limited and can introduce problems. We want our tooling to help us guard against missing environment variables. When `nil` is accidentally provided during the start up process it is preferable to fail fast with an explicit message. Without this `nil` can be passed down through the stack and cause strange behaviour where the code has been designed with it as a dependency. Instead of adding `nil` guards throughout the codebase for required environment variables (eg. `ENV.fetch('FOO', 'default')`, this should be managed centrally. We have previously used Figaro for this purpose but it was deprecated in 2016 https://github.com/laserlemon/figaro. We should only use supported gems to ensure we get support in the form of fixes and security patches. We also want to be able to stub our environment variables in our test suite. An easy example of this is when we use environment variables as a feature flag mechanism. We want to stub the value to test both scenarios without being influenced by real values being loaded. Mutating the actual ENV value (eg. `allow(ENV).to receive(:[]).with('BOX_ID').and_return("1234")`) is possible but may have unexpected consequences where more than 1 part of the same process under test uses the same variable. Figaro used to be a handy abstraction layer that we could stub eg. `allow(Figaro).to receive(:env).with(:foo).and_return('bar')`. We should then consider how we can stub environment variables.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to guard against missing environment variables and fail fast with explicit messages.
- Avoid adding nil guards throughout the codebase.
- Use supported gems to ensure ongoing support and security patches.
- Ability to stub environment variables easily in tests.
- Avoid overhead of managing multiple environment variable files.
- Maintainability and testability of environment variable management.
template_adherence.decision: Use DotEnv to load our environment variables.
template_adherence.consequences:
- When using Docker and Docker Compose, environment variables will need to be loaded with `docker-compose up --env-file=.env.development` rather than `docker-compose.env` which is a pattern previously used.
- Having two files for managing environment variables such as `.env*` and `docker-compose.env*` is undesirable due to overhead in keeping these in sync.
- DotEnv loads environment variables but doesn't offer an interface as Figaro did. Access is via `ENV['foo']` rather than `DotEnv.foo`.
- A supporting decision to use Climate Control will be needed to support testing.

alternatives.description: Continue using Figaro for environment variable management.
pros: Previously used and familiar.
Provided an abstraction layer that was easy to stub in tests.
cons: Deprecated since 2016.
No longer supported, no security patches or fixes.

alternatives.description: Access ENV directly without a wrapper.
pros: No additional dependencies.

cons: Limited and can introduce problems.

template_adherence.context: We want to keep our test coverage as high as possible without having to run manual checks as these take time and are easy to forget.

template_adherence.title: Use Architectural Decision Records
template_adherence.context: Architecture for agile projects has to be described and defined differently. Not all decisions will be made at once, nor will all of them be done when the project begins. Agile methods are not opposed to documentation, only to valueless documentation. Documents that assist the team itself can have value, but only if they are kept up to date. Large documents are never kept up to date. Small, modular documents have at least a chance at being updated. Nobody ever reads large documents, either. Most developers have been on at least one project where the specification document was larger (in bytes) than the total source code size. Those documents are too large to open, read, or update. Bite sized pieces are easier for for all stakeholders to consume. One of the hardest things to track during the life of a project is the motivation behind certain decisions. A new person coming on to a project may be perplexed, baffled, delighted, or infuriated by some past decision. Without understanding the rationale or consequences, this person has only two choices: 1. Blindly accept the decision. This response may be OK, if the decision is still valid. It may not be good, however, if the context has changed and the decision should really be revisited. If the project accumulates too many decisions accepted without understanding, then the development team becomes afraid to change anything and the project collapses under its own weight. 2. Blindly change it. Again, this may be OK if the decision needs to be reversed. On the other hand, changing the decision without understanding its motivation or consequences could mean damaging the project's overall value without realizing it. (E.g., the decision supported a non-functional requirement that hasn't been tested yet.) It's better to avoid either blind acceptance or blind reversal.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for lightweight, modular documentation that is easy to update and consume.
- Importance of capturing motivation behind architectural decisions to avoid blind acceptance or changes.
- Agile project context where decisions are made incrementally.
- Desire to keep records in a simple, accessible format within the project repository.
- Need to track status of decisions (proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded).
- Requirement to document consequences of decisions, both positive and negative.
template_adherence.decision: The team will keep a collection of Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) for architecturally significant decisions affecting structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques. ADRs will be short text files in a format similar to Alexandrian patterns, describing forces and a single decision. They will be stored in the project repository under doc/arch/adr-NNN.md, using lightweight markup like Markdown. ADRs will be numbered sequentially and monotonically, with old decisions kept but marked as superseded if reversed. The format will have a few parts: Title, Context, Decision, Status, and Consequences, each described clearly to facilitate understanding and maintenance.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Provides a clear, maintainable, and accessible way to document architectural decisions.
- Positive: Helps new team members understand the rationale behind decisions, reducing confusion.
- Positive: Encourages keeping documentation up to date and relevant.
- Positive: Facilitates tracking decision status and history.
- Negative: Requires discipline to maintain ADRs consistently.
- Negative: May add some overhead to the development process.
- Overall, the approach improves project transparency and decision traceability, supporting agile development practices.

alternatives.description: Not using Architectural Decision Records and relying on traditional large documentation or informal communication.
pros: No additional documentation overhead.
Familiar approach for teams used to traditional documentation.
cons: Large documents tend to become outdated and unreadable.
Lack of clear rationale for decisions leads to confusion and poor decision making.
New team members struggle to understand past decisions.
Decisions may be blindly accepted or changed without understanding consequences.

pros: Comprehensive documentation covering all aspects.
May satisfy strict compliance or regulatory requirements.
cons: High overhead and maintenance cost.
Documents may become too large and unwieldy.
Less agile and flexible, slowing down development.
Difficult to keep up to date and relevant.

- Allow both designers and engineers to edit the docs

[React Styleguidist](https://react-styleguidist.js.org/)

cons: Missing the action logger feature present in Storybook

template_adherence.title: 7. Publish Components
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to pull in these components to other apps as one or more NPM packages. There are pros and cons to a single-package approach versus one package per component.

The ADR discusses the pros and cons of two approaches: one package per component and a single package exporting all components. It also mentions the complication of the style guide's release cycle in relation to component versions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the complexity of setup and maintenance, ease of publishing, dependency management, impact on app bundle size, and how to handle component versioning and style guide representation.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to prefer a single package exporting all components, mitigating its cons by:
- Exporting changed components as new versions in separate folders (e.g., v1, v2) to avoid breaking changes.
- Avoiding internal React component imports; instead, passing needed components as props or children.
- Using Jest snapshot testing to detect visual changes and decide on version splits.
- Relying on apps to implement tree shaking to avoid bundling unused components.
This approach also naturally supports showing all component versions in the style guide.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simpler publishing and understanding, and controlled component versioning to avoid breaking changes. Negative consequences include the need for apps to implement tree shaking and the overhead of managing multiple component versions within the package.

alternatives.description: One Package Per Component
pros: Minimum dependencies pulled in with each component used.
Fixes to one component do not unintentionally change others.
cons: Tracking and installing dependencies per component is complex.
Developers must install each component package as needed.
Publishing is tricky, especially with interdependencies. Lerna + semantic-release may help, but repo structure may not be ideal.

alternatives.description: A Single Package Exporting All Components
pros: Install a single package to get all components.
Simpler publishing process.
Easier for developers to understand the style guide repo.
cons: Bumping dependency versions pulls in all component changes.
Extra work needed to ensure unused components are not bundled.

template_adherence.title: Use micro frontends
template_adherence.context:
We designed the API layer (known as the backend) to be a custom set of services. This allows the user to tailor it to their own requirements, and introduce custom code as needed.

The original plan was to make the presentation layer (known as the frontend) a monolith. That is, a single service that generates all the HTML pages.

As a monolith, it is hard, if not impossible, to change or replace parts without having to replace the whole. This would mean a lot of configuration options to support differing requirements. It would also limit adoption of the platform as it can't meet them.

We investigated the use of micro frontends in [#371][Spike].
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow customization and flexibility in the frontend layer, avoiding the limitations of a monolithic frontend that is hard to change or replace parts of, and to support differing requirements and adoption of the platform.
template_adherence.decision: We will create separate services for individual, and groups of, pages. The user will use a proxy to make them appear as a single service. The frontends are independent of each other, and are always optional.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The frontends will need to share knowledge of authentication.
- Each frontend will have its own assets.
- The user will need to configure each frontend so it knows how to generate links to other frontends.
- The user can choose which frontends to use.
- The user can add their own frontends as needed.

alternatives.description: Monolithic frontend service generating all HTML pages.
pros: Simpler deployment as a single service.
Easier to manage a single codebase for the frontend.
cons: Hard or impossible to change or replace parts without replacing the whole.
Would require many configuration options to support differing requirements.
Limits adoption of the platform as it can't meet diverse needs.

template_adherence.title: Use component-level micro frontends for the header and footer
template_adherence.context: Having separate micro frontends for pages requires duplication of the header and footer. We expect users will want to change the content of both, as well as their styling and behaviour. We investigated the use of micro frontends in #371 Spike.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid duplication of header and footer in separate micro frontends, user expectations to customize content, styling, and behaviour, and investigation results from a spike on micro frontends architecture.
template_adherence.decision: Create dedicated services for the header and footer, using Edge Side Includes (ESIs) limited to <esi:include> to transclude them into pages, with each component having two ESIs: one for the <head> and one for the <body>.
template_adherence.consequences: Compatibility with popular ESI processors like Varnish and Fastly; limitation that not all CDNs support ESI (e.g., AWS CloudFront), requiring page-level micro frontends to process ESIs themselves if no trusted proxy is available; ability for components to add CSS and JavaScript in the <head> ESI; need to avoid styling and behaviour clashes between page and components; flexibility for users to replace or omit header and footer services.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implied alternatives include duplicating header and footer in each micro frontend or not using ESIs for composition.
pros: Simpler implementation without ESI dependency.
cons: Duplication of header and footer code and styling.
Harder to maintain consistency across pages.

template_adherence.title: Why Service sign in pages aren't linked to from transaction pages using a content id
template_adherence.context: Currently, when content designers create a transaction page they enter a URL for the service that the start button should link to, and this service is usually an external (to GOV.UK) URL. Service sign in pages however will be GOV.UK content items, and ideally we should not link to specific content item URLs as they could change in future. Instead, the links should reference a content_id, which never changes. However as the field where content designers enter the URL that the start button should link to doesn't support content_ids currently, the only option available to them is to enter the URL for the service sign in page.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid linking to URLs that may change, the desire to use content_id which never changes, the current limitation of the content designers' URL field not supporting content_ids, and the risk assessment of linking directly to URLs.
template_adherence.decision: After discussing this with @kevindew from the publishing platform team, we identified that the risk of things breaking because we're linking directly to a URL is quite low because if the base_path of the service sign in page changes, the publishing API will automatically create a redirect.
template_adherence.consequences: Ideally we should ensure that we're referencing the content_id instead of the service sign in page URL so that all risk is mitigated, so in future we should look at how we can support providing a content_id instead of a URL on the edit transaction page in Publisher.

template_adherence.title: Why "Service sign in" is its own format
template_adherence.context: The Q3 Start Pages mission goal was to make it easier for users to choose a sign in option in order to access a service. It was decided that a page should sit in between the transaction/guide page and the service which allows users to select a sign in option such as GOV.UK Verify or Government Gateway, or to register for a new account (henceforth know as the service sign in page). We initially looked at whether we could use an existing format to house this page. At first glance, it felt that transaction pages might be a suitable place for it, as it would be tailored to the transaction. Alternatively we could create a new format for this page.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to make it easier for users to choose a sign in option.
- Service sign in pages could be linked from multiple formats (transactions and guides).
- Scope limitations: no consolidation of product debt around transactions.
- UI building for service sign in pages was out of scope.
- Need for flexibility to link service sign in pages from more than one format.
- Consideration of user experience for content designers.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to create a new `service_sign_in` format rather than incorporating service sign in pages into the transaction format. This was because service sign in pages need to be linked from multiple formats (not just transactions), consolidating product debt was out of scope, and building UI support for service sign in pages within transactions was not planned. The new format would house up to two pages: a required `choose_sign_in` page and an optional `create_new_account` page. Creating a separate format for `create_new_account` was considered but deemed unnecessary at this time.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Creating a dedicated `service_sign_in` format allows flexibility to link from multiple formats.
- It avoids the need to consolidate product debt in transactions.
- It may complicate publisher workflow compared to having a less flexible format or extension to transactions.
- If user needs evolve, it might make sense to have a less flexible format or extension to transactions for easier publisher workflow and consistent iterations.

alternatives.description: Incorporate service sign in pages into the transaction format.
pros: Tailored to the transaction, potentially more integrated experience.
cons: Not suitable for guides which also link to service sign in pages.
Requires consolidating product debt around transactions, which is out of scope.
Would require building UI support for service sign in pages within transactions, which is out of scope.

alternatives.description: Create a separate format for `create_new_account` page.
pros: Clear separation of concerns.
Potentially easier to manage distinct pages.
cons: Currently no need for a standalone page for this.
Adds complexity without immediate benefit.

template_adherence.title: Communications between bounded contexts
template_adherence.context: Some common data should be used by several bounded contexts (modules, in the case of monolith application).
template_adherence.decision:
Communication between bounded contexts asynchronous. Bounded contexts don't share data, it's forbidden to create a transaction which spans more than one bounded context.
- https://www.infoq.com/news/2014/11/sharing-data-bounded-contexts/
- http://www.kamilgrzybek.com/design/modular-monolith-primer/
- https://github.com/kgrzybek/modular-monolith-with-ddd#37-modules-integration
template_adherence.consequences: This solution reduces coupling of bounded contexts through data replication across contexts which results to higher bounded contexts independence.

alternatives.description: We will create the dependency between modules. After setting up the dependency, needed method can be called from another module.

The modules will not communicate by direct calls, so the dependency between modules is not needed. Common data can be duplicated inside the modules during executing the listener for particular events.

template_adherence.title: Use Pull Request Templates for GitHub
template_adherence.context:
The quality of information included in our pull requests varies greatly which can lead to code reviews which take longer and are harder for the person to understand the considerations, outcomes and consquences of a series of changes.

A couple of recent projects have found a GitHub pull request template to have been a positive change. Prompting what pull request descriptions should include has lead to better documented changes that have been easier to review on the whole.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Improve the quality and consistency of pull request descriptions to facilitate easier and more effective code reviews.
template_adherence.decision: Include a basic pull request template for GitHub so that every pull request prompts every author to fill it out.
template_adherence.consequences:
- a small overhead to every pull request which may prompt us to spend more time in creating a pull request. We accept the cost of this to gain the benefits of easier reviews, and better documented changes
- writing good pull request descriptions is not to be done instead of commit messages, they are the primary source of storing rationale that will persist. Commit messages may be duplicated into the pull request description.
- prompting authors to articulate their thought process and decision making can improve the quality of code before a reviewer becomes involved. Essentially you are following the process of [rubber ducking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber_duck_debugging) which gives you the final opportunity to amend your proposal
- this is not compatible when source code is hosted on other services eg. [GitLab requires a file of a different name](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/description_templates.html#creating-merge-request-templates), as all of our Rails projects are on GitHub this should be a minor issue
- asking for screenshots doesn't always make sense especially when production deployments are facilitated by pull requests from develop into main. We accept that in these cases the cost of editing the template is small enough to not be a problem. The first header that prompts to describe changes does still apply
- not all pull requests result in a frontend change that requires screenshots, we believe that these prompts can be removed quickly with a minor cost to the author

alternatives.description: Not using a pull request template and relying on individual authors to write good descriptions.
pros: No overhead of filling out a template for authors.
Flexibility for authors to write descriptions as they see fit.
cons: Inconsistent quality and completeness of pull request descriptions.
Longer and harder to understand code reviews.

alternatives.description: Using a more complex or customized pull request template.
pros: Potentially more detailed and comprehensive pull request descriptions.

cons: Increased overhead for authors to fill out the template.
May discourage some authors from thorough descriptions due to complexity.

template_adherence.title: Use DotEnv for managing environment variables
template_adherence.context:
Accessing ENV directly without a wrapper is limited and can introduce problems.

We want our tooling to help us guard against missing environment variables. When `nil` is accidentally provided during the start up process it is preferable to fail fast with an explicit message. Without this `nil` can be passed down through the stack and cause strange behaviour where the code has been designed with it as a dependency. Instead of adding `nil` guards throughout the codebase for required environment variables (eg. `ENV.fetch('FOO', 'default')`, this should be managed centrally.

We have previously used Figaro for this purpose but it was deprecated in 2016 https://github.com/laserlemon/figaro. We should only use supported gems to ensure we get support in the form of fixes and security patches.

We also want to be able to stub our environment variables in our test suite. An easy example of this is when we use environment variables as a feature flag mechanism. We want to stub the value to test both scenarios without being influenced by real values being loaded. Mutating the actual ENV value (eg. ` allow(ENV).to receive(:[]).with('BOX_ID').and_return("1234")`) is possible but may have unexpected consequences where more than 1 part of the same process under test uses the same variable. Figaro used to be a handy abstraction layer that we could stub eg. `allow(Figaro).to receive(:env).with(:foo).and_return('bar')`. We should then consider how we can stub environment variables.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid direct access to ENV without a wrapper to prevent issues with missing environment variables.
- Desire to fail fast with explicit messages when environment variables are missing.
- Avoid adding nil guards throughout the codebase.
- Use supported gems to ensure ongoing support and security patches (Figaro deprecated).
- Ability to stub environment variables easily in tests without side effects.
- Maintainability and consistency in environment variable management.
template_adherence.decision: Use DotEnv to load our environment variables.
template_adherence.consequences:
- When using Docker and Docker Compose, environment variables need to be loaded with `docker-compose up --env-file=.env.development` instead of the previously used `docker-compose.env` pattern.
- Having two files for managing environment variables (e.g., `.env*` and `docker-compose.env*`) is undesirable due to overhead in keeping them in sync.
- DotEnv loads environment variables but does not offer an interface like Figaro did; access is via `ENV['foo']` rather than `DotEnv.foo`.
- Need to make a supporting decision to use Climate Control to support testing and stubbing environment variables.

alternatives.description: Continue using Figaro for environment variable management.
pros: Figaro provides an abstraction layer that allows easy stubbing in tests.
Familiarity with existing tooling.
cons: Figaro was deprecated in 2016 and is no longer supported.
No security patches or fixes are provided for Figaro.
Using deprecated software increases risk.

alternatives.description: Access ENV directly with nil guards throughout the codebase.
pros: No additional dependencies required.
Direct access to environment variables.

template_adherence.title: Decision to not use Docker in development
template_adherence.context:
dxw do not set a preferred default for working in development. dxw do set a default stance of using docker in all live environments and CI.

Docker in development can be slow and it can require some experience to resolve situations where things go wrong, like a full disk space.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but implied drivers include developer experience, performance concerns, and environment parity.
template_adherence.decision: Use non-docker tools and packages to run the application in development. This includes web servers, rails consoles, tests, local dependencies eg, Sidekiq, NPM, etc.
template_adherence.consequences:
The current development team will be more productive using tools they are more comfortable with.

Getting the app set up on your local machine requires a longer process. There is more room for problems when setting up and starting several dependencies locally. We could automate this using Foreman or Make files.

Support teams who are rotated on will have to spend time going through the documentation to get set up before they can work on any issues.

We may have to come back later to add Docker Compose.

Debugging issues found on live environments on our local environments can be harder without the parity. We could add Docker Compose files if these edge cases come up but they will not be readily available.

Documentation for getting set up locally has more chance of being maintained compared to if there were 2 different options used by different team members. It is harder to keep to sets of documentation up to date.

alternatives.description: Use Docker in development as well as in live environments and CI.
pros: Consistency between development and production environments.
Easier debugging of live environment issues locally due to environment parity.
cons: Docker can be slow in development.
Requires experience to resolve issues like disk space problems.
May increase setup complexity for developers.

template_adherence.title: 19. use-data-migrations-to-update-live-data
template_adherence.context:
We need a way to modify existing data on live environments. A good example of this is the new field we made called `geography`. We made is a required field but missed the fact that existing data needed to be migrated based on the value of `recipient_region`. We missed this and needed to take action to correct the mistake on each environment.

We want to avoid having unstructured access to rails consoles on live environments to de-risk the process where possible.

We want to avoid the fact we have to remember to run a manual action before or after a deployment to snure they aren't forgotten.

Using conventional rails migrations as the mechanism for only change data is an option. Though we may wish to change the schema without changing the data migrations. Tieing these 2 responsibilities into the same mechanism seems like it could back us into a corner later.

We would like to document the actions we perform through our code. This would help us understand and debug the state of the service.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to modify existing live data safely and reliably.
Avoiding unstructured manual interventions on live environments.
Desire to separate schema changes from data changes to avoid coupling.
Need for automated, documented, and reversible data migration processes.
Reducing risk of forgetting manual migration steps during deployment.
template_adherence.decision:
Use the data-migrate gem[1] when we need to make changes to data without touching the schema.

Changes to the schema can still include changes relevant to data within the db:migrate. If we were to add the geography feature again, we would add the new column and set the value as a single transaction.

Include the `rake data:migrate` step in the deployment process so it is automatically run after `rake db:migrate`.

[1] https://github.com/ilyakatz/data-migrate
template_adherence.consequences:
Changing data on real environments has an automated process.

The team can rollback from data migrations if they need to.

Data migrations and "one-off tasks" are preserved and documented within the code base.

It may be unclear when to use data migrations and when to use db migrations despite including this in the README.

alternatives.description: Use conventional rails migrations for both schema and data changes.
pros: Single mechanism for schema and data changes.
Familiar to developers already using rails migrations.
cons: Couples schema and data changes, which may cause complexity.
May lead to difficulties in managing data-only changes separately.
Less clear documentation and separation of concerns.

alternatives.description: Perform manual data changes via rails console on live environments.
pros: Immediate and flexible changes.
No need to add new tooling or processes.
cons: Risky and error-prone.
Lack of documentation and audit trail.
Manual steps can be forgotten or done inconsistently.
Hard to rollback changes.

template_adherence.title: 20. use-skylight-application-performance-monitoring
template_adherence.context: To ensure the RODA application has the highest availability, we want to have confidence that the application is resourced properly in times of low and high usage.
template_adherence.decision:
dxw have used the Skylight gem in many other projects and there is a Skylight account available for use. We have prior knowledge of using Skylight in other projects.

Skylight provides a web interface and graphing so we can more easily identify pain points in our application which will cause it to become less performant under high load. It can identify slow-running parts of the service down to the controller action level, and indicate where - for example - excessive database calls or slow queries are causing degradation in the user's experience.

Common alternatives to Skylight are New Relic and DataDog. We do have some experience with DataDog at dxw, but we had more confidence within the team with using Skylight.
template_adherence.consequences: Skylight will turn performance data from our application into insights which we can use to make product decisions. Identifying pain points in advance of the application being put under high loads means we can have more confidence in the application's performance in public beta and live.

pros: We have some experience with DataDog at dxw.

We have easy access to the console via GOV.UK PaaS, so this is relatively painless. We have added a generator which creates an empty Ruby file with a timestamp and the name of the migration as the filename. Once the code is deployed, we run the migration on the production server. template_adherence.title: Replace PublicActivity with our own hand-rolled way of recording changes
template_adherence.context:

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly list decision drivers as a separate section or clearly under a heading. However, from the context and decision sections, the drivers can be inferred as: the existing `PublicActivity` gem is not fit for the needs, the information recorded has never been used or displayed, and the desire to have a more granular and user-visible change tracking system.
template_adherence.decision:
We have decided to introduce a `HistoricalEvent` model to record changes to models, starting with `Activity`s.

Once we have applied `HistoricalEvents` to all the models we need to track, we can remove all the calls to `PublicActivity` and remove the gem entirely.
template_adherence.consequences:
This change will allow us to record changes that have been made to various models in a much more granular fashion, allowing us to record what fields have been changed, as well as the associated report, as well as playing those changes back to the user.

When we move away from `PublicActivity` completely, we will have to decide what to do with the old `PublicActivity::Activity` records that have been created - do we delete all the data entirely, or do we use the data to create incomplete `HistoricalActivity` records to give us a complete, if patchy, history.

template_adherence.title: 3. Follow a cloud native design principle
template_adherence.context:
We need to design the building blocks of the Digital Citizenship platform. We will make decisions about the overall architecture and the building blocks we're going to use to satisfy the functional and non-functional requirements.

When deciding what technologies to use and how to satisfy those requirements, we're going to evaluate whether we want to build certain components from scratch, use open-source solutions managed by us or rely on existing public cloud components, managed by 3rd party providers.

As the world of cloud technologies continues to accelerate, we should absorb new developments into how we work. Leading technology organisations are rapidly embracing new tools like "serverless" computing.

At the infrastructure and application level we should expect our applications to be resilient, flexible and API-driven. We should have the tools and practices in place to manage and secure a distributed range of tools accessed over the internet.

Decision criteria will also include:

* elasticity and resilience
* pay-as-you-go pricing
* exploiting economies of scale
* exploiting falling costs of infrastructure over time
* quality of management tools
* best of breed security
* flexibility and opportunity costs

template_adherence.consequences:
We can maintain a record of how many times we use something that’s unique to a specific provider.

We should also keep track of indicative figures for the cost of exit from each cloud provider or feature.

In case of a significant commitment to a particular feature offered by a cloud provider, we should explain our strategy for reducing lock-in over time.

We should also consider sponsoring open source tools that work across multiple providers or developing equivalent feature functionality that works with other cloud providers.

template_adherence.title: 6. Choice of primary key for citizen data
template_adherence.context:
We are going to associate data to citizens, thus we need to define a primary key for identifying citizens in the data model.

Italian citizens have a "natural" identification key: the Fiscal Code (FC).

For natural persons, the [FC is made of 16 alphanumeric characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_fiscal_code_card#Fiscal_code_generation).

The FC is supposed to be unique and immutable but these properties are not always true: a person may have his FC revoked or changed (e.g. after a change of name or because his FC is not unique).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to uniquely identify citizens in the data model; existence of a natural identification key (Fiscal Code); issues with uniqueness and immutability of the Fiscal Code; need for system extensibility to other types of citizen keys.
template_adherence.decision: The citizen's Fiscal Code (FC) will be used as the primary key for a citizen entity. However, components should not assume the primary key is always an FC to allow future extensibility to other key types (e.g., foreign citizens).
template_adherence.consequences:
Entities representing citizens will be uniquely identified by the citizen's FC.

FCs should be stored in a normalized form (all upper case, no spaces).

Since FCs can change, the system must allow changing the association of data to a different FC.

Services cannot be used by people without an FC (e.g., most non-Italian citizens).

alternatives.description: Use a surrogate key (e.g., system-generated unique identifier) instead of the Fiscal Code.
pros: Ensures uniqueness and immutability independent of external factors.
Supports all citizens regardless of FC availability.
cons: Requires additional mapping between FC and surrogate key.
May complicate integration with external systems using FC.

alternatives.description: Use the Fiscal Code as the primary key without abstraction.
pros: Simplicity in using a natural key.
Direct mapping to an existing unique identifier.
cons: Assumes FC is always unique and immutable, which is not true.
Limits extensibility to other citizen types without FC.

template_adherence.title: 11. We have chosen a retry strategy in case of processing errors
template_adherence.context: To perform asynchronous operations we use Azure Storage Queues: enqueued messages are processed by Azure Functions using triggers. In case of errors in the message handler, it is necessary to re-schedule the message to be processed again later. The goal is to re-schedule processing at increasing intervals using an exponential back off strategy. The default behavior retries up to five times and then sends to a poison queue. The Function SDK does not provide an output binding to delay processing, so a custom retry policy is needed. Several alternatives were considered, including switching to ServiceBus, using Durable Functions, using a Custom Queue Processor, and updating the visibilityTimeout parameter. Currently, only a global visibilityTimeout setting is available, not per message.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to handle processing errors by retrying messages asynchronously with increasing delay intervals. Limitations of Azure Functions SDK in delaying message processing per message. Desire to avoid poison queues by retrying messages effectively. Consideration of cost, support, and documentation of alternatives.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to update the visibilityTimeout value using Azure Storage SDK methods and re-enqueue messages that caused errors. This uses the SDK's updateMessage() method to implement an exponential back off retry strategy with a maximum time to live of 7 days.
template_adherence.consequences: All message handlers must call updateMessageVisibilityTimeout() in their processing code to catch errors and schedule retries. Messages causing failures will not be sent to poison queues anymore because the retry mechanism resets the retry entry.

pros: Allows scheduling messages at specified points in time.
cons: Known issues suggest avoiding this approach.

pros: Provides orchestration capabilities for retries.
cons: Only supported in .NET environment.

alternatives.description: Using a Custom Queue Processor.

alternatives.description: Update the visibilityTimeout parameter in enqueued messages.

template_adherence.title: Using Machinist for Factories
template_adherence.context: [machinist][] is a ruby library that makes it easy to create objects for use in test. [Factories tend to be preferable to fixtures][factories-not-fixtures]. We decided to try switching over from [machinist][] to [factory_bot][]. Our primary decision behind switching was because machinist is unmaintained. The last commit to _master_ is from 2013. factory_bot is well maintained and is very popular. We had converted roughly a dozen factories over from machinist to factory_bot, starting from the leaf nodes of our object graph. As we moved to objects with associations, we encountered increasing degrees of friction. The differences in how [sequel][] and [active_record][] handle associations mean that factory_bot was not well suited. In active_record, associations are created by placing a foreign key on one of the two records. Specifically, the record with the `belongs_to` contains the foreign key for the record with the `has_one`. This means that any factory library can create the `has_one` record, generate its primary key 'A', then create the `belongs_to` record with a foreign key of 'A'. In our usage of sequel, some associations have mutual foreign keys on both of the two records. So, a factory library has to create the first record, generate its primary key 'A' with no association, then create the second record with primary key 'B' and foreign key 'A', then update the first record so that its foreign key is 'B'. This "create-create-update" workflow is tricky (but possible) in factory_bot and is clean in machinist.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a maintained and popular factory library.
- Compatibility with the database ORM's association handling (sequel vs active_record).
- Ease of creating complex associations in factories.
- Maintenance status of the library.
- Developer familiarity and onboarding considerations.
template_adherence.decision: We have reverted the conversion commits, remaining with machinist. We will switch to a maintained fork of machinist. (It turns out that other people use machinist too.)
template_adherence.consequences:
- New team members will have to learn machinist, whereas rubyists would probably be familiar with factory_bot.
- There will no longer be a state where both machinist and factory_bot are used while converting.

alternatives.description: Continue using factory_bot despite the friction with sequel associations.
pros: factory_bot is well maintained and popular.

cons: Difficulties handling complex associations with sequel ORM.
Requires workarounds for create-create-update workflow.

pros: Machinist handles complex associations cleanly.

cons: Less popular than factory_bot.
New team members may be less familiar with machinist.

template_adherence.title: Switching to Request Specs for Controllers
template_adherence.context:
There are two approaches to unit testing controllers, neither of which is very useful: If we mock most of the dependencies of the controller, our tests become tightly coupled to the implementation and do not give us a lot of confidence. If we make them more integration-style tests, we end up duplicating lots of tests between the controller and the request specs.

Additionally, writing controller specs is a discouraged pattern:

> Controller specs can be used to describe the behaviour of Rails controllers. As of version 3.5, however, controller specs are discouraged in favour of request specs (which also focus largely on controllers, but capture other critical aspects of application behaviour as well). Controller specs will continue to be supported until at least version 4.0 (see the release notes for details).

From [RSpec — Controller or Request Specs?][]

**Warning**: Request specs in the `cloud_controller_ng` codebase are not actually Rspec/Rails request specs (which would be [declared with `type: :request`](https://relishapp.com/rspec/rspec-rails/docs/request-specs/request-spec)), but use [Rack Test](https://github.com/rack-test/rack-test).  Rack Test has similar looking helper methods for making requests (e.g. `get`, `post`, etc), but these take different arguments than the equivalent Rspec methods.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce duplication in testing controllers
- Avoid tightly coupled tests that mock too many dependencies
- Follow community best practices discouraging controller specs in favor of request specs
- Maintain test coverage and confidence
- Adjust existing test helpers accordingly
template_adherence.decision: Moving forward, we will only write request specs for controllers.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Reduced duplication in testing controllers
- Controller spec helpers need to be adjusted to no longer mock out CC app directly - ie they need to be transformed into Request spec helpers.
- Delete controller specs once they've been transitioned to request specs.

alternatives.description: Continue using controller specs with mocks for dependencies.
pros: Tests can be more isolated and faster.
Familiar pattern for existing developers.
cons: Tests become tightly coupled to implementation details.
Low confidence in tests due to heavy mocking.
Contradicts community best practices.

alternatives.description: Use integration-style tests duplicating tests between controller and request specs.
pros: Tests cover more realistic scenarios.
Higher confidence in behavior.
cons: Duplication of tests between controller and request specs.
More maintenance overhead.
